data.title: Jim Ratcliffe lashes out at Labour as he mothballs factories
data.description:
Sir Jim Ratcliffe has accused Labour of “economic vandalism” after his petrochemicals business was forced to close three plants over soaring energy costs.

The facilities in Hull – which employ some 4,000 workers – normally produce raw materials for drugs, clothing, cosmetics, detergents, construction and explosives.

But Ineos, founded by Sir Jim, said they will now be temporarily shut down until further notice because of what he called “ridiculously high” energy prices.

Two have already ceased production, with the third due to come offline in a matter of days.

Sir Jim said the sites “just cannot compete”, pointing to soaring UK gas prices, despite claiming that its facilities are among the most energy-efficient and low-carbon of their kind in Europe.

The Ineos chief also blamed the Government’s energy policies for causing “economic vandalism on an industrial scale”.

He said: “I’m sure people will find it hard to believe that we are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe but with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and eight times that of China, we just cannot compete.

“Not only is the ridiculously high gas price in the UK destroying our manufacturing base and the jobs of hard-working people on Humberside, it is also massively increasing the environmental burden, with replacement products supplied from the USA at double the carbon emissions and from China at eight times the emission level.”

He added: “The UK Government’s energy policy is leading to economic vandalism on an industrial scale, exporting jobs to China and the United States and driving up global CO2 emissions at a stroke.”

It was not immediately clear whether Ineos was considering closing the three Hull plants permanently, but the company warned that such a closure would have a “dramatic” impact on the Humberside area.

Sir Jim, who has a personal fortune of around £15bn, said last weekend that he did not have “any confidence in Britain” and had no plans to return from his home in Monaco.

The Manchester United co-owner also urged ministers to address problems of immigration and the country’s soaring benefits bill, “otherwise the country ends up in a bad place and goes broke”.

Figures from the Institute for Fiscal Studies published on Tuesday show that British households and industry have to pay the highest electricity costs in Europe.

Electricity for industrial use cost 19.1p per kwh in Britain in 2025, far higher than Ireland, which was in second place at 17.7p.

The analysis showed that this was because British manufacturers have to pay the highest combined charges for network upgrades, taxes and levies, which made up 8.1p, or nearly half, of the total costs.

Industrial energy costs in Great Britain saw the third largest rise in Europe between 2017 and 2025, behind only Ireland and Poland.

Domestic electricity in Great Britain in 2025 cost 33.2p per kwh, after accounting for supply costs, network costs, taxes, levies and VAT, the IFS found. This was the highest level in Europe, above Germany at 33p per kwh.

Household electricity costs have also surged at the highest pace in Europe, climbing by 12.7p per kwh between 2017 and 2025.

UK and European gas prices have surged this summer as the prolonged US-Iran conflict continues to squeeze supplies of oil and gas coming out of the Strait of Hormuz.

There are also fears about European gas storage levels, which are below average for this time of year.

In the UK, the gas price last week hit its highest level for nearly four years at about 198p per therm. It traded at 173p per therm on Tuesday, amid reports that Washington and Tehran could broker a ceasefire.

But Ashley Kelty, an analyst at Panmure Liberum, said markets were “ignoring history” by going “all in on the prospect of a diplomatic solution”.

He added: “We see the intervention by China in asking Iran to try and rein the Houthi rebels in as being a more significant factor as China has stayed on the sidelines during the conflict.”

A government spokesman said: “While this is a commercial decision from Ineos, we know this will be a concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families.

“We’ve taken bold action to support our chemicals industry including £350m for strategically important chemicals producers, which will be available on a co-investment basis.

“We’ve also put trade measures in place on foreign chemicals imports and are tackling high electricity costs via our supercharger and British industrial competitiveness scheme to keep our chemicals sector competitive.”

data.title: JCB succession settled as Lord Bamford’s younger son triumphs
data.description:
JCB’s boss has appointed his younger son as co-chairman, ending a long-running saga about who would succeed him as head of the manufacturing giant.

Lord Bamford said George Bamford, his third child, would be elevated from deputy chairman to share the reins at the digger maker and UK export powerhouse.

The Telegraph reported in May that Lord Bamford, who turns 81 next month, had chosen George, 45, as his eventual successor rather than Joseph Bamford, his elder son and presumed heir.

The tycoon confirmed the move, the first change at the top of JCB in more than 50 years, as the firm reported higher global market share in 2025 despite zero growth in demand in North America and a contraction in India.

Lord Bamford said he was naming his successor as JCB “invested heavily” in its Staffordshire headquarters and a sprawling new plant in Texas.

He said: “We have never been a company that stands still, and these investments will ensure JCB is well placed to seize the opportunities ahead. As part of that next chapter, I’m delighted that my son George will become joint chairman of JCB.”

Lord Bamford previously told The Telegraph that a succession plan was “very important” in terms of JCB “remaining a family business” and that he had one in place, adding when asked who would eventually take over: “It will be George.”

It is understood that Joseph Bamford, 48, had earlier attempted to persuade his father to give up the day-to-day running of JCB in what Lord Bamford viewed as an attempted coup.

Joseph, known as Jo, is a successful industrialist in his own right, owning bus manufacturer Wrightbus, which employs 2,500 staff in Northern Ireland, and founding hydrogen producers Ryze and Hygen Energy.

Speaking with The Telegraph in June, he said George and his father had his “full support” and that his own ambitions lay in building a global hydrogen player to match JCB’s success.

JCB is producing the world’s first hydrogen-powered diggers as part of a £100m programme and has collaborated with Jo Bamford on some projects.

Alice Bamford, Lord Bamford’s eldest child, lives in California, where she is a film producer.

JCB’s sales were flat last year at £5.7bn, while profits fell 7pc amid a slump in machine sales.

Graeme Macdonald, the company’s chief executive, said it expected moderate growth this year “despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”, aided by the expansion in manufacturing capacity.

JCB, which has 20,000 employees worldwide, 8,000 of them in the UK, is spending £100m at its HQ in Rocester, where it has been based since 1950.

The new factory in San Antonio, Texas, which opens next month, cost $1bn (£750m) and will be JCB’s largest in the world, employing 1,500 people.

data.title: Octopus blocks £5m of withdrawals from inheritance tax scheme
data.description:
Octopus has blocked a financial adviser from withdrawing millions of pounds for his client from one of its inheritance tax schemes for seven months.

Mark Spendlove, of IPP Group, asked Octopus Investments, which manages a number of inheritance tax funds, to withdraw £5.4m from Terido, a scheme aimed at small businesses.

The scheme takes the spare cash from member businesses and invests it in asset-backed loans, mainly in property, ensuring that its investors can qualify for business relief.

Octopus originally told Mr Spendlove that the withdrawal process would take about four weeks, but said later that the money would be paid out over seven months, with the final payment of £2m not made until March 2027.

In correspondence seen by The Telegraph, Octopus told IPP Group that the phased withdrawal was “consistent with how we manage larger withdrawal requests”.

It would only be able to pay the final sum of £2m in March if the “partnership’s liquidity position develops as currently expected”, Octopus added.

In a complaint to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Mr Spendlove said he had previously arranged a number of large withdrawals across Octopus’s competitors and had never had to wait more than six weeks.

He added that the delay had led him to become concerned about the liquidity at Terido.

“Two to four weeks when we submitted a withdrawal request has suddenly gone to seven months when the last penny is going to be paid,” Mr Spendlove told FT Adviser, which first reported the news.

“My client, obviously, was not at all impressed. That’s completely, totally, not acceptable.”

Octopus’s best-known inheritance tax product is the Octopus Inheritance Tax Service (OITS), which has 18,000 customers, where investors have faced months of uncertainty after they were blocked from withdrawing their money.

The scheme allows savers to lower their inheritance tax bills by investing in businesses to qualify for relief.

Investors in OITS had been sold shares in Fern Trading, which owns about 300 energy, property and telecoms companies.

However, they were prevented from taking out their money for three months as Octopus held failed takeover talks for TalkTalk’s wholesale business.

OITS confirmed last week that it would split Fern in two, separating its fibre investments from its other holdings.

The fibre fund will now be permanently gated with money disbursed as its assets are sold down. Investors will be able to access their money from the other fund, although Octopus has warned that “withdrawals cannot be guaranteed”.

The unfrozen fund and Terido are linked, with money from Fern funnelled through Terido to provide its investors with access to asset-backed loans.

Octopus’s talks to take over TalkTalk’s wholesale business collapsed earlier this month, and the failing broadband business was bought out of administration by BT.

The investment firm said its fibre broadband assets have been its “biggest drag on performance”, but that it will not be possible to revalue them because of “ongoing merger and acquisition activity in the fibre sector”.

It had previously committed to revaluing the holdings after the acquisition, however, they may not be revalued now until July next year.

An FCA spokesman said: “As you’d expect as part of supervision, we’re in contact with the firm and aware of these developments.”

A spokesman for Octopus Investments said: “It would not be appropriate for us to comment publicly on individual client cases.

“We take our responsibilities to our clients seriously, and where concerns are raised with us, we look into them carefully and engage directly with the client and their adviser as appropriate.”

data.title: Angela Rayner accused of making housing crisis worse
data.description:
Angela Rayner has been accused of making the property crisis worse after a housebuilder lost its battle to construct hundreds of homes in south-east London.

Berkeley Group had mounted a legal challenge to revive plans to replace Peckham’s derelict 1980s Aylesham Centre with 867 homes, but its appeal was rejected by a judge on Monday.

Ms Rayner’s officials in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) have also frozen a second Berkeley project, for 586 homes, at the redundant Motspur Park gasworks in Kingston.

Rob Perrins, the chief executive of Berkeley Group, warned on Wednesday that the decisions underscored the “gulf between positive planning policies and what actually happens when you try to build homes in London”.

With its projects repeatedly rejected by councils and planning inspectors, Mr Perrins said the housebuilder was increasingly forced to rely on “hugely costly and slow” legal appeals or decisions by ministers to secure approval for developments.

Yet plans for its Motspur Park development were “immediately put on hold by central government” in August, Mr Perrins said, and now must be reviewed by Ms Rayner, despite securing consent from the Mayor of London’s office.

Mr Perrins said: “All of this creates extreme uncertainty and is undermining the Government’s housing agenda.

“Housing delivery in London is at a record low. At a time when we should be fighting to attract investment and build more homes, we’re fighting it off. The result is fewer homes, less growth and a worsening housing crisis.”

In Peckham, the housebuilder had applied to build homes in more than a dozen tower blocks running up to 20 storeys high, served by a new Morrisons supermarket.

But its proposals were rejected by the planning inspectorate in May on heritage grounds, which ruled they were “visually intrusive”.

Mr Perrins described the Peckham saga as a “10-year planning nightmare”, adding that Historic England, the heritage watchdog, had not objected to the plans.

“The outcome is no new investment, no jobs, no homes,” he added. “All the policies support housing, but the decisions block it time and time again.”

The site has been earmarked for housing since 2014. It is estimated the project would generate nearly 1,000 jobs along with £15m for the council to invest in the community.

But local groups protested against the project, including Aylesham Community Action, labelling it “gentrification [on] steroids”. The campaign was backed by Miatta Fahnbulleh, the local Labour MP who was appointed Energy Secretary in July.

Lord Khan , the Mayor of London, meanwhile, called in and approved Berkeley’s Motspur Park development after councillors rejected the proposal in March.

But the Housing Secretary issued a holding direction in August that bars City Hall from officially granting consent, despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to leave more control of building projects to mayors.

Separately on Wednesday, Taylor Wimpey, a competitor to Berkeley, said it had no more plans to build new homes in London and warned the city’s housing market was “fundamentally broken”.

Jennie Daly, the chief executive of Taylor Wimpey, told The Times: “Baseline viability is, I think, fundamentally broken in London.

“The reward for undertaking what is a very high-risk form of development in London has just evaporated.”

A spokesman for the MHCLG said its planning reforms had led to a 298pc increase in new London housing starts compared to a year ago. It is also investing £11.7bn into council housing in the capital.

He added: “We are also backing the Mayor of London and working closely with industry to get more homes built for Londoners – making sure good schemes are not left in limbo while unlocking jobs, growth and opportunity.”

data.title: Asos says hackers tricked employee to access customer data
data.description:
Asos has admitted that hackers were able to send a notification to customers threatening to leak their data after tricking an employee into sharing login details.

The online retailer said a staff member allowed hackers to access information about customers stored by a third party, understood to be US company Snowflake, a data handler.

An email to customers on Thursday said: “We discovered that an unauthorised party gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain login credentials.

“Those credentials were then used to access information on certain third-party platforms used by Asos.”

Asos said the databases affected by the breach were locked down “immediately”.

Customers of the online retailer received a message from Asos’s app on Tuesday that said: “Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it.”

Snowflake, the company mentioned in the hackers’ message, said it has found no evidence that its systems were breached.

The hackers, who identified themselves as Xuanye group, gave Asos a two-week deadline to pay a ransom or they would leak the customer data.

The hackers told The Telegraph they were seeking a ransom payment from Asos in exchange for deleting customer information.

Speaking on the messaging app Telegram, the group said: “Our message is clear and simple to recognise. The organisation must contact us or we will leak it, that is what we said.

“The two-week period is intended for them to make contact, they know what happened.”

Asos shares rose as much as 5.7pc on Thursday after it apologised to customers who received the notification and explained the breach.

It said a full investigation would continue in the coming weeks. It did not elaborate on whether it would pay the ransom demand.

It confirmed that hackers gained access to some personal information, including names and contact details.

However, no payment card information or account passwords were accessed in the incident.

Asos said customers did not need to take any action but added it would contact anyone directly where additional information, support or action may be required.

The email to customers added: “The Asos website and app were safe to use throughout and remain safe to use today.

“There is no action you need to take on your account. However, please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos.

“We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call.”

data.title: John Lewis lashes out over threat of Budget tax raid
data.description:
John Lewis has warned the Chancellor that a tax raid on retailers in the Budget would trigger a wave of catastrophic closures on the high street.

Jason Tarry, the chairman of John Lewis and Waitrose, said a tax raid on department stores and supermarkets by John Healey would “only harm our high streets” and threaten to prompt closures.

Mr Tarry said concern was mounting among major retailers that Andy Burnham will fund his promise to cut business rates for pubs and music venues by “piling more costs” on to large stores with a so-called “warehouse tax”.

Writing in The Telegraph, Mr Tarry mounted an unusually outspoken attack on the potential Budget raid, warning that it “would reveal a fundamental misunderstanding of how modern high streets work”.

The Prime Minister has signalled Labour will ramp up a tax on warehouses to help fund a tax cut for “businesses that bring social benefit”, such as pubs and restaurants.

Labour-linked think tanks are also piling pressure on the Chancellor to mount a wider £1.5bn raid on online retailers, including Amazon, to provide more “breathing space” for the high street.

UK businesses already face some of the highest property taxes in the industrialised world.

Taxes on business have soared since Labour came to power in 2024, most notoriously when Rachel Reeves raised employers’ National Insurance contributions by around £25bn a year to pay for government spending plans.

Other rising costs under Labour, such as increases in the national minimum wage, have been blamed for employers’ reluctance to take on young workers, triggering a spate of closures across Britain’s high streets.

Supporters of a warehouse tax targeting larger commercial properties claim it would rebalance competition between high street shops, which pay high business rates, and online retailers operating out of facilities on cheaper land.

However, Mr Tarry said it would hit “a far greater number of high street shops than warehouses”.

In John Lewis’s case, it would lead to higher charges on just 18 warehouse hubs, but hit 200 stores.

Mr Tarry, an influential retail veteran, warned that “when forced to balance the books” retailers would “inevitably look to their most expensive operations, namely their stores, and that can only harm our high streets”.

The intervention comes days before the Chancellor is scheduled to host retail and hospitality chiefs in Downing Street to hear their concerns before his first Budget this month.

It is understood Amazon executives have also been invited to what could be a tense meeting just days before he announces his tax and spending plans.

City trade associations also sent a letter to Mr Healey on Friday, calling for a commitment not to impose any new bank taxes.

Mr Burnham has previously argued that high streets have been “hollowed out” and overrun with vape and betting shops.

The Prime Minister said last month: “People don’t measure growth by looking at a spreadsheet. They measure it by looking at their local high street. Are shops opening or are the shutters down? Does the place feel like it’s moving forward or being left behind?”

Labour has already increased business rates on large warehouses, with changes that came into effect in April this year. These increased costs for larger properties with a rateable value above £500,000

The Prime Minister is now expected to push up rates on large warehouses further to pay for a 20pc rate cut for pubs, clubs and live music venues struggling under the weight of higher wage bills and taxes. Retailers have warned this would drive up prices for shoppers.

Mr Tarry called for a “clear commitment in the Budget” that “no high street shop should face higher taxes”.

He is the latest in a succession of senior figures in business and finance to warn the Chancellor against burdening high streets and hospitality businesses with further taxes.

Lord O’Neill, an influential economist and a former adviser to Mr Burnham, urged the Chancellor on Friday to rule out “stupid” extra wealth taxes and higher business levies to avoid hurting the economy.

Stuart Machin, the chief executive of Marks & Spencer, branded Labour’s previous two budgets “disasters” and a “crushing disappointment”.

Writing in the Daily Mail, Mr Machin urged the Chancellor to “get Britain growing by taking the handcuffs off business and putting money back into people’s pockets”.

Andrew Bailey, the Governor of the Bank of England, has also cautioned that imprudent tax and spending plans could trigger a repeat of the Liz Truss crisis of 2022.

Speaking on Thursday, Mr Bailey said spending plans must be “directed towards stability and be seen by markets as credible”.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, warned Labour’s tax rises were destroying jobs.

He said: “The Chancellor should be spending every day working out how to cut taxes, not how to put them up.”

The Treasury declined to comment.

Britain’s high streets need teamwork, not higher taxes

Jason Tarry, chairman of John Lewis Partnership

Walking through my local high street in North London on a Saturday morning shows what makes a community special. While the businesses may change, it still reminds me of when I started working in retail 35 years ago, watching families gather, friends grab a cup of tea and neighbours exchange news outside local shops.

Today, as chairman of the John Lewis Partnership, that sensory richness remains unmatched. High streets are not just commercial strips; they are the living manifestation of local pride and belonging.

As the Prime Minister drives forward his agenda to devolve power from Westminster to local leaders and create growth in every postcode, town centres stand as the most visible benchmark of whether local communities feel supported or left behind.

In January, the then chancellor raised hopes by announcing plans to work alongside businesses to develop a cross-government High Street Strategy. To date, there has been sparse engagement with the retail or hospitality sectors, and I’ve seen little appetite to co-design this roadmap with those who operate on the front line.

High streets are already evolving into multi-faceted hubs offering healthcare, housing, offices and cultural experiences alongside retail. Crafting a strategy for this new era requires intimate, practical knowledge.

In the past 15 years, four separate high street reviews – from Mary Portas OBE to Sir John Timpson – have been commissioned, published and ultimately left to gather dust on Whitehall shelves. We cannot afford a fifth exercise in academic optimism.

A prime opportunity exists to get this right, but recent policy signals give me cause for concern. The Government has trumpeted small-scale business rate relief for pubs and live music venues. While any relief is welcome, its scope is minimal. Worse, concern is mounting that ministers intend to fund these concessions by piling more costs on larger retailers through a so-called “warehouse” tax on online retailers.

This would reveal a fundamental misunderstanding of how modern high streets work. Town centres are complex ecosystems. A crude “large versus small” equation doesn’t add up.

Major department stores and supermarkets, including our 36 John Lewis stores and hundreds of Waitrose branches, act as vital anchor tenants. They generate the primary footfall that sustains surrounding independent shops, pubs, bakeries and cafes. Penalising anchor retailers through higher business rates risks harming the smaller businesses operating in their orbit.

Modern retail is also not a zero-sum game of physical shops vs online. Many modern retailers are omnichannel. At John Lewis, around 60pc of our sales take place online, yet our physical stores are the beating heart of our brand and our communities.

At around £170m per year, business rates are the highest tax we pay, and second only to wages as our biggest cost. In last year’s Budget, the Government introduced the “higher value multiplier” on business rates. It’s intended to level the playing field between online and physical retail by applying an extra tax to the business rates paid on large properties, including large warehouses used by online retailers.

The problem is it applies to a far greater number of high street shops than warehouses. In our case, the higher charge applies to just 18 distribution centres but more than 200 John Lewis and Waitrose stores. Almost 80p in every pound is levied on our shops, with around 20p on our warehouses.

Physical shops already carry heavy fixed operating costs. Imposing even higher rates on large stores would come on top of cumulative cost shocks, including higher employer National Insurance, packaging levies, rising energy bills and persistent inflation. It would directly undermine efforts to give households “breathing space”, in the words of our Prime Minister, such as Waitrose investing another £20m in reducing prices on everyday essentials.

Personally, I understand the case for online retail shouldering a fairer share of tax, particularly if channelled towards supporting local high street businesses.

But a higher-value property “surtax” worsens, not eases, the tax imbalance. When forced to balance the books, multi-channel retailers will inevitably look at their most expensive operations, namely their stores, and that can only harm our high streets.

The bedrock of any meaningful effort to revitalise town centres must be a clear commitment in the Budget: no high street shop should face higher taxes. If the Government wants to adjust property multipliers, bricks-and-mortar shops should be exempt. Any surtax should focus outside retail, hospitality or leisure properties – such as corporate offices.

Looking ahead, a genuine High Street Strategy must be optimistic and action-oriented, unlocking town centres as economic powerhouses and the first rung on the career ladder for young people. This year alone we’re investing £50m in John Lewis stores, opening three new Waitrose shops and refurbishing 28 others. We can only do this with a predictable and coherent policy environment.

Here are three ideas: First, deliver the Government’s manifesto pledge to reform the archaic business rates system so that it supports and incentivises businesses that are investing in their properties and rewards those that make an additive contribution to local civic life.

Second, the Government should introduce a modern digital tax-free shopping scheme for international visitors to reclaim lost foreign revenue. These could be trialled in tourist zones set by regional mayors before being rolled out more broadly.

Third, we should pioneer “BIDs 2.0”. Business Improvement Districts (BIDs) are defined areas, often town centres, where local businesses pool funds and work together to improve their trading environment by running festivals, providing deep cleaning of streets, private security and festive lights.

The High Street Strategy presents an opportunity to further empower them with greater local responsibility for parking, local transport and public realm improvements. Is there anything else that more directly aligns with the Prime Minister’s local devolution agenda than placing decision-making in the hands of those who know their streets best?

Britain’s high streets possess enormous resilience and potential. By working together to co-design a plan rooted in reality rather than tax increases, we can ensure our town centres thrive as vibrant centres of community life.

After all, in the words of our Prime Minister: people don’t measure growth by looking at a spreadsheet, they measure it by looking at their local high street.

data.title: The obstacles to Healey’s goal of re-industrialising Britain
data.description:
John Healey’s dream of reindustrialisation, illuminated by the handy metaphors provided by the miner’s lamp he keeps at home, already looks set to be snuffed out.

At his speech to the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, the Chancellor promised a “new age of industrialisation”, powered by businesses with “new levels of confidence, investment and yes, profits”.

“Those miners didn’t just use their lamps to light their own steps, they shone them to help others. A symbol of solidarity. A symbol of hope, that no matter the darkness, there’s always light at the end of the tunnel,” he told Labour’s conference, laying it on thick.

“And you know, the same goes now for Britain’s future.”

Yet fundamental problems with the nation’s economy mean British factories are heading rapidly in the opposite direction.

Stephen Phipson, the chief executive of industry group Make UK, welcomed the commitment to reindustrialisation, but questioned the basis on which it could take place.

Businesses “are still grappling with crippling energy costs, costly new employment regulation and sky-high business rates”, he said.

“The Government’s warm words will mean nothing to our members if they are not matched by action at the Budget and faster delivery of the Industrial Strategy.”

Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce, similarly welcomed Healey’s intent but cast doubt on the ability of businesses to invest in current conditions.

“This strategy is unlikely to succeed while the everyday cost of doing business is still soaring,” she said. “Firms are being asked to invest while facing a tsunami of rising costs from employment, energy and business rates.”

This is no mere grumbling from lobbyists.

Businesses in the room were distinctly underwhelmed by the speech.

One chief executive said: “It was quite a thin speech. They’re clearly saving things for the Budget.”

Bosses charged £6,600 a head for tickets to Labour’s “business day” said access to ministers was “massively improved” on previous conferences under Sir Keir Starmer, but they were left underwhelmed by the lack of detail behind the Prime Minister’s plan to reindustrialise Britain.

Referring to Jonathan Reynolds, who was brought back to the Cabinet as Business Secretary by Burnham, one person who attended the business day says: “Jonny keeps saying he’s back. That’s great, we all love Jonny. But now we need to hear what he’s actually going to do. And does he even have any power?”

An industry source added: “We get the big picture. But we need some detail. I’ve done so many round tables, that’s all fine and well. But you have to actually create the basic conditions for growth and investment. Right now the maths isn’t working.”

And major industrialists are doing more than just warn about the impact of high energy costs.

The Labour Party conference began with the mothballing of three vital chemicals plants in Hull – threatening a fresh wave of deindustrialisation.

On the eve of Andy Burnham’s first major set-piece event, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the boss of Ineos, accused Labour of “economic vandalism”.

“With gas prices now 12-times the level in the US and eight times that of China, we just cannot compete,” Sir Jim said.

Peter Huntsman, the American billionaire with a chemicals plant on Teesside, echoed the criticism over the weekend, warning energy bills were “getting progressively worse”.

It’s not just factories that are suffering: diesel prices hit fresh record highs on Monday, teetering on the brink of £2 per litre. That is worse even than the awful levels seen in the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

“I personally cannot think of an advanced economy less suited for an industrial resurgence,” said Liam Sides, the director of Oxford Economics, noting Britain’s high energy prices and the surge in cheap exports of advanced products – such as electric vehicles – from China.

Swati Dhingra, a member of the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee, said Britain should focus on its strengths in the services sector rather than trying to revive heavy industry.

“I don’t necessarily see tomorrow we can suddenly change immediately and become a manufacturing superpower – that is not going to happen,” she said in an interview with the Making Money podcast on Monday.

Meanwhile, even Healey suggested that he recognised the limits of the Government’s ability to get much done quickly.

Amid optimistic talk of “a greater resolve, a greater determination, and a greater hope” to turn the country around after “14 years of flatlining Tory growth and living standards”, the Chancellor also let slip the bad news for the party faithful: there is no money left.

The Conservatives “left Britain spending more on debt than the Home Office, Defence and Justice put together,” he said.

“It’s the money that we can’t spend on the NHS, on schools, on housing, on social care.”

Healey might rail against the “austerity [that] gutted our public services”, but he acknowledged that too much spending and borrowing was problem. The annual debt interest bill is poised to rise from more than £130bn this year to more than £160bn at the end of the decade.

Interest rates are still rising. The rate financial markets charge the Government on benchmark 10-year debt rose again to 5.43pc, hitting a fresh post-2007 high. Back then, the national debt stood at just over £500bn, compared to almost £3tn today.

Healey vowed “fiscal discipline”, sticking to the borrowing rules set out by Rachel Reeves, his predecessor. But she already loosened the debt targets compared to the Conservatives’ goals, allowing more borrowing.

The Chancellor told the conference hall: “It is simply not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill and a system which offers an income but doesn’t offer a future.”

But he set out little in the way of a path to bring borrowing under control.

Healey said he wanted fewer youngsters to be written off, stuck on benefits.

But Allan Simpson, at Hospitality UK, said government policies were getting in the way of hiring just those youngsters, with the apprenticeship levy a prime example of a misguided measure driving up costs.

“Employers trying to hire kids out of unemployment need complete freedom to use their levy to fund practical short courses in the sort of foundation skills you need to start a career,” he said.

“At the moment the levy is just another tax, it needs to be a fund for getting kids into work and keeping them there.”

Despite the call for businesses to lead the way with investment and jobs, bosses were rather abruptly pushed to one side in the speech.

Initially at the front of the room to hear the Chancellor, bosses were asked to move back to make way for apparatchiks to take the prime seats.

Without the money to fund the Government’s aspirations or the energy prices that would allow a business boom, Labour’s hopes already look as doomed as the coal industry Healey so touchingly recalled.

data.title: BT rival accuses bosses of cashing in on TalkTalk rescue
data.description:
A rival bidder for TalkTalk has accused BT executives of profiting from a rescue deal for the ailing broadband provider.

Opus Broadband, which had been bidding for TalkTalk’s 1.5 million retail customers, suggested BT bosses could benefit from higher bonuses after securing a dramatic last-ditch deal to buy the company out of administration.

This year, BT introduced a new incentive linking directors’ bonuses to the telecoms giant’s share of the UK retail market for both mobile and broadband.

In a letter to Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, Opus said BT’s TalkTalk takeover would raise its broadband market share from 30.8pc to around 36pc.

Mike Ellwood, the chairman of Opus, wrote: “From this year, BT’s directors are rewarded for growth in UK retail market share.

“This transaction delivers that growth by acquisition and removes a low-cost rival at the same time.”

A BT spokesman said the TalkTalk acquisition would not be factored into bonus calculations for the current financial year.

However, it is unclear whether the deal could pay off in future years. It is understood that BT would publish its bonus metrics for the next financial year in June 2027.

Retail market share carries a 5pc weighting in determining executive bonuses. Financial metrics account for the majority.

BT moved to buy TalkTalk out of administration on Monday in a £400m move that saved the debt-laden broadband provider from imminent collapse.

Typically, the former state monopoly would probably be blocked from buying its rival, the UK’s fourth-largest broadband company, because of concerns about its market power.

TalkTalk serves about 1.5 million households, plus another million customers through its wholesale division.

But Ms Nandy used pandemic-era legal powers to override competition concerns in mergers and acquisitions to protect public health.

The Culture Secretary described the situation as “unprecedented”, citing the risk a TalkTalk collapse posed to tens of thousands of vulnerable customers and the networks underpinning national security.

BT’s rescue deal includes TalkTalk’s consumer and wholesale divisions, which are closely interlinked. Allison Kirkby, BT’s chief executive, described her company’s bid as the “only viable option”.

But Opus has disputed this characterisation, arguing that its offer represented a viable alternative for TalkTalk’s retail customers.

The company said it entered the auction early this year and tabled a £100m bid, which officials cleared under national security laws.

Mr Ellwood argued that rescuing TalkTalk’s wholesale arm, which houses connections for hospitals, public services and users of emergency telecare alarms, did not require BT to take control of its household customers.

Opus also noted that BT had provided no guarantees on how many of TalkTalk’s 900 staff would remain in their jobs and for how long. BT’s workforce fell by 7pc last year, and it has raised its cost-saving target to £3.7bn by 2030.

Just one week before intervening to approve BT’s takeover of TalkTalk, Ms Nandy joined BT workers protesting against plans to close the company’s Liverpool office and relocate about 600 jobs.

Blackburn-based Opus, which employs around 250 people, said in the letter that it had intended to keep the consumer business as a standalone employer in the North West.

Mr Ellwood wrote: “In our view, the acquisition by BT of TalkTalk’s consumer business will plainly result in a substantial lessening of competition in retail broadband.

“Our plan was the opposite: to maintain TalkTalk as a vigorous, independent competitor, maintaining and enhancing, rather than reducing, competition.”

Ms Nandy has directed the ​Competition and ‌Markets Authority ​to report ​⁠on BT’s rescue deal by Oct ⁠19, after which she will make a final decision.

data.title: Louise Botting, founding presenter of Radio 4’s Money Box treasured by listeners for her financial nous
data.description:
Louise Botting, who has died aged 87, became one of the BBC’s most recognisable voices during 15 years as co-presenter of Radio 4’s long-running series Money Box.

Devised by Vincent Duggleby, the weekly series made its debut in October 1977, with Louise Botting, a former City investment analyst, and Peter Hobday as its first presenters. Pink Floyd’s Money, with its “ker-ching” cash-register sound effects, was its theme tune.

The programme proved a hit, attracting a faithful weekly audience of more than a million listeners, picking up numerous awards and spawning a range of spin-offs.

At midday every Saturday, in crisp, authoritative tones – “superior, yet laced with honey”, according to one reviewer – Louise Botting delivered complicated financial information as if it were no more difficult than two plus two, helping listeners to dispel the brain fog associated with such acronyms as TESSA and PEPS.

“What we have to do”, she explained, “is teach people to look after themselves.” So in 1992 she surprised one interviewer when she admitted that while she was not overdrawn, her own finances were “not in as impeccable order”, as might be expected.

“But,” she went on, “one thing I do know is that the only person who is going to keep me out of the workhouse is me. I don’t ever want to hear my daughters say, ‘What are we going to do about Mum?’”.

One of three children of Robert Young and his wife Edith, née Roberts, she was born Elizabeth Louise Young in Liverpool on September 19 1939, two weeks after the outbreak of the Second World War.

Her parents had both been brought up in impecunious circumstances, but her father, after service in the Army, became prosperous through insurance broking, and the family moved to Sutton Coldfield, where Louise attended the High School for Girls.

Keen on maths –“I loved algebra” – 16-year-old Louise was just becoming interested in her father’s business chat when he suddenly died, leaving his financially naive widow vulnerable to bad advice.

“By the time I was 20, she had run out of money,” Louise remembered, “and it struck me that if I was going to do anything in life, I’d like to pick up where my father left off.”

After graduating in Economics from LSE, she joined the merchant bank Kleinwort Benson as an investment analyst. There were no other women on the investment analysts’ floor at the time, so the bank had to build a lavatory especially for her.

She worked there for three years before marrying the travel, biography and history writer Douglas Botting in 1964. They travelled the world together – “we lived in South America, we sailed up the Amazon, we travelled through Morocco” – and had two daughters.

But the joys of full-time motherhood soon palled and in the late 1960s, at a time when there was growing public interest in protecting investments from inflation, Louise Botting began to research the world of bonds and unit trusts: “I’d grown out of the City, which left me wondering what young matrons like me could do. I asked my friends and they all said market research.”

In 1970 Margo Naylor, editor of the Daily Mail’s money page, recruited her as the paper’s personal finance editor.

Her postbag soon grew to 600-700 letters a week and as she recalled, “Many of them said ‘if only I could pop in and see you’, and I thought, ‘why not?’” So in 1974 she founded the private wealth management firm Douglas Deakin Young, serving as its managing director, and later chairman, until the firm was sold in 2005.

Her career in broadcasting began inauspiciously with British Forces Broadcasting (BFBS) when an interviewer at her first audition described her as sounding like a cross between a calculator and a wet dishmop and told her that she could not use the name Botting because people would laugh.

Nevertheless she presented programmes for BFBS until 1981, by which time she had landed her seat on Money Box.

In 1984, with Vincent Duggleby, she published Making the Most of Your Money. In 1987 she was appointed to the Top Salaries Review Body and the following year was invited to replace Valerie Singleton on BBC Two’s The Money Programme. She refused, not wanting people “to see me grow old on television”.

Not all her investment tips paid off. In 1991 she encouraged what she called “sugar daddies” (including her own boss, the BBC chairman Marmaduke Hussey) to invest in an art gallery that subsequently folded. But she had no regrets: “They were all big boys, they knew what they were doing. We had some smashing parties in the gallery and nobody cared. I never lost a night’s sleep over it.”

The Chancellor’s annual budget was the biggest event in the Money Box calendar and Louise Botting was in her element explaining what it all meant for people’s personal finances. However she and the BBC parted company a week before Budget Day 1992, when her bosses objected to her taking a position on the board of their rivals London Weekend Television.

In addition to LWT, after leaving Money Box, she notched up a substantial portfolio of appointments, including on the boards of General Accident, Trinity Mirror and Camelot.

She was appointed CBE in 1993.

Louise Botting’s marriage to Douglas Botting was dissolved, and in 1989 she married Leslie Carpenter, the former chairman of Reed International. He died in 2020 and she is survived by the two daughters of her first marriage, one of whom is the Sky News presenter Anna Botting.

Louise Botting, born September 19 1939, died September 22 2026

data.title: ‘Just forget it’: Labour has no answer to London’s housing crisis
data.description:
Housebuilders are all too aware that London is ground zero when it comes to Britain’s housebuilding crisis.

“Nothing is viable in London at the moment,” says Andy Hill, the chief executive of housebuilder The Hill Group.

The number of new houses under way plummeted by 72pc year-on-year in the capital in 2024-25, with London on track for its lowest delivery rates since the Second World War.

“We’re building at the slowest rate we’ve ever developed at,” says Hill.

And while some might have been hopeful that Andy Burnham’s revived Help to Buy scheme, announced last weekend, could provide some relief to the industry, they have since been sorely disappointed.

The plan appears set to fail to increase building rates meaningfully in the capital.

The Prime Minister’s new first-time buyer support scheme – called Your First Home – will provide prospective homeowners with a 20pc government-backed equity loan on a 2.5pc deposit to purchase a new-build property.

It is similar to the Help to Buy programme launched by George Osborne in 2013 to help the housing sector in the wake of the financial crisis. That scheme resulted in 387,000 transactions until it ended in 2023.

North to benefit most

But there are some key differences, which are particularly problematic for London.

Under the previous scheme, to account for far higher property prices in the capital, London buyers had access to an equity loan that was twice as large, at 40pc. There is no suggestion of any such treatment this time around.

Analysts warn that London property prices are so wildly out of kilter with earnings that access to a 20pc equity loan will not meaningfully improve affordability for first-time buyers.

“I don’t believe that a 20pc equity loan is enough to make a huge difference,” says Hill.

Savills analysis, based on local incomes and mortgage affordability criteria, found that in half of London boroughs, no more than 10pc of privately renting households would be able to afford an average-priced new build home with a 5pc deposit – there is an expectation that developers will be asked to make a 2.5pc contribution – and a 20pc equity loan.

The share of renter households that will benefit is particularly low in the expensive boroughs of Kensington & Chelsea and Westminster – at 0pc and 3pc respectively.

But the trend is also evident across cheaper outer boroughs, where households typically have lower incomes. In Enfield and in Barking and Dagenham, for example, the shares were also exceptionally low, at just 1pc and 3pc respectively.

Hill says: “The announcement was a really good move in the right direction, but it is in the North where I think it will move the dial.”

London left out

Developers are nervously awaiting October’s Budget, when John Healey is expected to outline the details of another key difference with the previous Help to Buy scheme.

Your First Home loans will be subject not only to local property price caps, but also to household income caps.

Emily Williams, who leads Savills’ planning research, warns that the lack of the larger 40pc equity loan means these caps will need to be set high to boost building in London.

Under Help to Buy, the equity loans were available in London on new-build homes up to the value of £600,000, and there was no income cap.

Banks typically only allow buyers to borrow up to 4.5 times their income when buying a home. To buy a £600,000 home with a 5pc deposit and a 40pc equity loan, a buyer would need to take out a £330,000 mortgage. This means they need to have a household income of at least £73,000.

This time around, with the smaller 20pc loan, the Government would need to set an income cap of around £120,000 for anyone to be able to use it in London, says Williams.

This is because a buyer purchasing a £600,000 home with a 5pc deposit and a 20pc equity loan would need to borrow £450,000, leaving them needing a £100,000 salary to get sign off from the bank.

Few analysts think Burnham is likely to announce a policy giving handouts to households earning £100,000 per year.

“As a Left of centre Labour government, it is unlikely that they’re going to set a significant price threshold in London,” says Marcus Dixon, the head of residential research at JLL.

“I hope that they realise that setting that price threshold too low will exclude a lot of people from buying in the majority of London.”

Developers are also worried that the price caps for the properties will be set too low.

Building in London is often more expensive than other parts of the country, partly because there are much more stringent regulations on high-rise blocks.

If the cap were set at £500,000 it could be useful in London’s outer boroughs, but it would do nothing to boost building rates in the centre of the city, says Bob Weston, the chairman of Weston Homes.

“Not central London, just forget it. Zone one is out, zone two is out, zone three is probably out,” he says.

James Moody, the chief operating officer at property developer Seven Capital, says the price cap would need to be as high as £800,000 for the policy to have an effect in central London.

“It is very difficult to build anything in [central] London below £1,000 per sq ft in sales value. That’s giving you a one-bed flat in zones two or three for £550,000 and a two-bed probably at £750,000,” he says.

This all matters even more because high mortgage rates have hammered buyer affordability.

For most of the duration of the previous Help to Buy scheme, mortgage rates hovered around 2pc. Since then, they have more than doubled. Bank of England data show average new fixed-rate mortgages hit 4.65pc in August.

This means that since the start of 2022, the monthly cost of borrowing £450,000 – the mortgage necessary to purchase a £600,000 home for a buyer with a 5pc deposit and a 20pc equity loan – has increased from £1,817 to £2,540.

A government spokesman said: “Your First Home is designed to help people currently unable to buy because of deposit barriers, while supporting the construction of new homes.

“The scheme will also set a household income cap with local property price caps to ensure support is targeted at those who need it.”

Hill welcomes Your First Home, but he is far from optimistic that it will help him build more homes in the capital.

“We don’t have that many homes on our books for less than £500,000. For a lot of what we do, it is not going to touch the sides.”

data.title: Burnham oversaw £55m taxpayer loan to UAE businesses
data.description:
Andy Burnham oversaw a £55m taxpayer loan to United Arab Emirates-owned businesses while he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, The Telegraph can disclose.

The money was awarded to three Jersey-based property companies ultimately controlled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan, the owner of Manchester City FC.

He is also a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family and vice president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

The decisions to issue the loans were taken in two meetings in 2017, both of which Mr Burnham chaired as mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA).

They are the first pieces of evidence that the Prime Minister was directly involved in decisions that favoured Abu Dhabi. 

Last month Mr Burnham became embroiled in a row over Manchester City after the Premier League found the club guilty of financial irregularities.

The Prime Minister initially said he would be “really concerned” if the UAE decided to sell Manchester City, before rowing back on the comments, with Downing Street insisting that no one was above the rules. 

The UAE is appealing against the decision and has threatened to pull out of major UK investment projects in retaliation against the Premier League’s verdict.

The financing for the property companies came from the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loan Fund (GMHILF), a pot of taxpayers’ money lent to the region by central government on the basis that it would be used to tackle the housing crisis.

The £300m fund was supposed to be lent to private developers to “kickstart housing projects that would otherwise be difficult to fund from elsewhere”, according to a GMCA press release in which Mr Burnham was quoted.

The Prime Minister is likely to face questions over how well GMCA adhered to this brief by authorising the loan of public money to companies controlled by one of the wealthiest men in the world.

Louie French, the shadow sports minister, said: “We need to know why these firms got loans from a fund intended for housing projects that would not otherwise be viable. 

“They could easily have got competitively priced loans on the private market, so why did the taxpayer have to finance them instead, thanks to approval at meetings chaired by Burnham when he was mayor?”

John Leech, the Liberal Democrat chairman of the GMCA overview and scrutiny committee, said: “Clearly, there would be no suggestion that the money couldn’t come from somewhere else in the case of Sheikh Mansour.”

Mr Leech added that the loans appeared out of kilter with the “stated aim” of the funds, and that the committee would look into “this issue of public loans for housing schemes in Greater Manchester”.

The disclosures raise fresh questions about the links between Abu Dhabi and Manchester. Mr Burnham has repeatedly praised the UAE for investment that helped to transform the city, but it has not been clear until now that Sheikh Mansour’s contribution was partly financed by loans from taxpayers’ money.

Sheikh Mansour’s investment vehicle, Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), has repaid the loans with interest. The rate of interest is not known.

Mr Burnham has come under mounting scrutiny for property deals which favoured Abu Dhabi, carried out by Manchester city council.

The Telegraph revealed last week that the council used public money to pay millions of pounds more than its nearest competitor for a dilapidated retail park that it intended to reserve for development by Abu Dhabi.

Mr French said: “Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Man City case was completely extraordinary and totally out of touch. But now it is beginning to make sense. The Prime Minister needs to come clean: why did he let these loans proceed?”

Sources close to Mr Burnham have previously played down his involvement in controversial decisions favouring Abu Dhabi, saying either that they were taken before he became mayor or by Manchester city council, one of the 10 councils that made up his combined authority.

However, GMCA minutes show that he chaired the meeting at which the enormous loans were approved.

The decisions to approve them were taken collectively by GMCA members, rather than by Mr Burnham alone. His office declined to comment, including on whether he raised any objections to the loan. GMCA also declined to comment.

All three loans went to companies that were ultimately owned by ADUG.

Two of the loans, totalling more than £30m, went to New Little Mill Developments Ltd and Vesta Street Developments Ltd. Subsequent filings show that the ultimate beneficiary of the Jersey-based companies was Sheikh Mansour.

According to University of Sheffield research on Manchester city council’s joint venture with ADUG, Sheikh Mansour’s investment vehicle was also the ultimate beneficiary of the third company, Lampwick Developments Ltd, at the time the GMCA approved a loan to it of £24.5m.

A separate council document, obtained by The Telegraph, states that the money would be used to build 213 apartments on privately owned land that already had planning permission, and that, along with Vesta Street and New Little Mill, was one of three schemes that were “brought forward by Manchester Life”.

Manchester Life is a joint venture between Manchester city council, and ADUG.

‘We will invest it wisely’

The GMCA minutes show that Richard Leese, who was the deputy mayor of the GMCA – who is also a director of the Manchester Life joint venture – recused himself from discussions about the loans.

“Councillor Richard Leese declared a prejudicial interest in this report... and left the room during the discussion of the report,” the September minutes said.

Council documents claim that in addition to the Lampwick apartments, the loans would be used to create 68 apartments at New Little Mill, and 169 apartments and three townhouses at Vesta Street, New Islington.

The money for the GMHILF was provided by central government. The GMCA was entrusted with approving loans from the fund to developers in order to accelerate building projects.

Speaking about the fund after it launched in 2015, Bill Enevoldson, GMCA’s chief investment officer, said: “It is not designed to finance unviable projects but can unlock currently unfundable ones…

“Greater Manchester is in a unique position. This money is at our disposal and we will invest it wisely to help speed up the delivery of much-needed new housing of all types right across the region.”

Developers borrowing money do so on the basis that they will repay it with interest, so that it can be lent out again.

The GMCA must return at least 80 per cent of the pot to central government by April 2028. The pot has been lent more than three times over, delivering 11,000 new homes.

‘Competitive terms offered’

However, an “evaluation report” commissioned by GMCA from analysis firm GC Insight suggests that developers have been attracted to its favourable terms.

They told GC Insight that they had borrowed through the fund “not out of necessity” but owing to “competitive terms offered by the fund, particularly in relation to interest rates, funding limits, and flexibility on loan-value ratios” and because it was perceived to be a “more flexible/understanding lender should progress on the development go awry”.

The terms of the GMHILF loans to the three Abu Dhabi-backed companies have not been made public.

A Manchester Life spokesman stressed that ADUG put its own capital into projects before accessing loans from GMHILF, and that these loans were repayable external debt financing, commonly used by property developers.

The spokesman said: “The £55.7m represented the external debt financing for the three relevant developments. It did not form part of the private-sector equity investment in Manchester Life. Presenting them as though they constituted the investment in Manchester Life materially overstates their role.”

He added that Sheikh Mansour’s investment vehicle invested more than £160m into the first two phases of the building scheme, and that it could only draw down the GMHILF funds once the the projects had been brought to a certain stage.

He said: “ADUG provided the equity and risk capital required to bring the schemes through planning and design and to the point at which the development-finance facilities became available.”

The Manchester Life spokesman added that it was “not in a position to comment on the objectives, eligibility criteria, approval process or individual lending decisions” of the fund. But he said that Manchester Life completed 453 homes, and that the three loans were all repaid in full with interest.

Lampwick has since been sold to a US investor, although the properties are still marketed by Manchester Life. The Lampwick Developments Ltd which was awarded the loan is unrelated to the UK-based company of the same name.

data.title: Where to put £100k savings right now for the highest return
data.description:
Have you got a savings strategy to maximise your returns? We want to hear from you. Email money@telegraph.co.uk

The great savings rate decline may not happen this year, as conflict in Iran has halted plans for further Bank Rate reductions. While this is good news for your savings, it’s tempered by the fact that inflation is expected to rise, eating away at your returns.

To protect your money, it’s worth putting some effort into finding the accounts paying the best rates possible.

But with so many to choose from, all with differing rates and conditions, finding the best home for your cash can be difficult. Everyone’s circumstances are different: some can afford to lock cash away for years, while others only feel comfortable if they can make instant withdrawals in case of emergencies.

Telegraph Money asked Katie Horne of Flagstone, a cash deposit platform, to give her views on three scenarios that represent common questions we get asked by readers.

For simplicity’s sake, we have not considered tax. In reality, tax on savings interest would be a problem for any money held outside an Isa.

Once you earn interest over £1,000 a year (for most basic-rate taxpayers) or £500 (for higher-rate payers), returns are subject to income tax, due to the personal savings allowance.

Scenario 1

A retired couple in their 70s with £100,000 in cash. They are happy to lock up £80,000 for more than a year, but need access to the rest – though not necessarily daily

Katie says: “The retired couple could take advantage of some longer-term fixed accounts, specifically the Investec 12-month Fixed Term Deposit, which pays 5.01pc.

“They can place £80,000 into this product, earning themselves interest of £4,008 a year. If they are comfortable securing a longer fixed term, and concerned that rates might be significantly lower in 12 months’ time, another option is Chetwood Bank’s 5 Year Fixed Term Deposit, paying 4.95pc AER, which would generate £3,960 a year in interest.

“For the remaining £20,000, they could use their Isa allowance – Aldermore Bank Instant Access Cash Isa pays 3.77pc AER, generating interest of £754 a year.

“However, if they have used their Isa allowance, they could choose the Investec instant access account, paying 4.06pc AER, earning £812 in interest.

“All of these accounts would be covered by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS). This balanced portfolio would meet their near-term liquidity requirements and generate a blended interest rate of 4.71pc to 4.82pc, equivalent to between £4,714 and £4,820 a year.”

Scenario 2

A working woman in her 50s with £100,000 in cash. She needs ready access to £80,000 but can lock up £20,000 for up to three years

Katie says: “She could opt to place £80,000 into an instant-access account from Investec, which pays 4.06pc AER.

“This account allows unlimited withdrawals without any restrictions and would earn her £3,248 in interest a year.

“If she is willing to restrict access somewhat, she could achieve a slightly higher rate with Standard Charter Bank’s three-month fixed term product, currently paying 4.11pc AER, earning £3,288 in interest a year.

“For the remaining £20,000, she could secure the Chetwood Bank 3 Year Fixed Term Deposit, currently paying 4.92pc, earning £984 a year in interest. Alternatively, she could lock in for a shorter period and secure a slightly higher rate of 5.01pc with the Investec 12 Month Fixed Term Deposit, earning £1,002 a year.

“Her selection here would probably be driven how much she values certainty versus flexibility. Fixing for longer provides certainty over the rate she’ll receive, while a shorter term would allow her to reassess sooner as the interest rate environment evolves.

“This balanced portfolio would meet her near-term liquidity requirements and generate a blended interest rate of 4.23pc to 4.29pc, or £4,232 to £4,290, again covered by the FSCS.”

Scenario 3

A working man in his 40s. Has no savings, but can put aside £1,500 a month for the next five years. Doesn’t need access for five years

Katie says: “A number of big banks offer good savings rates with specific requirements. For example, Santander Edge Saver offers 6pc AER with a minimum deposit of £1 and a maximum deposit of £4,000, or £233 a year in interest. Once his savings have grown, he can reassess and diversify his investments.

“We would also suggest that he look into cash Isas to take advantage of the tax-free status. You can currently invest up to £20,000 in Isas each year without paying tax on the interest you earn.

“The best rates over the past 12 months have been around the 4.5pc mark. Currently, Trading 212 offers a cash Isa at 5.01pc with no minimum required. If he puts in £300 a month, he’ll get a return of £97 a year.”

Scenario 4

A saver in their 60s with £100,000 in cash. They don’t need access to all of this money immediately, but want to generate a steady return while keeping some flexibility

Katie says: “For savers who want to strike a balance between flexibility and income, laddering fixed-term deposits can be a really effective strategy. It allows you to earn higher returns on money you don’t need straight away, while keeping some accessible in case of emergencies.

“In this example, £25,000 could be held in an easy access account with Investec, paying 4.06pc AER, earning £1,015 in annual interest.

“A further £25,000 could be placed in a six-month fixed term account with ABC International Bank, paying 4.5pc AER, earning £1,125 in interest over the year.

“For the next portion, £25,000 could be locked into a 12-month fixed term deposit from Investec, paying 5.01pc, which would generate £1,222.50 in annual interest.

“The final £25,000 could go into a 24-month fixed term deposit from ICICI Bank, paying 4.46pc AER, earning £1,115 a year.

“This combination would provide access to a portion of funds at all times, while maintaining steady income from staggered maturities. It also ensures full FSCS protection across four banks, a key advantage of spreading deposits.

“Altogether, this portfolio would achieve an average blended rate of 4.6pc, generating around £4,615 in annual interest, with funds maturing every six to 12 months to allow reinvestment at new market rates.”

data.title: Here’s how the new billionaire owners of Boots can save it
data.description:
The decision to take Boots off the stock market almost two decades ago has proven to be disastrous.

Away from the glare of public ownership, in the hands of a series of private owners, one of this country’s most important high-street names has been subjected to extreme neglect.

You only have to pop into one of the many hundreds of Boots stores dotted all across Britain and Ireland to see the massive challenge that Canada’s wealthy Weston family faces to rejuvenate the business after their £6.8bn swoop.

My own local Boots branch offers about as forgettable a shopping experience as there is to be had. On some days it’s hard to find a member of staff, other than the poor, overworked pharmacist – plural on a rare good day – dishing out pills and prescriptions to a long line of equally weary-looking customers.

The shelves look half-stocked, the tills like something from another era and I’d be surprised if the walls have seen a paintbrush since the turn of the century. The sense of abandonment is overwhelming.

With Stefano Pessina, a serial dealmaker, leading the charge, Boots has long been locked in a state of purgatory. First under the ownership of private equity’s original Barbarians at the Gate, KKR, then as a forgotten overseas outpost of American pharmacy giant Walgreens.

When it passed to the Wall Street investment giant Sycamore Partners last year, it was clear Boots would soon be jettisoned as Sycamore set about breaking up the sprawling Walgreens empire Pessina had created.

What all these supposedly sophisticated investors never seemed to understand is that Boots is more than just another bog-standard retailer: it’s a critical piece of Britain’s national infrastructure.

For it to stand a chance of being revived, the Weston family must recognise that Boots isn’t just a purveyor of lipstick, toothpaste and industrial-sized tubs of chewing gum. It’s an integral part of the NHS, and it does far more than just dish out old people’s daily pills too.

It’s why, for all the retrenchment the high street has been subjected to over the years, Boots still has a staggering 1,800 stores in the UK and Ireland, employing an army of more than 50,000 people.

However, what limited investment there has been over the years has been disproportionately focused on a much smaller number of stores on the basis that the return from refitting the others would be paltry.

A former executive once described Boots to me as a “two-speed” company. There are around 500, larger shops that have essentially been designated as “the powerhouse of the business” and have been revamped to a greater or lesser degree.

The rest are much smaller shops and – despite being no less vital to their respective surrounding communities – many have been almost deliberately neglected.

It is estimated that each one would cost somewhere in the region of £50,000 to £100,000 to refurbish. However, the resulting boost to turnover from such makeovers is often negligible, making it difficult for management to justify the outlay to the number crunchers sitting thousands of miles away in Walgreens corporate headquarters in Deerfield, Illinois.

Yet the counterargument to this short-sighted approach is surely that stores which are allowed to fall into disrepair end up becoming somewhere shoppers increasingly avoid where they can.

At times, Boots’ owners have been guilty not just of underinvestment but of prioritising heavy cost-cutting instead. Its last round of store closures was accompanied by a statement explaining that in all cases there was an alternative store less than three miles away, which obviously risks being too far for someone who is under the weather, never mind sporting an angry verruca.

Boots’ prospects aren’t helped by the fact that the Government has put the squeeze on pharmacies after the Department of Health and Social Care’s decision to freeze NHS prescription charges for the second year running.

Nevertheless, the opportunities to make money through other services are improving all the time. With the NHS stuck in a seemingly never-ending state of chaos and mismanagement, and growing numbers of people unable to secure a GP appointment, Boots is becoming an increasingly important provider of online consultations, vaccinations and blood-pressure checks.

In some outlets you can get specialised treatments for skin and hair loss, as well as so-called “at-home” testing kits for high cholesterol and other health concerns. These are all things that an overwhelmed NHS would happily outsource more of, which means your local Boots is becoming more vital to many local communities, not less.

There are other glaring failings. It is commonplace in other major retailers around the world to come across so-called “line-busting” – staff walking around the store carrying handheld payment devices, removing the need for customers to queue at automated tills, or worse those that should be manned but are frequently left unattended as is often the case in Boots branches.

Some pharmacy chains in the UK offer round-the-clock prescription collection from lockers. On a recent weekend trip to Valencia with my wife and friends, I was intrigued by the sight of vending machines attached to local pharmacies, dispensing pregnancy tests, basic first-aid items and other standard over-the-counter items. Boots offers neither of these services, yet it was once the industry trailblazer.

It has also been extraordinarily, and almost unforgivably late to capitalise on the boom in beauty products fuelled by far more innovative rivals like Sephora. The opening of a huge standalone beauty store to much fanfare in Battersea, south-west London, in 2023, has been followed by just one more in Bristol earlier this year. The pedestrian pace is indicative of an organisation either lacking the capital to compete or a willingness to part with it.

All of this needs to change if Boots is to emerge from a prolonged slumber. It was a mistake to allow it to fall into the wrong hands without even a whimper in the first place.

Where were the ministers standing up for Britain’s interests and those of the many people for whom their local Boots is a provider – often uniquely so – of many vital services? The complacency is astonishing.

That nobody in government gave it a second thought is indicative of a deeper national habit of allowing the country’s most important assets to fall into the hands of profit-obsessed, dispassionate owners without a thought for the wider consequences. Britain is almost unique in allowing this to happen right across the economy.

In Alex Baldock, Boots has a highly capable chief executive who turned around Currys, another UK big high street name that at one stage looked destined for irrelevance.

For him to repeat the feat, the Weston family must demonstrate that its boast of “deep expertise in pharmacy-led retail excellence” isn’t a meaningless sound-bite.
