data.title: Legoland’s owner is falling apart brick by brick
data.description:
For many children, a trip to Sea Life in London can sound like the highlight of a holiday.

Yet recent visitors have complained it is “a little tired”, “boring, empty and overpriced”, and “fine, not remarkable”.

Tripadvisor reviews are subjective, but they offer a glimpse of the broader challenges facing theme park and entertainment juggernaut Merlin Entertainments.

Sea Life is one of London-headquartered Merlin’s biggest global brands, alongside Legoland resorts, Madame Tussauds and Peppa Pig World of Play. The company also owns the London Dungeons, Alton Towers, Thorpe Park and the London Eye.

Over the course of two decades, the British company has become the world’s second-biggest operator of visitor attractions, behind only Disney.

But a poorly timed, debt-fuelled deal to go private on the eve of the pandemic has derailed its finances and left executives scrambling to stave off a debt squeeze.

At the same time, Merlin must contend with a wave of newer attractions, from escape rooms to virtual reality, vying for people’s attention.

A decade ago, Merlin’s success attracted the attention of private equity giant Blackstone, which in 2019 took the company private alongside Kirkbi, the investment firm of the family behind Lego, and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB), a Canadian pension giant.

The consortium paid £4.7bn to take Merlin off the stock market – a valuation equivalent to 12 times its annual earnings. Merlin’s new owners promised “significant long-term investment” to secure the future of its attractions and drive further growth.

Mounting debt burdens

In 2018, the year before it went private, Merlin made a pre-tax profit of £285m on revenues of £1.68bn. Some 67 million people visited its attractions.

But the deal came at the wrong time. Merlin’s net debt rose from £1.1bn in 2018 to £4.7bn by the end of 2020, just as Covid-19 forced places such as Legoland to close.

As interest rates have soared since the pandemic, the company’s net financing costs have risen nearly tenfold, from £38m in 2018 to £368m last year.

As the cost of living crisis has squeezed disposable income worldwide, Merlin has been forced to write down its brand value by hundreds of millions of pounds.

Merlin made a pre-tax loss of £426m last year. Visitors to one of its attractions numbered 60.5 million, down almost 10pc since the company went private.

Some challenges were beyond the company’s control: the pandemic, soaring interest rates and a cost of living crisis.

But Helen Rodriguez, an analyst at CreditSights, says the company hasn’t helped itself. Executives have spent years spreading money across a sprawling collection of attractions instead of focusing on the best performers.

“Instead of pursuing a very focused investment strategy towards their more successful concepts, they’ve gone wide and broad, and they’ve acquired and invested in a lot of different things over the last 15 to 20 years,” Rodriguez said. “The investment strategy hasn’t been terribly effective.”

Some of the more puzzling projects include a £20m Bear Grylls adventure park in Birmingham, closed in 2024, and a Peter Rabbit-themed attraction in Blackpool.

A lack of focus has followed a high turnover of chief executives in recent years. Merlin’s long-time boss, Sir Nick Varney, left in 2022 after 23 years in charge.

Scott O’Neil, an American sports executive who ran the Philadelphia 76ers basketball team, replaced him, but he left two years later to run LIV Golf, the breakaway Saudi league.

Fiona Eastwood, a former executive at the BBC’s commercial arm, was parachuted in last year and launched a turnaround plan.

Since then, Merlin has narrowed its focus. The company handed back Blackpool Tower, which it managed for 15 years, to the council in June, along with the Peter Rabbit attraction.

Meanwhile, Merlin has spent £70m on new indoor roller coasters at Legoland parks in Florida and California, and new attractions based on the popular children’s shows Bluey and Paw Patrol have come to its British parks.

The new rides aim to capture the attention of a new generation of children as Merlin tries to revive theme parks that have been losing appeal in the smartphone era.

This pressure is showing elsewhere in the company.

Pressing financial challenges

Merlin wrote down Madame Tussauds by £262m last year. A further £48m was written off against other attractions in 2024.

But the company’s most pressing challenge is financial. Merlin had more than £600m of debt due in 2027, a deadline looming over the entire business.

Merlin needed to push out repayment “in order to give them a couple of years to continue to try and turn around the business”, Rodriguez said.

The sale of Merlin’s Lego Discovery Centres to the Lego Group for more than £200m in February eased pressure, but selling assets has traditionally been difficult.

“They tried to sell Sea Life, but there were no attractive offers,” Rodriguez says.

Instead, the company has effectively been mortgaging its attractions. Merlin recently agreed a £657m loan to help refinance around £630m of debt due next year, securing the lending against attractions including the London Eye, the London Dungeon and Shrek’s Adventure London.

Yet this leaves holders of older bonds with fewer assets to fall back on if the company runs into serious financial trouble.

As a result, Merlin’s bonds have plunged in recent months. Some of its debt now trades at around 65c on the euro, down from about 80c in the summer.

One credit investor says: “Every time you put another one of those good assets under some different securitisation, you can rule that out to be part of your recovery calculation. If you do enough of that, recovery starts to move closer to zero.”

The yields on some of Merlin’s pre-refinancing bonds have risen from roughly 7pc when the bonds were issued to about 21pc today.

“If you wanted to be involved in this bond now, you’d really need to be a distressed debt specialist,” the credit investor says.

As a result, Merlin is relying on an ever-smaller pool of potential lenders.

The next few years will show whether the refinancing has given Merlin enough time to rebuild the appeal of its attractions, or whether it has simply delayed the next reckoning with its debts.

A Merlin spokesman said: “We are making good progress in our transformation, investing in our strongest destinations, bringing iconic brands to life and welcoming more guests as a result.

“We have secured commitments to proactively refinance our 2027 bonds in good time so that we have the right funding in place for the business and our growth plans.”

data.title: Britain’s race to supersize grocers gathers pace
data.description:
It was a three-month flirtation that fizzled out. Move on, nothing to see here.

But while the merger talks between Britain’s second and sixth biggest supermarket chains, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons, may have run their course by February, the dust raised by the unwanted public outing of the talks last week has far from settled.

Retail analysts believe the disclosure of the discussions between Simon Roberts, the chief executive of Sainsbury’s chief, and Sir Terry Leahy, the chairman of Morrisons and former boss of Tesco, has fired a starting gun on a potentially turbulent period of consolidation.

All over the Square Mile investment bankers are running the rule over every possible permutation of takeover and merger in a vast £200bn grocery industry that has seen remarkably little consolidation in the past 20 years.

Indeed, not since “Mozzers” swooped on Safeway in a £3bn takeover in 2004 has one major UK supermarket chain swallowed another. That may soon change.

As veteran retail watcher Richard Hyman, a partner at RAH Advisory, put it: “Nothing is certain, but I think now it is more likely to be when, rather than, if.”

The underlying drivers for the urge to merge are not hard to identify. Wafer-thin margins of 3pc to 4pc – at best – at a time of rising costs, cut-throat competition and intense political pressure to keep a lid on prices mean it is a constant battle to deliver the returns investors crave. Greater scale gives supermarkets greater buying power, allowing them to squeeze even better deals out of suppliers.

At the same time, the market has evolved from the big four to the big six with the arrival and ascent of the German discounters Aldi and Lidl, making the regulatory hurdles to any merger rather less formidable.

Indeed new realities of the grocery landscape are now being formally recognised by the Competition and Markets Authority in a proposal to reclassify the pair as “large grocery retailers” rather than “limited assortment discounters” as they were before.

The change may sound technical, and it has yet to be formally adopted, but it has profound implications when the next merger or takeover proposal comes bowling along.

The assumption that any combination of the biggest players will be stymied by the regulators – as happened with Sainsbury’s and Asda’s ill-fated engagement in 2019 – no longer applies. Deals could go through with far fewer supermarket sites having to be sold and far less risk of reduced competition harming consumers.

Putting the orange-liveried grocer together with Morrisons would have created Britain’s second biggest supermarket chain with 23.6pc of the market, just behind Tesco’s 27.8pc.

So when will the mergers and acquisitions dam burst? “I’m not Mystic Meg, but stories like this act as a catalyst,” says Clive Black of Shore Capital. “It’s not a given that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons will merge, but it puts the whole sector in play.”

Tesco is probably barred from a takeover of a major rival because of its dominant share. Under Ken Murphy’s leadership, it appears to have gone down a different route with its current interest in acquiring Majestic Wine.

Meanwhile, the German twins are unlikely to want to acquire a full-service supermarket chain, according to Hyman. It would add complication to business models built around stripping out costs.

The options for purely UK consolidation within the big six are therefore limited. But Asda – which, like Morrisons, is a private equity-owned, debt-laden laggard – is probably going to have to find a dance partner at some point. Some combination of Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrison’s now looks inevitable.

Another longer-term scenario, raised by a leading industry figure this week, is a pan-European wave of consolidation creating champions hefty enough to take on US and Chinese giants who will ultimately look to muscle in on their patch.

“Alone we will be equal to one US state or one province in China,” the industry source says. “But together, we may have chance. Alone, there is no chance. So yes to consolidation. Sometimes it is desirable.”

Black is more sceptical, pointing out that many of the world’s biggest grocery retailers spent much of the first two decades of the 21st century unwinding global empires laboriously assembled by previous chief executives.

He points out that Tesco once operated in territories as far flung as America, Japan, China, India, Thailand, and Malaysia. Now only the central European outposts in the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary remain outside the British Isles, and even they look destined to be cast off soon.

More plausible, believes Black, is a raid from Amazon. The US tech giant has a balance sheet big enough to take on even Tesco, but has so far failed – by its own standards – in its own efforts to crack the UK grocery sector. 

Amazon closed its 19 grocery stores last September after its till-free format failed to catch on with shoppers. The tech giant still has grocery operations here, though, in the form of Whole Foods, the US organic food chain it bought for $13.7bn in 2017.

Black believes there is scope for one or two more big mergers in the UK, likely involving Sainsbury’s, Morrisons or Asda, before a new phase that nobody has yet seriously considered.

He believes that if a new oligopoly is created through a spasm of consolidation, the next opportunity to create value for shareholders could be deconstruction and break up. He points to the food manufacturing sector, where, for example Unilever has demerged its Magnums ice cream business.

In the end, Sainsbury’s and Morrison’s nuzzling came to nothing. But the conversation, now in the open, has lit a spark that could trigger more corporate upheaval in the UK’s hyper-competitive supermarket scene than we have seen for a generation. 

It is a prospect that the fee-hungry advisers and funders of the City will relish.

data.title: Metal business could quit London stock market after almost a century
data.description:
One of Britain’s oldest manufacturers could quit the London stock market after nearly a century following a £1.4bn takeover offer.

Vesuvius, which has had a presence on Britain’s flagship exchange since 1930, said on Tuesday that it was “carefully evaluating” a bid from rival RHI Magnesita.

The unsolicited offer of 551p per share values the FTSE 250-listed group at £1.4bn.

Anglo-Swedish activist fund Cevian Capital, which holds a 23pc stake in Vesuvius, has backed the acquisition, although the board has yet to agree to the bid.

Vesuvius said: “The company appreciates Cevian’s commitment and engagement during this time and remains focused on the interests of and delivering maximum value for all shareholders.”

A takeover would end 96 years as a standalone company on the London Stock Exchange.

Vesuvius, which handles molten metal, was spun out of the manufacturing brand Cookson Group in 2012.

Cookson was an august name in British manufacturing, with a lineage dating back to 1704 when Isaac Cookson founded a series of metal and glass works on Tyneside.

It was first listed on the London Stock Exchange in 1930 under its original name, Goodlass Wall and Lead Industries, before rebranding as Cookson in 1982.

After a 2012 demerger, the parent entity adopted the Vesuvius name while retaining the original 1930 Cookson listing.

Vesuvius, which helped supply the Allied war effort during the Second World War, has drifted away from the UK operationally in recent years and expanded internationally.

RHI Magnesita’s bid for the group is the latest in a series of offers.

These include a 550p cash offer in March 2026 and a cash-and-shares bid in June 2026, both of which Vesuvius rejected.

RHI Magnesita has until Oct 27 to announce a firm intention to make an offer or walk away.

The potential sale follows a string of recent foreign acquisitions of UK companies.

French energy giant Engie purchased UK Power Networks for £10.5bn, while Swedish private equity firm EQT acquired Intertek Group for $14bn (£10.6bn).

Meanwhile, American asset manager Nuveen bought Schroders for $13bn and Swiss insurer Zurich took over Beazley for £8bn.

John Healey, the Chancellor, has pledged to arrest a slide in British manufacturing.

He told the Labour Party conference in Liverpool on Monday that he would usher in “a new age of industrialisation, for growth made here by British firms and British workers”.

data.title: Lotus halves British workforce after Trump tariff blow
data.description:
Lotus has cut its UK workforce by more than half after Donald Trump’s tariffs triggered a collapse in sales.

The sports car manufacturer had 600 employees at the end of last year, less than half the 1,300 staff it had before US import duties stunted demand in its biggest market.

The workforce cuts, revealed in newly published accounts, appear to go deeper than Lotus indicated in August last year, when it planned to let go of 550 staff.

Sales at the carmaker – which is based in Hethel, Norfolk – fell 71pc to just 1,539 vehicles in 2025 after the US president raised tariffs on British vehicle imports by 25pc.

While the levy was later reduced after ministers reached a deal with Washington, deliveries in the first half of 2026 remained flat at 896 cars.

Lotus – founded in 1952 by Colin Chapman, an engineer – said it had been forced to cut production as “global tariff uncertainty and evolving trade conditions” hit demand for British sports cars. Lotus’s full-year losses climbed more than 90pc to £263m.

The carmaker, which is owned by China’s Geely, said: “The imposition of 25pc tariffs by the US government in the early part of the year led to a significant reduction in orders from dealers and consumers in Lotus’s largest single market.

“Although tariffs for UK manufacturers were subsequently reduced to 10pc, the introduction of a 100,000-unit quota at this rate has constrained market potential.”

It added that the US tariffs, combined with “softer global demand” across other key markets, had “necessitated the careful alignment of production levels with distributor requirements”.

Lotus Cars, as the UK business is known, was combined in August with Lotus Technology, a Chinese offshoot created after the marque was taken over by Geely in 2017.

The UK business shipped 1pc more cars in the first six months of this year, mostly petrol-engined Emiras priced at between £80,000 and £125,000.

The Chinese business, which makes electric saloon cars and SUVs largely for the domestic market, lifted deliveries 57pc to 3,008.

The imbalance will add to concerns about the future of the Hethel plant after reports last year that Geely, which also owns Sweden’s Volvo, was considering moving production to the US to escape American tariffs.

After the rumours, Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, held emergency talks with Geely, which denied that there were plans to close the plant.

Qingfeng Feng, the chief executive of Lotus, said in August that the expansion of the company’s China-made “lifestyle brands” was part of plans to shift Lotus’s product mix away from traditional sports cars.

However, he said Lotus remained committed to producing British sporting models – including a proposed 1,000-horsepower Type 135 hybrid supercar.

data.title: Tories pledge to cut £50k from cost of new homes
data.description:
The Conservatives plan to reduce the price of a new-build home by £50,000 in a bonfire of red tape.

Party leaders will use the second day of their annual conference to launch “the biggest deregulation project in a generation” to scrap net zero rules, cut grocery costs and pave the way for a third runway at Heathrow.

In her first speech at the conference on Sunday, Kemi Badenoch declared her party was “for the future” and revealed a plan modelled on Margaret Thatcher’s years in opposition to bring the Tories back to power.

Andrew Griffith, her shadow chancellor, will announce plans on Monday to scrap the Future Homes Standard, which will require developers to include heat pumps or other low-carbon technology in their designs from 2027.

He will also pledge to abolish the “Grocery Tax” – a packaging levy that has pushed up food inflation by 0.5 per cent under Labour – and to simplify the UK’s tax code, which he will say has become a “cat’s cradle of complexity”.

Writing for The Telegraph, Mr Griffith said he would reverse Andy Burnham’s “socialist fever dream of the 1970s” if the Conservatives win the next election, by winning a “battle of ideas over the very basis of prosperity”.

Praising Mrs Badenoch as a “leader with a backbone”, he said: “We will start by cutting up to £50,000 off the price of a home, through a combination of removing red tape and net zero building regulations that have driven up construction costs.”

The savings include around £30,000 from abolishing net zero rules for builders, which require them to consider more expensive energy-efficient heating systems, including heat pumps and solar panels, rather than gas boilers.

Rules on water efficiency are thought to add another £3,100 to the cost of an average new build, with further costs from requirements to install electric vehicle chargers and wider internal staircases.

The announcement comes after Mrs Badenoch’s pledge in 2025 to abolish stamp duty to cut the cost of home ownership. She has not denied speculation that she will announce plans to scrap inheritance tax in her speech on Wednesday, claiming in a pre-conference interview it would be “morally right” to axe it.

Mrs Badenoch said on Sunday that she had been inspired by Baroness Thatcher to write a 90-page pamphlet on her plan to rebuild the Conservatives, modelled on a similar book published in 1976.

She said her party “governed for 18 years after that, because we started with the right foundations” and pledged to “do the same again”.

In the pamphlet, called The Right Way, Mrs Badenoch criticised her predecessors for their approach to immigration, net zero and post-Brexit trade policy by “[leaving] the European Union without the economic plan that should have gone with it”.

She also warned that “little ghettos of separatist communities” risk “ruining” the UK and called for the return of a “high-trust society” with the “return of consequences” for criminals.

The conference marks the Tories’ first major attempt to respond to Mr Burnham’s announcements last week that Labour will reopen a national debate on membership of the EU and scrap the pensions triple lock to partially fund a new care service.

The Tories have pledged to keep the triple lock in their next manifesto, although some shadow ministers are privately concerned that the policy will become unaffordable over the next decade.

Show where the money is coming from

Mr Griffith said that by refusing to explain how he will pay for his pledges, the Prime Minister risks repeating the mistakes of Liz Truss’s mini-Budget.

“As a former finance director for over a decade, it is second nature to always show where the money is coming from to show our workings,” he said.

“That was the mistake of Liz Truss’s mini budget. It’s a mistake the Government is making again today.”

Since entering Downing Street in July, Mr Burnham has announced measures to give people and businesses “breathing space”, including by cutting VAT from energy bills and slashing business rates for pubs and clubs.

John Healey, the Chancellor, is expected to lay out how the Government will pay for these measures in the Budget on Oct 28, but opponents say the policies have been announced to fuel a “Burnham bounce” in the polls for Labour, which now has a marginal lead over Reform UK.

On Monday Mr Griffith will pledge to speed up the planning system by scrapping mechanisms known as Section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy.

These two planning obligations, imposed on developers, fund the cost of new infrastructure such as roads and doctors’ surgeries when new housing estates are built.

But the shadow chancellor says the bureaucracy involved can delay the construction of housing by up to 17 months and does not give communities enough control over the infrastructure developers are funding.

They will be replaced by a new infrastructure levy which will impose less red tape on builders and give local councillors more control over how the funds are spent.

Support for third Heathrow runway

Mr Griffith will also come out in support of a third runway at Heathrow a week after Mr Burnham refused to back expansion.

The airport itself has warned that a new runway may not be operational until 2039.

Responding to the announcement about Heathrow, Thomas Woldbye, the airport’s chief executive, said: “We welcome the growing ‘can do’ consensus behind Heathrow expansion and the Conservative leadership’s recognition of the role we can play in driving growth across the UK.

“Heathrow and our investors stand ready to work with politicians from across the spectrum to finally get the third runway built.”

To speed up the delivery of national infrastructure projects, the shadow chancellor will also promise to leave the Aarhus Convention.

The convention, signed in 1998, is blamed for slowing down the planning process by making it too easy for people to launch judicial reviews against major infrastructure projects.

The treaty ensures that legal challenges against planning schemes are not prohibitively expensive, thereby removing the normal financial risk of going to court.

To comply with this, British courts impose a cost cap of £5,000 for individuals and £10,000 for organisations if they challenge a major project.

Speed up building nuclear power plants

Mr Griffith will say he will withdraw from the convention, as this is the only way to remove these cost caps.

He will pledge to speed up the construction of nuclear plants and warn the Scottish National Party that it cannot block new nuclear power stations in Scotland.

In addition, he will announce plans to scrap a net zero “grocery tax” which increases the cost of the weekly shop and imposes a £1.5bn burden on business.

The tax, known officially as “extended producer responsibility”, is intended to encourage food producers to minimise waste, but almost all of the cost of the levy is passed to consumers through higher prices.

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, said it was “high time to review these taxes”, adding: “Packaging costs have soared and producers are now paying three taxes to recycle the same materials to the tune of nearly £3bn a year – costs which push up prices and hold back hiring.”

Every Treasury minister in the next Conservative government will be given a mission to simplify Britain’s tax code.

And Mr Griffith will pledge to abolish two “dysfunctional” quangos, Natural England and the Environment Agency, which have been accused of subjecting farmers and developers to needless red tape.

Natural England is accused of stopping 160,000 homes being built by insisting that developers abide by strict nutrient neutrality regulations, which are designed to lower river pollution.

They also imposed a £700m “fish disco” acoustic deterrent system on Hinkley Point C, which will save one salmon every 12 years.

The Environment Agency is accused of doing too little to help prevent floods, and even investigating volunteers for cleaning up rivers without a permit.

Their necessary functions will be brought back under the control of ministers in the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.

Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment minister, told The Telegraph: “Both of these arm’s-length bodies were set up with the best of intentions, and they contain very good officials.

“But they have morphed into organisations with powers that extend far beyond what was originally envisaged.

“There is an awful lot of duplication and gold-plating, and there is now one Defra-related civil servant for every five farmers.

“Charities tell me that nature has been in decline since the 1970s, so we must ask whether these quangos are succeeding in the aims they have.”

Robert Jenrick, Reform’s economy spokesman, said: “The Tories are once again copying our policies.

“But they can’t raise the tax-free personal allowance for £15,000 because they refuse to cut migrant welfare, net zero subsidies and the ballooning benefits bill.”

data.title: South West Water owner seeks £550m cash injection after parasite outbreak
data.description:
The owner of South West Water is seeking £550m from shareholders as its boss tries to turn around the struggling business after a parasite scandal.

Pennon Group shares plunged by nearly 19pc on Tuesday after it said it would cut its dividend and ask investors to stump up more cash to fund a £3.6bn investment in its pipes and services.

The supplier was at the centre of a contaminated water outbreak in 2024 that led to a string of customers falling ill in Devon. It was forced to issue a warning to 17,000 households because of the presence of a parasite that can cause diarrhoea.

Keith Haslett, the chief executive at Pennon, said the company would seek to raise £550m by selling new shares to existing investors so it could put in “more investment where our assets need it most”.

He said: “It’s clear from my comprehensive review that Pennon has real strengths, but there are areas where we need to improve and deliver better outcomes for our customers and communities.

“I have looked hard at how we operate, maintain and invest in our assets and today we are setting out in detail what we are doing.”

He added: “I am confident this plan will deliver a better service for customers, improve our environmental performance and generate sustainable, growing value for our shareholders.”

Pennon said its investment plan was £1bn more than was required under the terms set out in a review by regulator Ofwat in 2024.

Those requirements were set out weeks after residents in Brixham, Devon, were told to boil their tap water after the discovery of an outbreak of cryptosporidiosis, which left hundreds of people ill.

Pennon also said it would reduce its dividend payments from £138m in its 2026 financial year to around £125m in 2027 as it seeks to put itself on a firmer footing.

It said it would continue to use debt funding and proposed the sale of its renewable energy investment vehicle Pennon Power to cut debt.

The investment plans come as Andy Burnham raises the prospect of “greater public control” of essential services such as utilities.

Mr Burnham faced a backlash from Labour MPs after shelving plans to place struggling Thames Water into emergency administration.

The Government is working on whether there is a viable alternative to putting the utility into a special administration regime, a type of nationalisation, after officials baulked at the cost.

data.title: One in eight Britons to take weight loss drugs by 2027
data.description:
One in eight Britons will be taking weight loss drugs by 2027, a new report has predicted.

The number of UK adults taking glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) weight loss medication will more than double from three million to seven million by next year, according to analysis by consulting firm PwC Strategy&, accounting for 13pc of the population.

This uptick will be fuelled by the approval of a new Wegovy pill, which will make weight loss treatment easier and more accessible.

This is expected to trigger a sharp drop in the sale of sweets and crisps, according to PwC, as the rollout dramatically changes consumer spending patterns.

Those already taking the medication cut their spending on snacks and sweet treats by 70pc and spent 60pc less on sugary drinks, PwC Strategy& found in a survey of more than 2,300 adults.

The latest findings have been released just weeks after the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) approved a tablet version of the blockbuster weight loss drug Wegovy.

This is the UK’s first GLP-1 pill for weight loss and can now be prescribed to adults with obesity.

It means that millions of Britons can access GLP-1 drugs, which mimic gut hormones to regulate people’s appetites, without needing to administer them by a weekly injection.

The pills will soon be rolled out across major retailers including Boots, Morrisons and Superdrug.

However, they are not yet available on the NHS. Before this can happen, the pill will need to be evaluated by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

While businesses selling confectionery or fast food will suffer from a drop-off in spending on unhealthy foods, those selling healthy products are likely to see a surge in sales.

GLP-1 users spent 60pc more on fresh food, 54pc more on high-protein options and 40pc more on vitamins and supplements, PwC Strategy& found.

They also spent 30pc more on fitness and an additional 40pc on clothing.

These spending patterns are likely to continue even after they have lost weight and stopped taking the drugs.

More than 80pc of those who had stopped treatment said they maintained at least some of the dietary changes they had made while taking the GLP-1s.

Jacqueline Windsor, head of retail at PwC UK, said: “GLP-1 is the most consumerised medication today. Who your GLP-1 customers are, and how your category changes, will dictate how brands and retailers compete.

“We’ll see consumer businesses reshape their portfolios to manage near-term risk.”

More than a quarter (28pc) of GLP-1 users said they would maintain their current levels of spending on the drugs even if the cost of living rose.

The drugs, which are only prescribed on the NHS for those with severe obesity, have predominantly been purchased by wealthier households, but are becoming increasingly mainstream.

Of current users, 6pc came from lower-income households, compared to 20pc for wealthier households.

Adoption of weight loss drugs has so far been highest among women, who account for 60pc of current users.

data.title: Bank tax raid will hurt the economy, Healey is warned
data.description:
John Healey has been warned that unleashing a tax raid on banks in the Budget would hurt the entire economy.

Chris Hayward, the policy chairman at the City of London Corporation, said he was “hugely concerned” that the Chancellor would unveil higher levies on Britain’s banking sector later this month.

Andy Burnham has refused to rule out a tax raid on banks to fund his wave of spending announcements since arriving in No 10. Unions have lobbied Labour to increase the bank levy, a tax on bank profits, to help fund cost of living measures.

Mr Hayward said higher taxes would mean banks “will not be able to afford to lend as much” and risked driving investment abroad.

He said: “We want them [banks] to lend to small businesses; we want them to help drive the economy.

“Governments don’t drive growth; businesses drive growth. It’s very important that the financial services sector is respected across the country.”

Mr Healey and Lucy Rigby, the City minister, met chief executives of major British banks in Downing Street on Tuesday morning. It marked the bank chiefs’ first in-person meeting with the Chancellor since he took up the role in July.

The chief executives of Lloyds, HSBC, NatWest and Barclays attended the gathering, where Mr Healey was warned that a bank tax risked driving away international investors who tend to own shares in UK lenders.

Some executives are reportedly concerned that the Treasury is planning to hit only UK banks with a higher windfall tax, exempting international lenders.

Jamie Dimon, the boss of JP Morgan, warned that exempting international lenders would be unfair.

“I’m not in favour of things that lack principle,” Mr Dimon said in an interview with Bloomberg TV on Tuesday. “It’s easy to say, Charge my friends over here.’ I think that’s wrong.”

The Chancellor told bank chiefs on Tuesday that Britain faced a tough fiscal position, but Bloomberg reported that no decisions had yet been made on bank taxes.

Growing fears of higher taxes have caused Lloyds shares to drop 7.3pc in the last month, while Barclays shares have fallen 9.8pc in the same period.

Fears of tax rises in the Budget have prompted UK investors to sell out of stock funds for the fifth month in a row.

According to Calastone, a data provider, UK investors withdrew a net £858m from stock funds in September, with £708m coming out of British stocks alone. It was the 15th month of outflows in the last 16.

Edward Glyn, of Calastone, said: “Speculation about higher taxes means some investors will be taking profits now.”

‘Banks need to be competitive’

Mr Hayward said that the Burnham Government needed to see banks as “drivers of growth”, rather than businesses that could be squeezed for more government revenue.

He added: “We’ve seen minimal growth in the economy for the past 30 years, so this is the biggest challenge.”

Mr Hayward warned that higher taxes would make British banks less competitive internationally.

He said: “Our banks are already substantially higher taxed than our European counterparts, so they’re already under pressure. Banks need to be competitive.”

British banks already pay one of the highest tax rates in the world at nearly 47pc, according to UK Finance.

Dame Jane Fraser, the Scottish-born chief executive of Citigroup’s investment bank, warned earlier this year that any tax increase risked making the UK a prohibitively expensive place to do business.

“It makes it a tougher decision. You know, it’s already one of the most expensive centres in the world,” she said during a visit to London in August.

Separate figures from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW) show UK business sentiment is in its longest downturn since the global financial crisis.

The ICAEW’s business confidence monitor was negative in September, meaning the index has been below zero for seven consecutive quarters, matching the length of the record downturn in 2008.

Alan Vallance, the ICAEW chief executive, said: “Firms have frozen recruitment. They’ve reduced headcount. They’ve reduced investment. They’ve delayed or cancelled expansion.”

There has been talk in the City of a compromise on bank tax that would allow the Government to raise more funds without raising the headline rate of tax.

At the moment, banks can limit their tax liability by offsetting past losses against profits. The Treasury could restrict banks’ ability to do this.

An analyst note by Jefferies, published in September and circulated across the City, suggested that banks could offer a five-year pause on using past losses to cut their tax bills.

The Treasury would see a short-term uptick in cash tax, and banks wouldn’t feel the full brunt of a significant increase in the bank surcharge.

The City of London Corporation is urging the Government to “do no harm” to the financial and professional services sector at the Budget.

The Treasury was contacted for comment.

data.title: Britain risks running out of gas by end of winter
data.description:
Britain risks running out of gas reserves by the end of winter, raising fears of an energy crisis crippling the country.

A new report from Europe’s gas transmission operators said on Thursday that UK storage facilities could be completely depleted if harsh conditions sweep the country in the next few months.

EU backup gas storage facilities, which Britain relies on to plug the gap when stocks run out, are also running low.

It means the UK could be forced to seek out costly imports of US liquefied natural gas (LNG) to stay afloat, driving up bills for households.

The report, from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG), says the UK is one of the most vulnerable countries to a gas crisis, with its forecasts showing a cold snap would send reserves to zero.

The EU is also under threat, with capacity set to fall to 11pc, far below the 30pc minimum seen as safe.

“Maintaining strong LNG deliveries throughout the winter remains important to support the European gas balance and preserve storage levels,” the report said.

“If LNG availability remains limited, storage levels could fall well below 30pc by the end of the winter, increasing impact in the event of potential cold spells later in the season.”

The warnings coincide with increased pressure for Andy Burnham to approve the Jackdaw North Sea gas field, which could boost UK gas supplies by 3pc.

Mr Burnham has already warned that the UK is facing an “energy crisis”, saying the winter will be “very challenging” after analysts at Cornwall Insight predicted a 16pc rise in bills from January.

EU gas reserves are currently just 72pc filled going into the winter, far below the 88pc level seen as the minimum needed.

The Iran conflict means LNG imports will come mostly from the US – meaning the UK and EU will also be increasingly vulnerable to political interference from Donald Trump’s administration.

Andrew Bowie, the Conservative shadow energy secretary, said: “Britain’s gas supplies are at the mercy of foreign tankers and the weather.

“Labour have banned new drilling, taxed the producers we have left and left Jackdaw gathering dust, so every cubic metre we do not produce at home must be bought from abroad.”

The UK’s plight is worsened because energy giant Centrica has shut down the Rough gas storage facility which has the capacity to support the UK for weeks.

A Centrica spokesman said the facility was scheduled for decommissioning in April after government delays in prolonging its life.

They added that Rough contains just two days’ worth of gas – a fraction of its capacity.

The Government has repeatedly delayed approval for the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, which contains an estimated 15 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas.

If switched on, it could produce 1.4bcm per year – about 2.5pc of total UK demand. However, the decision has been repeatedly delayed because of objections from green groups and Labour backbenchers.

Seb Kennedy, an analyst at Energy Flux, said: “Even when full, UK storage holds less than eight days of average winter demand; today it holds under four. Germany has roughly six weeks in the tank, and Italy and France more than 10.

“Approving Jackdaw will not help this winter ... Even with a quick approval it would take time to ramp up, and it would supply a small share of UK demand.”

The analyst added: “Britain’s gas price is set by the last LNG cargo it has to attract. Jackdaw’s value is longer term: slowing the rise in import dependence as North Sea output falls.”

A government spokesman downplayed the risk. “We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply. Gas is sold on the international market and the price is not connected to our storage capacity – which was only 5pc of our supply last winter,” the spokesman said.

data.title: School coaches face the axe as diesel prices soar
data.description:
Thousands of school coach services are facing the axe as soaring diesel prices make it impossible for operators to turn a profit.

Almost half the coach firms that take 600,000 children to school each weekday plan to quit if fuel prices do not fall soon, according to the Confederation of Passenger Transport (CPT).

It would leave pupils in rural locations struggling to get to lessons and heap costs on local authorities, who have a duty to provide them with free transport if the nearest school is too far to walk.

Graham Vidler, the CPT’s chief executive, said school contracts were negotiated for the full academic year at fixed rates, leaving coach operators haemorrhaging cash after a jump of more than 40pc in diesel prices since the start of the Iran war.

Mr Vidler called on John Healey, the Chancellor, to grant school coaches a fuel duty rebate of 20p per litre of diesel in the Budget.

He said: “This industry operates on narrow margins and school work is generally done on a fixed-price basis – so if your costs go up, you have to take a loss or hand the contract back.

“Our members are on a knife edge. A quarter have already reduced operations, two thirds say they’re concerned about their viability and some operators have gone out of business.”

Coach operators that once relied on school contracts for steady income have come to regard them as a burden, the CPT said.

A survey last week of more than 500 members, which operate around 10,000 coaches, found that 45pc were planning to pull out of school services next year.

Mr Vidler warned this would have a “huge impact on local authorities, independent schools and people trying to get their children to school”.

He added that a 20p rebate from the Chancellor would reduce the cost of diesel for coach businesses by about 13pc. Coach operators can claim back the VAT on their diesel, paying about 160p a litre.

If coach companies pull out of school contracts, Mr Vidler said commitments under the Education Act could compel authorities to ferry children to school in taxis or fleets of minibuses.

Pupils under eight must be provided with free transport for journeys of more than two miles, rising to three miles for older children.

While the Government has provided a one-off payment of £30m to help mitigate soaring diesel prices, Mr Vidler said that had gone overwhelmingly to urban bus operators.

Coaches for tourist excursions, sporting events and rail replacement services are generally negotiated at shorter notice than school contracts, making them more sustainable for businesses, he said.

He said the industry nevertheless expected to see fewer trips in the coming months to attractions such as Christmas markets.

The situation is particularly acute because coach operators – which provide 450 million passenger journeys each year, equivalent to 25pc of the total for rail – are mostly family-owned and have more limited financial resources than major urban bus operators.

Operators have formed a new association, Coach UK, to help press their concerns with ministers.

data.title: Lisa Nandy delays publication of critical report on UAE
data.description:
The Culture Secretary has further delayed the publication of a critical report on the failed United Arab Emirates (UAE) bid for The Telegraph, two and a half years after it was completed.

Amid anger from the Gulf autocracy because of the Premier League’s damning investigation of Manchester City, Lisa Nandy’s department has this week declined to release to Parliament an Ofcom report on the bid for The Telegraph.

The media regulator investigated the attempted takeover by RedBird IMI, a UAE investment vehicle, as a potential threat to press freedom.

Although the bid was ultimately blocked, the Culture Secretary is required by law to make Ofcom’s findings, handed to the Government in March 2024, public. However, her department has refused requests to release it, including under the Freedom of Information Act.

Ms Nandy’s latest refusal was delivered to Parliament by Baroness Mackenzie of Sherwood, her junior minister.

In response to a written question from Baroness Stowell of Beeston, a Conservative peer, Baroness Mackenzie said only that the report would be released “shortly”.

The further delay is likely to stoke speculation that the Government is suppressing it to avoid potential embarrassment for the rulers of the UAE.

Ofcom reviewed evidence from journalists, press freedom and human rights groups on the state’s chequered record, including on its conduct in relation to Manchester City.

Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the Emirati royal, is behind both the club and RedBird IMI.

Baroness Stowell said: “It is troubling that the Government is taking so long to publish regulatory documentation it is required by law to do without offering any explanation for the delay.

“Ministers should remedy this situation swiftly if they want to avoid more questions and not fuel speculation and unnecessary concerns.”

Andy Burnham’s approach to the UAE and its money is under close scrutiny as a result of the Gulf state’s role in the regeneration of Manchester under his mayoralty. The Telegraph revealed that a former council official resigned in protest against a proposed deal to reserve a parcel of land for the Gulf state.

The Prime Minister stoked the controversy last week by appearing to express sympathy with the UAE in the Manchester City case, in comments that were swiftly back-pedalled by No 10.

The UAE has threatened to pull billions of pounds of investment in the UK after Manchester City were found guilty of breaking Premier League spending rules, putting the club at risk of heavy fines, point deductions or even being stripped of its trophies.

The row has raised further questions about Britain’s reliance on investment from the oil-rich state. The Telegraph takeover saga triggered a comparable diplomatic row and economic threats.

Conservative ministers intervened in RedBird IMI’s complex bid in late 2023, amid a cross-party outcry.

Ofcom and competition regulators were instructed to investigate the effect of the deal on media plurality and freedom of expression.

While the contents of the reports remain private, Lucy Frazer, the former culture secretary, revealed in a letter to RedBird IMI that Ofcom had uncovered evidence that “may indicate IMI’s propensity to exercise influence to curtail freedom of expression in the Telegraph titles”.

The regulator added that the UAE fund had “clear political and broader commercial incentives” to influence The Telegraph’s editorial line “in a way which could negatively affect the accurate presentation of news and free expression of opinion”.

RedBird IMI was blocked from buying The Telegraph after the Government brought in new laws banning foreign state ownership of British newspapers.

The Telegraph was then put back up for auction and ultimately bought by the German publishing giant Axel Springer in a £575m deal this summer.

The Government has been contacted for comment.

data.title: Burnham wants to revive British industry. This is why he’ll fail
data.description:
A giant crane slowly eats its way through vast, derelict buildings at the Llanwern steelworks.

At its peak, the site on the outskirts of Newport was a crucial cog in one of the biggest industrial hubs in the world.

Now, workers can only watch as the complex is torn apart.

“We’re literally watching as the place we work is destroyed in front of us,” says one veteran employee.

The facility, owned by Indian conglomerate Tata, produces galvanised steel today but its role has been dramatically reduced over time.

More recently, the steelworks has been threatened by high energy costs and an influx of cheaper, foreign steel that has followed a loosening of tariff restrictions.

As of August, it was only operating at half capacity with hundreds of jobs feared to be at risk.

“It feels like a perfect storm,” frets the employee.

Further along the Welsh coast, in Port Talbot, Tata has also cut some 2,000 jobs as part of plans to close its historic blast furnaces.

These struggles – and those of Britain’s wider steel industry – are among the most visceral examples of the UK’s fading industrial power.

Domestic businesses in carmaking, chemicals and other sectors are struggling to compete with global rivals.

But at Labour’s annual conference last week, Andy Burnham and John Healey vowed to buck this trend with a “new era of industrialisation”.

They have talked up manufacturing, arguing it is vital for national security in an age of instability, winning a rapturous reception from the party faithful.

But what does it mean in practice? And is it just a ridiculous fantasy?

Stephen Phipson, chief executive of manufacturing body Make UK, warns that far from a resurgence, industry is facing threats from “every direction”.

“Reindustrialisation won’t be delivered through speeches, strategies or slogans from Whitehall,” he says.

“It will be delivered by thousands of individual businesses making decisions to recruit, invest and expand.

“And right now too many of those decisions are being postponed.”

Car crash

In the 19th century, Britain was at the heart of the industrial revolution that unleashed an era of breakneck economic growth.

But in the post-war period, the nation’s industrial muscles have gradually atrophied as the global economy’s centre of gravity has shifted.

In the 1970s manufacturing made up around 30pc of all jobs domestically. Since then, that has dwindled to just 7.8pc of workers.

The dramatic decline has transformed once-bustling industrial towns into hotspots of joblessness after major employers shut their factories and moved overseas.

Now, some are worried Healey’s pledge to usher in “a new age of industrialisation” risks harking back to a bygone era.

Reindustrialisation would need to reverse a trend “that has been going on for decades”, says Paul Johnson, the former director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, when “actually, our strength is as a service-based economy”.

The data reflect just that. Last year manufacturing made up 8.3pc of total UK economic output (GVA), compared to an 81pc contribution from the services sector.

As the fortunes of the country’s manufacturers started to turn in the Eighties, a rare bright spot for the sector was Margaret Thatcher’s successful lobbying to bring in Japanese car manufacturers, with Nissan opening its first UK factory in Sunderland in 1984.

But China’s emergence as a manufacturing superpower has put further pressure on British industry since then, along with skills shortages and soaring energy costs.

Today, even Nissan’s highly efficient Sunderland plant has been reduced to running at 50pc capacity.

Top executives have blamed rising costs as a key reason for the idleness, warning that the plant “pays more for electricity than any other Nissan plant in the world”.

“Ultimately, the UK is not a competitive place to be building cars today,” said Alan Johnson, a senior vice president for manufacturing at Nissan, in a parliamentary hearing last year.

There are few signs that the decline is slowing. Stellantis closed its historic Vauxhall plant in Luton last year, putting around 1,000 jobs at risk. Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) – Britain’s biggest domestic car maker – is cutting 4,000 jobs over the next two years as it struggles with tariffs and tough competition overseas.

Against this backdrop, ministers have been courting Chinese brands such as BYD, Jaecoo owner Chery and SAIC Motor, the owner of MG, in the hope they will invest.

But industry sources say even they are wary about the costs of doing business in Britain. Meanwhile, western brands fear the Chinese will undercut them on price – partly thanks to state support from Beijing.

It has prompted questions of whether Britain should embrace China’s carmakers fully or follow the European Union and impose tariffs to protect domestic industry – a demand Brussels has reportedly made a condition of any deal on its “Made in Europe” supply chain standards.

Corroded chemicals sector

But automotive is just one area where competition from China has dramatically altered the landscape.

Since China transformed itself into an export powerhouse and joined the World Trade Organisation in 2001, the UK, like many western economies, has failed to keep up with the influx of cheap imports, leaving many domestic manufacturing companies falling behind.

British petrochemicals tycoon Sir Jim Ratcliffe warned last month that China was “overbuilding” factory capacity for polyvinyl chloride (PVC) – used in sanitation, healthcare, construction and food packaging – and then “dumping” the excess output on Europe.

“The result is an accelerating rate of closure of our chemical industry,” said Sir Jim, whose company Ineos has filed an official complaint with Europe’s competition regulators.

Chemicals used to be the crown jewel of UK industry. But bosses have since found themselves issuing desperate warnings to the Government amid a wave of factory closures – 25 and counting since 2021.

This has been accompanied by a collapse in the sector’s output, falling 60pc over the same period, according to the Chemical Industries Association.

Some economists have nevertheless suggested the flow of ultra-cheap Chinese goods is ultimately to Europe’s benefit.

But Sander Tordoir, chief economist at the Centre for European Reform, warns the West’s “dangerous” dependency on imports is one of the main reasons policymakers in the US and Europe are pushing for reindustrialisation – with Beijing seen as a far from benevolent trading partner.

“There is a deeper geostrategic rationale underlying the desire to reindustrialise,” Tordoir adds.

Unlike the UK’s car manufacturers, a number of other industries have survived and even kept growing.

“We have a very strong pharmaceutical base and a broader life sciences industry that isn’t likely to go anywhere any time soon, in part because it’s so research and development-intensive,” says Liam Sides, director at Oxford Economics.

The defence sector and aerospace engineering are also held up as parts of UK manufacturing that are growing significantly thanks to new advancements.

Yet for many other companies the question remains: will Burnham’s plan to boost industry really work, or are they stuck on a path to irrelevance?

A new age of industrialisation

As thousands of Labour apparatchiks mingled at the party’s annual conference last week, the merchandise shop in Liverpool was stuffed with memorabilia commemorating former leader Harold Wilson.

It has been 60 years since Wilson’s second election victory in 1966 – and 63 since he vowed to reforge British industry in the “white heat” of technology.

The plan ultimately rested on a sweeping, state-led reorganisation of manufacturing that created behemoths including carmaker British Leyland, the General Electric Company (GEC) and International Computers Ltd, which collectively employed more than half a million people.

Yet Wilson’s policy is now largely viewed as having failed on its own terms.

The boost to economic growth he hoped it would deliver never turned up, while all three of the big companies created through government-orchestrated mergers had gone bust or been broken up 40 years later.

Meanwhile, the Government’s shaky finances in the face of global headwinds also put a ceiling on Wilson’s ambitions – forcing him into a humiliating devaluation of the pound in 1967.

Much of the British state’s involvement in industry was then unwound under Thatcher in the Eighties with the privatisation of businesses including British Aerospace, British Telecom, British Gas, British Airways, Rolls-Royce and British Steel.

Ironically, however, Burnham and Healey, his Chancellor, are now pushing for the Government to resume a more muscular role in a “new era of industrialisation”.

In his Labour conference speech, Healey gave a nostalgic account of the “industrial heartlands” that once powered Britain’s economy while stressing that some sources of employment, such as coal-mining, were “not coming back”.

Instead the Chancellor chose to channel Wilson with an argument that manufacturing had to be “remade for the modern world”. He has also set out plans for the Government to stimulate demand by “buying British”.

“This is the new age of industrialisation,” he told delegates. “Don’t tell me it’s not possible.”

Burnham similarly argued that Britain should seek to lead the world in the deployment and regulation of AI, while name-checking Gordon Brown’s proposal for an “innovation nation” that supports start-ups.

“We led the world first’s industrial revolution from the Midlands and the North of England,” Burnham said. “So why can’t we lead the next?”

As critics have pointed out however, the plan for reindustrialisation so far looks somewhat scattershot.

The most expensive announcement was £6bn for domestic shipbuilders to construct new floating submarine docks – important infrastructure, no doubt, but hardly the technologies of the future.

There are also signs of a mismatch between what ministers are pitching and the more sweeping ambitions of Labour’s union backers.

Unite, the GMB, Unison, the RMT, the Communication Workers Union and the Trades Union Congress have variously called for the nationalisation of the energy, water, transport, postal, telecoms, shipbuilding and steel sectors.

“If they pull it off, reindustrialisation should mean reinvigorating the working-class communities and industrial heartlands of the UK,” says Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, the GMB’s national officer for manufacturing.

“It means apprenticeship opportunities for kids that can’t go to university and communities like Scunthorpe, where I’m from, thriving rather than just managing decline.”

She believes the decline of British industry since the Eighties is proof that privatisation hasn’t worked, leaving “foreign entities owning some of our most strategically important industries”.

However, nationalising more of the economy could initially cost the Government hundreds of billions of pounds – and risk saddling taxpayers with huge losses if the investments go bad.

A decision to nationalise British Steel, for instance, is already proving costly, with accounts showing the struggling business is losing almost £700,000 a day.

Turning the situation around will require time, commitment and hefty investments, says Gareth Stace, director general of lobby group UK Steel, as well as a decision on when to close the last blast furnaces in Scunthorpe and replace them with newer electric arc furnaces.

The Government has committed £2.5bn to the steel sector and on Tuesday Blair McDougall, the steel minister, said officials viewed it as “important for our national security”.

“There will be difficult decisions ahead,” he told attendees at an industry drinks reception.

“But our commitment… is to make sure that we do move on... that we do invest, and that we take those decisions we need to take to make sure this is a profitable, resilient and again world-class industry.”

Yet again, there is ambiguity about what Labour wants to achieve.

Last month, MPs on the public accounts committee said the Government had so far failed to set out a plan for British Steel beyond simply “propping up” the business.

One model for success that ministers have pointed to is a cluster of businesses that have based themselves in South Yorkshire.

There, the focus of the economy has moved from coal-mining to high-tech manufacturing with top businesses including Rolls-Royce, Boeing and McLaren now located in a business park built on top of the former Orgreave pit.

This is also where the University of Sheffield opened the Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre (AMRC) in 2004, aiming to bring together academics and companies to develop cutting-edge production techniques.

Chris Read, head of Rotherham city council, says these partnerships are the bedrock of the AMRC’s success.

“None of those partners on their own would have been able to do it,” he says, adding that “kids who live in my borough can now get apprenticeships with companies they’d never be able to work for otherwise” in industries such as clean energy.

But he also believes the era where “you’d have tens of thousands of men” working in traditional industries is probably gone – even as crises including Covid and Donald Trump’s trade wars provide a case for boosting domestic production.

Ministers claim they’re on the same page. Last week, Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, insisted the Government wanted to focus on “future-facing” technologies.

He also said the state wanted to play a more active role supporting innovation, using data to proactively identify businesses that deserve investment from the British Business Bank.

A source close to Reynolds disputes suggestions that the Government’s plan lacks substance, arguing that Labour stands by the “industrial strategy” ministers published under Sir Keir Starmer in summer 2025.

Yet businesses say that document did not go far enough and was sparse on detail, pointing out that Burnham’s promised “10-year plan” for Britain may also diverge from it in significant ways.

In the resulting vacuum, some of Labour’s biggest beasts are jostling for influence. Gordon Brown will gather business titans in Manchester next week for a conference to discuss his “innovation nation” idea, while Sir Tony Blair is calling for the rapid embrace of AI.

Like Wilson, Burnham has vowed to make sure Britain helps to steer the coming technological revolution instead of being swept up by it.

But experts warn there is another, less comfortable parallel between the two leaders: namely that Burnham’s promises depend on forces that are not all under his control.

Eye-watering energy costs

On the banks of the Humber in Hull, the sprawling Saltend chemicals park has been a vital hub of manufacturing for more than a century.

Yet in recent weeks, three factories there have fallen silent – potentially putting some 4,000 jobs at risk.

Ineos, the owner, has laid the blame on one of the Government’s biggest headaches: Britain’s soaring energy costs.

“I’m sure people will find it hard to believe that we are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe,” said Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the founder of Ineos.

“But with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and eight times that of China, we just cannot compete.”

It isn’t just gas, either. Across the board, British businesses electricity prices have reached crippling levels.

Official statistics published have previously shown that industrial businesses in Britain faced higher power costs than those in any other developed country.

Separate data from the International Energy Agency also show wholesale electricity prices in the UK have been nearly 200pc higher than the US, 45pc higher than Japan and 41pc higher than France over the past year.

This is a particularly potent threat because cheap electricity is needed to operate many of the “future-facing” industries ministers want to cultivate, from electric arc-forged steel to battery production and electric vehicle manufacturing, says the CER’s Tordoir.

He believes the correct approach is for the UK and European governments to provide targeted support to promising areas, for instance Britain’s semiconductor and aerospace sectors.

Others are more sceptical that Labour’s focus on industry is the right approach, however.

Sides, at Oxford Economics, warned last week: “I personally cannot think of an advanced economy less suited for an industrial resurgence.”

Simon French, chief economist at Panmure Liberum, also warns there will be “no reindustrialisation” unless Labour can improve the country’s economic fundamentals more broadly, including the costs of energy, capital, construction, and employment.

Many businesses complain Starmer and now Burnham are doing the opposite – raising taxes and imposing onerous employment laws and regulations.

“If you don’t get the pre-conditions for economic growth right, no amount of industrial planning will get over that,” French says.

Any attempt by ministers to focus on specific sectors or companies, rather than fix these basic foundations, “will fail miserably”, he adds.

Former IFS boss Johnson is similarly sceptical of the focus on manufacturing specifically.

“A growth strategy is a growth strategy for the economy as a whole, rather than for metal bashing,” he says.

He argues that the nation’s convoluted planning rules and building regulations are hampering investment and making it harder for businesses to expand.

Andrew Sentance, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, also believes the plan for reindustrialisation risks “heading in the wrong direction” and that Britain would be better off focusing on the “knowledge industries” that it excels at today.

“There was a time when manufacturing was the third of our economy back in the Sixties,” he says.

“But we can’t pretend we’re still in that world.”

Businesses are nevertheless lobbying hard for relief. The Confederation of British Industry, will warn next week that British companies are paying 45pc more to power their businesses than those in other rich nations.

Research by Britain’s biggest business group will show that energy bills have doubled.

Time to deliver

Phipson, of Make UK, also warns that before ministers can reindustrialise Britain, they must “first stop making it more expensive to manufacture here”.

“The autumn Budget therefore presents a simple test.”

Yet that is a big ask as Healey prepares for a difficult Budget on Oct 28.

According to economists, the war in the Middle East has blown a £10bn hole in the public finances that the Chancellor will have to plug to keep the bond markets happy. 

He has already warned Labour delegates in Liverpool that “the money New Labour had in the Nineties is simply not there now”.

It raises further questions about whether Burnham can afford to back up his Government’s soaring rhetoric on reindustrialisation with action.

But a failure to meet his party’s expectations will carry its own costs ahead of the next general election, warns the GMB’s Brumpton-Childs.

“If they don’t follow through on what they’ve promised, then it’ll be electoral suicide,” she says.

“The most important thing about hope is delivering, isn’t it?”

Back in Llanwern, the stakes feel all too real for the workers whose jobs are on the line.

Here, Labour’s promises to revive the steel industry have gone down well. But there are real doubts about whether a plan will materialise in time.

“You don’t want to sound too blue about everything,” says the veteran worker. “But it feels like we’ve got some tough times ahead before anything starts improving.”

data.title: Thousands of homes no longer subject to bats and newts rules
data.description:
Housing developers will no longer need to seek approval for new homes from Natural England, putting an end to the prospect of bats and newts holding up routine planning applications.

Natural England, the environmental quango, had been required to examine more than 22,000 planning applications for new developments annually.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, last year criticised nature rules for prioritising the needs of wildlife such as “bats and newts” over new developments.

She said: “As a country, we’ve cared more about the bats than we have about the commuter times for people in Leeds and West Yorkshire, and we’ve got to change that.”

The body has been criticised for its excessive caution in its consultation responses, holding up planning applications. Some of its rules have resulted in a de facto ban on new residential construction in several areas across England because of worries about water pollution.

Natural England was also criticised after it was consulted on a £100m “bat tunnel”, constructed over the High Speed 2 railway, and for its advice on a £700m underwater sound system – dubbed the “fish disco” – at the Hinkley Point C nuclear power station.

Legislation had required Natural England to reply to all large-scale planning applications, irrespective of whether they were a risk to the environment or not.

The environmental body could answer “no comment” to proposals that it felt did not require its engagement. However, this led to a large number of consultations where planning applications were registered and replied to with a “no comment” response.

New guidance means that councils will be able to rely on pre-written advice on whether they should seek input from Natural England, and they will be able to wave through more routine developments without consulting the quango.

The reforms will allow the environmental watchdog to focus on responding to planning proposals “which present the greatest risks or opportunities for nature”.

The changes mean Natural England will shift away from offering repeated advice on individual planning applications and instead provides more tailored advice for larger-scale projects.

The Government hopes this will speed up the planning application process for thousands of new developments as Labour races to accelerate housebuilding across the country.

Neil Hornby, the chief executive of Natural England, said: “This change of approach will help us focus our expertise where it can have the greatest impact for nature, while supporting efficient decision making across the planning system.

“Natural England is laser focused on advancing nature recovery and meeting key legal Environment Act targets, while supporting the Government’s ambition for good growth in every postcode.”

data.title: Healey urged to cut stamp duty on new homes to reap £4bn windfall
data.description:
John Healey has been urged to cut stamp duty on newly built homes in a move that one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders estimates could hand the Treasury a £4.2bn windfall.

In its Budget submission, Berkeley Group told the Chancellor that cutting the levy could revive a market that it warned was “sliding over an economic cliff edge”.

In the submission, seen by The Telegraph, the listed property developer called for stamp duty to be capped at 1pc for first-time buyers and downsizers.

It also urged Mr Healey to scrap a 5pc surcharge levied on investors in new-build rental homes.

The housebuilder estimated that the package could deliver an extra 60,000 homes per year.

Rob Perrins, the executive chairman of Berkeley, said: “Our position has always been that a stamp duty reduction on new-builds – especially around the investor surcharge, first-time buyers and downsizers – is the best and quickest lever.

“This is still needed alongside Your First Home to restart homebuilding in urban areas.”

The intervention came after Andy Burnham unveiled Your First Home, an equity loan scheme aimed at assisting more young people on to the housing ladder.

Designed as a scaled-back version of the previous Help to Buy initiative, the policy will be open to first-time buyers with a 2.5pc deposit, with backing from a 20pc equity loan from the Government.

Mr Healey is expected to formally launch the new policy in the Budget later this month.

However, Berkeley’s submission suggested the scheme would not be enough to solve an “acute crisis, particularly in London”.

The Treasury also reportedly rejected calls for a stamp duty break for downsizing homebuyers earlier this month.

Berkeley argued that higher interest rates, geopolitical uncertainty and rising taxes had led to a “significant slowdown in the rate of new housing sales”.

Only 8,840 private homes were sold in the capital last year, according to the document, down 56pc since 2022.

The housebuilder acknowledged that a cap for first-time buyers could cost the Treasury money, but argued this would be more than offset by extra revenue for the public purse from investors and buyers downsizing.

Berkeley calculated that removing the 5pc investor surcharge would save the typical investor around £13,000, meaning sales would need to rise by just 7pc for the Treasury to break even.

Using figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility, Berkeley estimated that scrapping the charge would unlock sales growth of at least 30pc, providing £4.2bn to the Exchequer.

The housebuilder added that a cap for those moving to a smaller home would probably be even “more lucrative for the Treasury”.

While older homeowners would pay less stamp duty on their own purchase, each move would trigger a chain of moves involving transactions that attract the full amount.

Outside stamp duty, each newly built home is thought to produce around £49,800 in taxes, such as corporation tax and the building safety levy.

Berkeley said: “If the Government wants to increase housing supply as measured against its high-profile commitment to deliver 1.5 million homes this Parliament, there are few policy measures available with the potential to deliver such an immediate impact, whilst sticking to a tight fiscal envelope.”

The Government has been contacted for comment.

data.title: Billionaire family behind Primark nears £7bn deal for Boots
data.description:
The billionaire family behind Primark is closing in on a £7bn deal to buy Boots from its private equity owners.

The Westons are in advanced talks to buy the British pharmacy chain from Sycamore Partners, with a deal expected to be confirmed in the coming days.

The two sides have been in talks for months about a potential deal after Boots was carved off from its former parent company, Walgreens Boots Alliance.

While the sale has yet to be finalised, the Wall Street Journal reported a deal could be reached as soon as next week.

The Telegraph previously reported that an earlier bid from the Westons for Boots had been rejected after its offer for the high street chain was reduced.

The Westons, a Canadian business dynasty, are one of the world’s richest families.

The Canadian branch of the family, which is in talks with Boots, owns Loblaw, the country’s largest supermarket. The UK arm of the family, meanwhile, owns brands including Fortnum & Mason and Primark-owner Associated British Foods.

The future of Boots has been in the balance for months as Sycamore weighed a potential London listing for the chemists after buying Walgreens Boots Alliance for $24bn (£18bn) last year.

Previously, Walgreens had explored a sale of Boots in 2022.

The sale to Sycamore saw Italian billionaire Stefano Pessina, who originally helped take Boots private in 2007, reinvest in the chain as it was split into a standalone business in preparation for sale or listing.

Sycamore had previously also held talks with Sigma Healthcare, an Australian pharmacy group.

Talks between the Westons and Sycamore stalled this summer after the Iran war and the accompanying economic shocks of higher inflation and rising interest rates dented business confidence.

The Westons are also exploring plans to demerge Primark from Associated British Foods and list it separately on the London Stock Exchange.

The family were also the owners of Selfridges for more than two decades, before it was sold in 2022 for £4bn.

Boots has in recent years been forced to close hundreds of UK stores as it grapples with cost-cutting and the widespread pressures affecting high streets across Britain.

Some 1,500 UK pharmacies have been forced to close in the past decade, according to industry figures.

Boots and Sycamore declined to comment. The Weston family was also contacted for comment.
