data.title: UK’s net zero strategy is an ‘abject failure’, says chemicals plant boss
data.description:
One of America’s most prominent industrialists has launched a withering attack on Britain’s “absurd” energy policy, branding the pursuit of net zero an “abject failure”.

Unable to compete with global rivals because of sky-high energy prices, UK manufacturers spanning the entire industrial base are shutting down operations or leaving altogether, billionaire Peter Huntsman warned.

Mr Huntsman, whose eponymous industrial empire includes a critical chemicals plant in Wilton, Teesside, said the charge towards renewables doesn’t make “any sense whatsoever”.

The environmental benefits of green zealotry are outweighed by “the destruction to society” caused by widespread job losses.

With energy costs “getting progressively worse”, manufacturers are asking “‘how do I get out?’ rather than ‘where can I invest?’” he added.

Yet there is an alarming “lack of urgency” from those in charge, Mr Huntsman said, with officials still intent on hitting net zero by 2050.

His criticism echoes that of Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who accused Labour of “economic vandalism on an industrial scale” after the tycoon mothballed three vital chemical plants in Hull last week.

Sir Jim blamed “ridiculously high” gas prices for the decision, claiming that UK factories are paying up to 12 times more than their rivals in the US.

This has been blamed largely on carbon taxes and the decline in domestic gas production, which has forced many factories to rely on expensive imports.

Mr Huntsman warned in March that his company could be forced to close its Wilton factory, which makes aniline, a chemical used in everything from car seats to aircraft components, if the cost of gas remained high.

The plant is the last of its kind in the country.

It is understood Huntsman is in negotiations with the Department for Business about propping up the Wilton site with funds from the Government’s £350m Critical Chemicals Resilience Fund, which was created in May to assist strategically important chemical manufacturers.

However, it is still waiting for confirmation that it qualifies for support.

“We’re still somewhat confused as to exactly what we are supposed to do to get the funds,” he said. “What are they looking for?”

Mr Huntsman said he was alarmed at suggestions that companies may have to agree to commit to using any state support for new “energy efficient” projects.

“Nobody’s putting money into new projects,” he said. “That’s just absurd.”

The Wilton plant, which employs up to 100 people, is one of the last surviving remnants of Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI), Britain’s largest manufacturer in the 20th century.

The businessman was one of the driving forces behind Huntsman’s £1.7bn takeover of what was then ICI’s industrial chemicals division in 1999.

The deal doubled Huntsman’s global workforce to 16,000 overnight and Peter became chief executive the following year, taking over from his late father Jon, who started the business in 1970 after serving in President Richard Nixon’s administration.

Within a few years, the company had shot to prominence with the invention of the “clamshell” styrofoam McDonald’s Big Mac container, and it now runs more than 55 manufacturing sites worldwide.

However, in recent years, the company’s UK operations have been bogged down energy policies that aren’t “grounded in reality”, said Mr Huntsman.

This has been compounded by the Government’s broken promises on net zero, particularly its failure to deliver a “hydrogen economy”.

“We were all told that consumers would demand carbon-free products. That never materialised,” he said.

“We were also told we were going to have cheap electricity, cheap wind power, solar power – essentially free power. Well, that didn’t work either.”

Prominent figures like himself have long warned about the dangers of allowing swathes of the steel industry and the chemicals industry to vanish.

Yet the exodus of critical manufacturers continues, he said.

“The part manufacturers that make the components for the automobile, aerospace, and pharmaceutical industries – they’re all leaving,” he said.

He added: “The question is, how bad can it get?”

Mr Huntsman said he’s not “anti-wind or anti-solar” but claimed that renewables alone couldn’t fuel an entire economy.

“Just look at energy prices,” he said. “None of this makes any sense to me whatsoever, yet I don’t see anybody seriously addressing this in government”.

He said the UK is simply “outsourcing its pollutants” by swapping domestic fossil fuel supplies for those imported from abroad, therefore “the climate is suffering too” from the Government’s net zero commitments.

As a result, Mr Huntsman said he was perplexed by Labour’s decision to ban new drilling in the North Sea while continuing to import vast quantities of oil and gas from Norway, Qatar and other overseas suppliers.

“As long as you’re buying it from somebody, you might as well buy it from yourself,” he said.

“If the UK can get to a place where it no longer uses natural gas and petrochemicals, terrific. That really would be an example to the rest of the world.

“But the simple fact of the matter is, you’re going to become more dependent on it [oil and gas] than ever before in the coming technological age.”

The UK’s preference for importing Norwegian fossil fuels over the exploitation of its own resources in the North Sea was “astounding” given that its reserves came from the same region, he said.

“Half the gas that you [Britain] consume is from Norway, and the gas that they are supplying in many parts comes from joint fields,” he said.

“They are taking hydrocarbons from underground formations that probably straddle the UK and selling it back to you.

“I don’t understand how people can look at that and say, ‘Well, it’s good that we’ve got Norway as a supplier to supply us with our own gas.’ I can’t even process that because it’s so idiotic.”

Mr Huntsman said he thought the UK’s North Sea operations were probably still doomed even if the Tories or Reform win the next election because investors won’t be willing to take the risk of Labour returning to power.

“When they do, guess who gets shut down again?” he said.

He urged the UK to take a similarly pragmatic approach to fracking and let local people decide whether it takes place in their communities.

“If they don’t want the economic benefit, that’s fine,” he said. But it should be “a national priority to try to extract it in the most economical and the most environmentally feasible way” rather than banning it on safety grounds.

“Usually in society – particularly in the UK – when something was declared unsafe, you didn’t abandon it,” he said. “You just made it better.

“The first steam engines that were ever built were blowing up all the time. The first railroads were terribly unsafe, but we got better and in the United States we have made fracking work.”

As for the threat from cheap Chinese imports, he urged Britain to follow America’s path by getting tougher on trade.

“Does that mean going to war with China? Of course it doesn’t. But it does mean choosing the industries that you’re going to protect, just like the Chinese protect certain industries in their country, and just like we do in the US,” he said.

He also warned against partnering with the Chinese in the way that Nissan is proposing doing with Chery at its Sunderland plant: “I would say be very careful. The Chinese are going to import batteries, motors, frames.

“They’ll say the car’s made in the UK. It might be glued together [in the UK], but that’s not a car built in the UK. You’re not getting the economic benefit.”

In June, Huntsman unveiled a blockbuster all-stock merger with American rival Olin to create a new chemicals giant with $12.5bn (£9.5bn) of combined annual turnover.

However, with energy prices still elevated in Britain, Mr Huntsman admitted that the future of the company’s Wilton site remained uncertain.

There was a moment during the summer when a fall in energy prices meant it was breaking even, but he warned that the site was now back to losing money.

He says its future rests on two things: firstly, whether the energy shocks of the last few years are “event-driven” or “systemic”; and secondly, “How long can you withstand the tides with a government that just doesn’t seem to care?”

Mr Huntsman will be watching closely to see how the Government responds to Ineos’s decision to mothball three plants in Hull.

“I’ve read that Jim Ratcliffe is playing chicken with the Government,” he said. “That’s a hell of a game of chicken.

“As soon as you shut down a plant, three things happen: you start losing employees, you’re putting strain on your operations, and you’re losing your customers. It’s not a question of just flipping the switch back on again.”

data.title: Airline bosses warn of major cuts with ‘tough winter’ ahead
data.description:
Airline bosses have warned that the industry faces a “crisis” in the coming months because of high fuel prices.

The aviation industry is entering its first winter since the outbreak of war in Iran, which caused the cost of fuel to soar. The price of jet fuel is around $208 (£155) per tonne. A year ago, it was around $90.

Soaring costs have already forced airlines to cut flights and delay payments on leased aircraft.

EasyJet, Europe’s fifth biggest airline, as well as Germany’s Lufthansa, is set to scale back operations over the winter season. It claims its margins are as low as just £6.08 per passenger and a dramatic rise in the price of fuel could mean that flights are no longer viable.

Michael O’Leary, the boss of Ryanair, another low-cost airline, told the Financial Times that the situation was dire: “This is a full-blown crisis. Everybody is going to be hurting next year. We are just trying to trim the ship as much as we possibly can.”

In recent years, Ryanair has sought to make up falling passenger numbers by selling scratch cards and high-margin food and drink on board their flights.

It is understood there are concerns that some airlines could go bust this winter season, which runs in the industry through to March.

Last month, AirBaltic filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the United States and Spirit Airlines, an ultra-low-cost airline based in Florida, stopped flying in May.

EasyJet has said it will cut up to 700,000 seats from its winter schedule. The carrier normally offers 50 million seats during the winter season. 

Data group Cirium has estimated that the industry as a whole has cut six million seats for the rest of the year.

The reports will come as a blow to Christmas holidaymakers. It is understood that although bookings for easyJet flights have been weak, it is anticipating a last-minute rush.

Mr O’Leary said he expects the fuel crisis to last until 2028.

Kenton Jarvis, the chief executive of easyJet, said that airlines are hedging on fuel, but that even if they buy it six months out, they are paying double industry norms.

John Strickland, an aviation analyst, also told the Financial Times that this winter could be bleak for the industry: “It does look like it’s going to be a tough winter. Even for airlines that are hedged.”

He added: “We’re going to see substantial cancellations and it even puts life in question for some.”

data.title: Diesel car values crash as pump prices reach record high
data.description:
The price of second-hand diesel cars is falling sharply as the fuel hits a new high at the pumps.

Used diesel vehicles were advertised at an average of £13,802 last month, according to Autotrader. That was £850 lower than at the start of the US war with Tehran and just £400 higher than in September 2016.

By comparison, Autotrader figures showed the average asking price for a used diesel peaked at almost £18,000 in January 2022, up 25pc in less than a year.

The drop in recent months comes as diesel prices reach new highs in the UK. Donald Trump’s threat to ring-fence diesel supplies for American drivers has seen pump prices climb to a record £2 a litre during the weekend, with analysts suggesting it could hit £2.50 or even £3 if the Iran war drags on.

Second-hand diesels rode a price boom in the years leading to 2022, amid moves by successive governments to take internal-combustion-engine cars off British roads. That culminated in the Zero Emission Vehicle mandate that will outlaw their sale from 2030.

Diesel car production has consequently dropped 60pc in a decade, increasing the scarcity value of the cars and funnelling buyers into the second-hand market.

Some motorists favour diesel because of engine efficiency, and the latest models comply with tighter emissions standards. Diesel cars deliver anywhere between 12pc and 19pc more miles to the gallon than petrol equivalents.

However, valuations have dropped in recent years as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the outbreak of the Iran conflict have pushed up oil prices and the fuels derived from it.

Prices for used petrol vehicles have also declined, though by much less, reflecting higher fuel supply from refineries. Diesel is priced at around 14pc more than petrol across UK forecourts.

Philip Gomm at the RAC Foundation said: “Thousands of people who are in the market for a second-hand diesel car will be doing back-of-the-envelope calculations to decide whether it’s time to change fuel type.

“Drivers are acutely aware of pump prices because it’s the only product we buy on a daily basis where the cost is displayed in front of us to a tenth of a penny.”

The cost of a tank of diesel may be nearing the point where the greater efficiency of diesel cars compared with petrol models was outweighed by the cost of the fuel, Mr Gomm said.

The improving availability of cheap electric vehicles may also hasten the retreat of diesel.

The RAC Foundation said that while private motorists could change fuel types, that was not the case for the owners of Britain’s fleet of 4.8 million diesel vans.

Mr Gomm said: “For the small businesses that rely on these vehicles, there aren’t practical alternatives. They are hostage to high diesel prices and so are their customers.”

data.title: The rise and fall of British helicopters
data.description:
Do you have a favourite helicopter? Mine, as a child, was Airwolf. But it could have been the helicopter that dropped Anneka Rice off at so many castles in the pioneering 1980s Channel 4 game-show Treasure Hunt, or the Blue Thunder choppers that ferry our elite SAS teams around Britain, tackling emergencies.

Today, in addition to their use by armed forces, they are status symbols for the 0.01 per cent. Donald Trump used to owned a fleet of three Sikorsky S-76 helicopters, with predictably gilded interiors. Yet not so long ago, some believed this form of transport would be used regularly by the hoi polloi; hopping into a chopper would be as common as hailing a black cab.

This month marks 40 years since the demise of British Airways Helicopters, and that brief moment in time when it seemed scheduled passenger helicopter services might actually catch on. So why did the helicopter never go truly mainstream?

Up in the Airlink

Focke-Wulf’s FW61 was unveiled in the 1930s, before Russian-American pioneer Igor Sikorsky took up the baton in the 1940s. The US company he founded would go on to dominate these machines’ development for half a century.

But passenger helicopter services actually began in the UK. The route? From Liverpool to Cardiff, launched by BEA in 1950, with an intriguing stop in Wrexham that would have suited Rob McElhenney and Ryan Reynolds if it were operating today.

More BEA routes followed, such as Birmingham to Northolt, and on to Heathrow. Birmingham got a pioneering “Rotorstation” for helicopters to land at. It was opened at Heybarnes Recreation Ground in Hay Mills – Peaky Blinders territory. Three flights left for London daily.

Between 1978 and 1986, a helicopter shuttle service, dubbed the Airlink, connected Gatwick and Heathrow. This was before the M25 was finished and when the journey between the two main London airports was tortuous. Helicopters ferried transit passengers from apron to apron in minutes.

A vision of the future

The thinking among many was that helicopters would be omnipresent. During the Festival of Britain, there was a helicopter landing pad on the Southbank in London. The Southbank was earmarked for a more permanent heliport, which explains the brutalist design of the Queen Elizabeth Hall. It was supposed to protect against the noise and vibrations of helicopters.

In the end a heliport at Battersea was opened, further along the River Thames, and is still in use today. Architects’ designs for Sixties new towns always showed two things: a monorail, and helicopters fluttering in the sky. This was the vision of the future – back when we believed in a future that would be better.

Even the GPO became enamoured with helicopters and trialled their use to deliver post to the rural towns of Norfolk. Quite what Farmer Giles, drinking a pint of warm Bullard’s outside The Railway Inn in Docking on a Sunday afternoon in 1948, would have made of the sight of a GPO Sikorsky S-51 on a post run to Wells-Next-The-Sea is anyone’s guess.

In the Fifties, Britain ramped up its own helicopter production at Westland’s Yeovil site, which became the home of the British helicopter. The Dragonfly, Widgeon, Whirlwind and Wessex became instantly recognisable machines built in Somerset. The Sea King, Wasp and Scout followed, then it was into the era of more modern machines like the Puma, Gazelle and Lynx.

Away with the Faireys

Among the more bizarre ideas was the Fairey Rotodyne: a hybrid between a plane and a helicopter that doesn’t look a million miles away from the stretched fuselage of the Chinook. In 1959 it flew from Heathrow to Paris via Dover and Brussels, but it wouldn’t catch on. One of the problems was the immense noise its rotors generated. This was going to be a problem when it was clattering over the roofs of densely populated areas of South London on the way to Battersea Heliport.

Westland took over Fairey in the 1960s, but domestic helicopter production was to become a hot political potato. Britain’s varied and incredibly successful aerospace entities were walking a tightrope between innovating, investing, exporting and balancing the books. Their designs were legendary, but of course not everything worked. There was always a tussle between nationalising everything into what would become British Aerospace and selling parts off to foreign investors.

Westland became a political football during the so-called Westland Affair in 1985, which pitted different factions of Margaret Thatcher’s Conservative government against each other, as arguments raged over whether to maintain this facility in Yeovil, who should run it and who would pay for it.

End of an era

Why did helicopters fade away? As with other futuristic transport ideas like hovertrains, monorails, hovercraft and other “gadgetbahns”, their relatively high cost and niggling technical problems could never be fully resolved.

Aeroplanes, trains and cars driving on motorways won the transport arms race because they could be easily scaled, and eventually mass uptake drastically reduced costs. These forms of transport made money rather than costing it.

Motorways connect us. With the M40 complete, there was no need to take a helicopter from Birmingham to London. Helicopters are also gas guzzlers – even Porsche owners would baulk at the price of a full tank. Sabena wanted to follow the Rotodyne’s first international flight and start a helicopter from London to Brussels – but Eurostar does that journey more efficiently.

In the US, where traffic is terrible and public transport is worse, Blade has put up a fight, offering relatively affordable flights from JFK to Manhattan, but without the drama of the former Pan Am helicopter, which whisked passengers to the top of the Pan Am HQ in Midtown in the 1960s.

Helicopters are still popular as niche forms of transport, and incredibly useful for medical evacuations, police and military use, and VIP transport. UK Air Sea Rescue has used helicopters to rescue the lives of countless sailors around our shores, and helicopters have ferried thousands of workers to oil and gas rigs in the North Sea and beyond, from Aberdeen, Norwich, Humberside and other hubs.

But their mass-market use has dwindled in the face of competition – which is sad, because they have a real value. The experience of being in one is not like regular flying because you’re so low you can see everything below you. The feeling of rising into the sky for the first time is surreal.

Rare survivors

The Scilly Isles are one of the rare examples of a route where helicopters make sense, and these flights have continued on and off from 1964 to this day. My honeymooning parents cannot have been the only holidaymakers caught out by rough seas who needed to use the helicopter as a way to swiftly get off the islands. For locals, they are a lifeline back to the shops, schools and health services of Penzance. This is now the last surviving scheduled British helicopter service.

Nice to Monaco and Saint-Tropez are other popular services going strong, as are Helity’s routes from Malaga and Algeciras to the headline-grabbing Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Hong Kong to Macau is another example. Faroese flag carrier Atlantic Airways runs domestic helicopter flights. But anyone who’s gone puffin-spotting in Mykines, and found themselves stuck on the island for days due to bad weather, will know that helicopters aren’t much use in storms or low visibility, which is pretty much every day in a Faroe Islands winter.

For the super-rich class there will always be helicopters ready to take them to the British Grand Prix or Goodwood (two of the biggest weekends for the Battersea Heliport). But for the rest of us, the dream of flying everywhere by helicopter is elusive. It’s not impossible though – this is why helicopter aficionados specifically head to Tresco or Tórshavn.

data.title: All aboard! Princess of Wales escorts elderly to lunch on minibus
data.description:
The Princess of Wales jumped aboard a community minibus to take elderly people who live alone to a village lunch club.

The Princess, who has spoken regularly about the importance of community, went door-to-door with volunteers from the West Sussex Minibus service.

Her first stop of the morning was the tidy bungalow of Stella Drewett, 94, a former school cook.

Mrs Drewett was told of her VIP guest shortly beforehand and said: “I couldn’t quite believe it. I am quite a new member.

“It’s a great service. I used to drive myself until I decided to spare the other road users. Everyone said to me: ‘But what are you going to do now?’

“But they take me to the supermarket once a week and we go down to the village hall for the lunch club. It’s a very valuable service. It’s wonderful.”

The Princess put a reassuring hand on Mrs Drewett’s arm as she manoeuvred her walking frame along the garden path and told her: “Well done.”

She then stood behind Mrs Drewett as she climbed on board the minibus, putting her hands against her back as a precaution.

When the Princess asked about her trips out for lunch, the 94-year-old quipped that they meant “one day of not cooking”.

The Princess took a seat next to Mrs Drewett and joked about always forgetting her handbag.

“Everyone always runs after me [shouting] ‘you forgot your handbag’,” she said.

Encouraging her to put her seatbelt on, the Princess added: “I have to remind my children to put their seatbelts on too.”

All the passengers, including the Princess, were taken to Pulborough village hall for lunch and other activities.

Inside the hall, the Princess sat down at a table with Lynda Jones, 75, and discussed the washing up.

“I love washing up. I really do,” she said.

“Oh good, a volunteer!” joked another guest.

Asked whether her husband, the Prince of Wales, helped, the Princess said: “He does the drying. We are a good double act. And we get the children involved.”

Examining the food on the table, the Princess noted there was a bowl of crisps.

“I bet you never eat crisps,” Mrs Jones teased her.

“I do. I love salted,” the Princess replied, eating one as they spoke.

Sarah Broadhurst, 87, stopped by to thank the Princess for coming to Pulborough and they held hands as they chatted.

“I think it’s amazing she has come to our little place. It can be isolating so it is lovely to have a royal visit,” she said.

Outside the village hall, a small crowd had gathered after word spread about the visit, which had been kept secret.

The Princess also stopped to speak to Thea Botley, 25, with her sons Albie, 1, and Arthur, 3.

Albie held the Princess’s hand to jump off the curb.

“Look at your cool boots!” the Princess told him. “Jump? Well done. One more? Well done.”

“Sorry I’ve started something,” she laughed as Albie continued to jump as she walked off.

The Princess also said hello to Beatrix, 3, and stroked the ears of three-year old cocker spaniel Jack, as she chatted.

The Princess, who has two cocker spaniels herself, asked her: “Is he cheeky? Does he steal your food? Whenever there is cereal on the floor our doggies always eat the cereal!”

The day out was part of the Princess’s commitment to encourage real-life connection.

West Sussex Minibus is a member of the Community Transport Association, described by Kensington Palace as a “vital lifeline for people who cannot easily access public transport due to isolation, mobility challenges or financial barriers”.

The minibus service boarded by the Princess on Wednesday celebrates 50 years of service this year. It’s an all-volunteer community transport organisation supporting people living in rural West Sussex.

Established in response to the decline of rural public transport, the organisation has grown from a single volunteer-led minibus into a community transport network operating from eight village hubs, supported by 284 volunteers and a fleet of 11 minibuses.

Its fleet travels approximately 60,000 miles each year, providing around 13,000 passenger journeys.

data.title: Lifeline flights to Scottish islands cut as jet fuel costs soar
data.description:
Scotland’s largest airline has cut flights to the Outer Hebrides and Shetland as rising jet fuel prices make the routes unprofitable.

Loganair said it will scrap up to 15pc of its schedule in its winter timetable after kerosene costs climbed more than 50pc above levels seen before the Iran war.

The routes affected include lifeline services to Stornoway on Lewis, Kirkwall in Orkney and Sumburgh on Shetland.

Loganair said it was conducting a review of its wider network and could not rule out further cuts without state support to keep otherwise non-viable flights going.

The cuts are already among the deepest imposed by carriers before the seasonal travel slump.

It comes as airlines brace for a hit to their profits from the full effect of higher oil prices. Most airlines had previously locked in more favourable fuel rates, with these deals now coming to an end.

EasyJet said on Thursday that it would trim its winter capacity by 1.4pc, or about 700,000 seats. Ryanair has reduced capacity by 4pc and warned that fuel prices could remain close to current levels throughout next year.

‘Cherry picking routes’

Ronnie Matheson, Loganair’s chief commercial officer, told the Scottish Parliament’s transport committee it was making a profit of just £4 per passenger.

He said: “This is about managing our costs and retaining financial sustainability through a tough winter period ahead.

“We have made the decision to trim a number of flights out of our network. This is a fairly normal practice for winter but this year we have stepped that number up.”

Mr Matheson said no location will lose flights entirely, although journey times to Edinburgh would be longer as some planes are forced to make multiple stops as a result of routes being combined.

He said: “We’ve tried to minimise cancellations and maintain a service to our island base as smooth as we possibly can.”

Willie Rennie, a Scottish Liberal Democrat Member of the Scottish Parliament (MSP), told Mr Matheson he was concerned that Loganair was “cherry picking routes”.

He added that since Loganair already receives state aid on some flights, it should subsidise other less-profitable routes.

He said: “If you take a route-by-route, almost day-by-day, consideration, then you are abdicating your responsibility for looking at the whole network.”

Loganair said legislation governing so-called Public Service Obligation flights recognised that airlines should still be able to make a profit after receiving state aid.

It came after Loganair said it would withdraw island flights from Inverness unless ministers stumped up additional funding.

Weekday flights were terminated in July, but will resume on Oct 26 after the Scottish National Party agreed to inject more than £1m.

However, Mr Matheson said the new money will run out in March, warning MSPs: “We don’t want to be in the same position again with flights being withdrawn.”

data.title: Channel 5 pays out £215m to US owner Paramount
data.description:
Channel 5’s US parent company Paramount has extracted £215m from the British broadcaster even as it suffered a sharp drop in profits.

The payout, which is among the largest in the channel’s history, was taken from retained earnings in Paramount’s first year under the leadership of David Ellison, the son of Oracle tycoon Larry Ellison.

It came despite Channel 5’s pre-tax profits slumping by two-thirds to £11.9m, while revenues fell 8pc to £292m, according to newly filed accounts.

The All Creatures Great and Small broadcaster blamed the decline on “challenging” conditions in the advertising market as brands continued to divert their spending away from traditional TV.

Channel 5’s travails underscore the challenge facing Mr Ellison, who closed an $8bn (£6bn) deal to take control of Paramount last summer.

He has since pulled off an even more audacious swoop on Warner Bros. The $110bn merger, which closed this week, is set to reshape Hollywood.

But the newly formed company, which has been rebranded Skydance, is already facing questions over eye-watering debt levels.

The company is heavily reliant on its declining linear television business to generate cash to service its debt.

As a result, bosses are also preparing at least $6bn in cost cuts in an effort to balance the books. The dividends suggest Mr Ellison will also squeeze subsidiaries for additional cash.

Channel 5 has previously handed significant dividends to its parent company, including a £740m payout in 2020.

Channel 5, which has an older audience than its rival public-service broadcasters, still attracts much of its viewing through traditional linear TV.

However, the channel has been investing heavily in its streaming service, which relaunched last year under the new brand name “5”.

Bosses said the investment had started to pay off as Channel 5’s streaming viewing rose by more than a third in 2025, outpacing the BBC, ITV and Channel 4.

The company was also boosted by a one-off gain of £19.1m after its investment in a subsidiary was transferred to another part of the Paramount group.

Paramount’s tie-up with Warner Bros, which owns CNN, TNT Sports and the eponymous film studios, has triggered concerns over media plurality and the effect on news provision in the UK.

Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, threatened to intervene in the deal, but ultimately waved it through after Paramount pledged to pump an extra £80m into Channel 5 over the next three years.

The cash will be used to fund news, original children’s programming and an additional 20 hours of drama programming each year.

Channel 5 spent more than £200m on programming last year as it splashed out on new dramas and rights for sports fixtures including the Fifa Club World Cup.

The tournament’s final between Chelsea and Paris St Germain delivered the channel’s biggest ever live sports audience, with a peak of 2.4 million on the main channel and 459,000 streaming it.

Channel 5, which appointed Reemah Sakaan as its new boss at the start of this year, recently struck a deal to shift its £300m advertising sales business from Sky to Channel 4.

Channel 4, which posted a deficit of £10m last year, is also struggling with a decline in the TV ad market and has outlined plans to cut around a quarter of its workforce in the biggest redundancy round in its four-decade history.

data.title: Giant solar farm approval is ‘wanton vandalism’, say locals
data.description:
Ministers have been accused of “wanton vandalism” after a massive new solar farm on prime Northamptonshire farmland was approved despite objections from thousands of residents.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, approved the Green Hill solar plant on Thursday. The site is roughly the size of Heathrow airport, covering 3,600 acres of prime arable land, including the solar arrays, batteries and landscaping.

The decision has triggered anger from residents who say the development will ruin the area.

Shena Howell, who co-leads the Stop Green Hill protest group, said on Friday that the scheme was “wanton vandalism” that would destroy food production and wreck the landscape.

“This solar plant will surround historic local villages like Grendon, a settlement mentioned in the Domesday Book of 1086, along with Easton Maudit and Mears Ashby. And it will take swathes of prime farmland out of production.”

Ms Howell, whose home village of Grendon will be at the heart of the development, said locals were still “reeling from the decision” to approve the farm, but were determined to keep fighting with options including a judicial review.

Martin Griffiths, a Reform councillor and the leader of North Northamptonshire council, said he was furious at the decision: “I am bitterly disappointed with the Secretary of State’s decision that will impact our rural communities for a generation.

“The industrialisation of our countryside is a national disgrace, and a future Reform government will follow Italy in banning ground-mounted solar panels on all agricultural land.”

The site, which is owned by Australian bank Macquarie, is highly controversial because it will take thousands of acres of prime arable farmland out of food production.

Public footpaths and bridleways running across the existing fields will remain, but will now run through corridors enclosed by security fencing and solar arrays rather than open countryside.

The solar plant will lie along a 20-mile-long strip of land between Northampton and Wellingborough.

The dozen or so landowners set to cash in on the scheme include Oxford University and Spencer Compton, the seventh Marquess of Northampton, whose inherited estate covers part of the area.

Island Green Power, the name of the Macquarie business which owns the Green Hill scheme, claims the plant will produce enough green electricity to power 200,000 homes on a sunny day.

However, residents in the area have objected to Ms Fahnbulleh’s decision to give Island Green powers of compulsory purchase.

It means Island Green can force landowners to give up their property to build the solar plant and lay cables.

Sarah Bool, the MP for South Northamptonshire, and Stuart Andrew, the MP for Daventry, joined locals to present a petition at 10 Downing Street opposing the scheme earlier this year.

UK government policy is that solar plant developments should avoid prime farmland, but this is only a recommendation and can be overruled by ministers.

In reality, the primary factor driving the way solar plant sites are chosen is proximity to substations that can offer a grid connection.

It means developers have drawn up maps of UK substations and are now targeting any land within a roughly 15-mile radius of a substation.

There is no national planning guidance controlling such schemes, resulting in clusters of giant solar farms close to substations in Lincolnshire, Northamptonshire and East Anglia.

Baroness Curran, the junior energy minister who approved the project on Ms Fahnbulleh’s behalf, said: “Solar power is crucial to delivering energy security for the country and financial security for communities, families and businesses.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Grid operator puts power stations on alert over electricity shortfall
data.description:
Britain’s grid operator has put power stations on alert to cover a potential energy shortfall as low winds weaken output from turbines.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) issued an electricity margin notice (EMN) early on Tuesday to ensure it meets demand later in the day.

An EMN sends a message to the electricity market that the operator would like a greater safety cushion, or margin, between power demand and supply for a limited period.

It does not signal that power cuts are imminent nor that there is not enough generation to meet demand.

Neso said on Tuesday it was expecting a system margin shortfall of 1,880 megawatts (MW) from 3pm to 11pm.

This was reduced to 321MW from 4pm to 11pm, and Neso later cancelled the notice on Tuesday evening.

A spokesman said: “The routine, precautionary notice was used to increase the margin between expected demand and available supply.”

However, Kathryn Porter, an energy analyst, said the notice had included an “unusually wide timeframe covering far more than just the evening peak”.

The notice came after forecasters predicted overnight that winds would be low on Tuesday, meaning output is expected to be around 40pc what was previously forecast.

The forecast for wind generation is 2,200MW at 6pm, according to market operator Elexon, which is a quarter of the average for this year.

A Neso spokesman said: “Neso has cancelled the electricity margin notice issued for this evening’s peak. 

“The routine, precautionary notice was used to increase the margin between expected demand and available supply. Demand was expected to be met throughout, with customer supplies not at risk.”

However, the warning underlines some of the challenges facing the Government as ministers switch to a power system based predominantly on intermittent wind and solar farms, with wind becoming the country’s single largest power source in 2024.

The energy operator issued several calls for additional energy supplies over the summer as Britain’s network grappled with a series of sweltering heatwaves and a rise in electricity usage from air conditioning units and fans.

Calm and cloudy weather conditions also triggered a drop in renewable energy supplies last month.

The UK entered a period of still and gloomy weather that causes renewable power generation to plummet.

Neso cancelled a notice that had been issued early last week after the potential margin shortfall was addressed by companies in the market.

Ms Porter added: “Typically, after an EMN is issued, the shortfall progressively reduces as generators make more generation available, grid maintenance is moved around and some demand reductions are found.”

data.title: BT’s TalkTalk rescue deal branded a ‘stitch-up’
data.description:
BT’s rivals have complained of a “stitch-up” after it secured a £400m takeover of TalkTalk to save it from collapse.

The FTSE 100 telecoms giant has bought the struggling broadband provider and its wholesale business out of administration, saving 900 jobs.

TalkTalk, which serves 2.5 million customers including tens of thousands of elderly and vulnerable people, had been seeking a buyer urgently as it struggled under the weight of a £1.4bn debt pile.

Allison Kirkby, BT’s chief executive, described TalkTalk’s near-collapse as a “genuinely unprecedented situation” and warned of “catastrophic” consequences if the company had been allowed to go under.

But BT’s swoop has triggered a furious response from rivals, who warned that the deal would cement the former state monopoly’s dominant position in the market and undermine competition.

A spokesman for Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) said: “This has all the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest.”

The deal follows an intervention by ministers, who have reserved the right to override competition rules given the risk to vulnerable customers if TalkTalk collapsed.

The Government is particularly concerned about the number of TalkTalk customers who use medical devices connected to Britain’s legacy copper network.

Security officials also raised concerns because TalkTalk connections support critical national infrastructure providers across health, emergency services, defence, education, transport, banking and government.

‘Genuine risk to life’

Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, used legal powers introduced during the pandemic that allowed the Government to intervene in mergers and acquisitions to maintain public health.

Ministers said there were also public-interest grounds to ensure continuity of supply of telecoms services.

TalkTalk faced rival bids from private equity, a rival broadband firm, and its lenders, but negotiations fell through.

Ms Nandy has directed the ​Competition and ‌Markets Authority (CMA) ​to report ​back ⁠by Oct ⁠19, after which she will make a decision on the deal.

The Culture Secretary said: “Phone and broadband services are vital national infrastructure. If TalkTalk services fail, there is a genuine risk to life and public services – including hospitals, schools and emergency care.

“These are unprecedented circumstances that require action now. That is why I am acting with urgency to ensure that impacts on public health, critical national infrastructure and supply to vulnerable customers are fully considered as part of this process.”

Ms Kirkby said the process would take up to six weeks and that customers would not be disrupted during that time.

She added: “Our immediate priority is to stabilise the business and provide a safety net for the households and businesses who rely on TalkTalk.”

‘Absolutely furious’

However, BT is gearing up for a fight with rivals who warned that allowing the telecoms giant to acquire TalkTalk’s wholesale network, PlatformX, and its 1.5 million retail customers would effectively re-establish it as a monopoly.

It came days after the CMA threatened to block VMO2’s £2bn takeover of broadband start-up Netomnia amid competition concerns.

Bonds tied to Virgin Media O2’s debts dropped to record lows on Monday after the CMA’s warning, with one note falling more than five cents in European trading to just over 70.3 cents.

VMO2 accused ministers of allowing BT to “roll its tanks over competition and further tighten its grip on the market”.

A spokesman added: “The logic simply doesn’t add up. We don’t believe rules should be thrown out the window to allow TalkTalk to fall into BT’s lap without a proper process, and we will be raising our concerns directly with Government and regulators.”

A source at one of Virgin Media O2’s shareholders said they were “absolutely furious”. Other broadband providers, including Vodafone and CityFibre, are also expected to raise concerns about the deal.

TalkTalk’s lenders had threatened to sue if BT was allowed to snap up the company, amid concerns about heavy losses.

Ares Management, the US private credit giant that has lent TalkTalk hundreds of millions of pounds, said on Monday that it supported the BT deal. As part of the transaction, Ares is understood to receive £100m. KKR, another of TalkTalk’s lenders, is in line to receive around £60m.

However, scores of other creditors are set to be wiped out, including a significant debt owed to BT’s network division, Openreach.

One creditor told The Telegraph they were “shocked but not surprised” that the Government had stepped in to clear the way for the deal.

They added: “There is no urgency any more: creditors like us will be wiped in the wash despite our impeccable behaviour and the Government is not going to help us.”

The rescue deal will leave TalkTalk debt-free. Overall, BT said the deal would hit its 2027 financial results with a £400m cash charge.

Ms Kirkby said the saga highlighted the “criticality” of broadband services to the UK’s safety and resilience and warned of the risk of further collapses among dozens of debt-laden broadband providers known as “alt-nets”.

She said: “It just shows that you really need to be looking at the fragility of some of these businesses, particularly the ones that have been loaded up with debt over the years.”

Ms Kirkby said she was ready to engage with the Government and regulator Ofcom on how to mitigate the risk of future insolvencies, including by establishing a supplier-of-last-resort regime similar to the energy sector.

Dame Melanie Dawes, Ofcom’s chief executive, said: “After a prolonged period of uncertainty around TalkTalk Group’s future, we welcome the prospect of a commercial solution that protects customers and secures continuity of critical communications services.”

data.title: Chinese imports ‘threaten to wipe out UK industries in five years’
data.description:
Cut-price Chinese manufacturers could wipe out whole chunks of British industry within five years, a think tank has warned.

Chatham House said European and UK industries ranging from electric vehicles and machine tools, to wind turbines and pharmaceuticals were “on a trajectory to lose” to China’s fast-growing and technologically dominant companies.

“There is a real possibility that over the next five years, Europe will lose much of its industrial base to Chinese competition,” said James Kynge, a Chatham House fellow and author of a new report on the economic threat from China.

“Not only will this result in the further loss of jobs and expertise; it may also mean the loss of companies with long histories of technological excellence and contributions to local communities.”

Mr Kynge said Chinese companies were winning because the country’s huge domestic market gave them greater economies of scale. China also boasted world-class universities, cutting-edge technological innovation and generous state subsidies.

He warned that British companies were losing market share to Chinese rivals not only at home in the UK, but also in China and in other countries where they competed.

“Chinese competitors are going global and rising to the forefront of global technology. That means that a UK business anywhere in the world is going to experience blowback from these uber-competitors coming out of China,” he said.

The soaring cost of energy is hindering British industry’s ability to compete and last week Britain’s biggest pharmaceutical companies warned of “a slow agony of decline” in the face of China’s growing dominance.

The Chatham House report found that in the pharmaceutical sector, China could rip through the clinical development of new drugs at three times the pace of Europe, for half the cost.

Mr Kynge said British and European pharmaceutical firms were now getting Chinese players to develop drugs for them. “They are outsourcing their brains to China. The collateral damage will be an atrophication of the UK’s own ability to innovate in drugs in the future,” he said.

The report also looked at China’s increasing takeover of industries such as wind turbines, machine tools and cars, where Europe until recently still held the upper hand.

The EU is reportedly about to launch new measures to protect its industries from cut-price Chinese imports. But Britain has remained more open to Chinese trade.

‘We need to do a reverse-China on China’

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, told The Telegraph this month that “if you put trade protections up, you’ve got to understand that they’ll probably be reciprocated and you’ll lose out”.

Britain had a £52.5bn deficit in its goods trade with China in the 12 months to the end of March. Goods exports to China declined 0.5pc to £18.5bn, while imports rose 2.4pc to £71bn.

Mr Kynge said the Government needed to reduce the regulatory burden and speed up bureaucratic processes to help British companies compete. Britain also needed to build more infrastructure, and increase the tech skills of its workforce.

Britain should welcome Chinese investment in non-sensitive sectors, he added, as long as the investors transferred technology, used local suppliers or hired and trained British workers.

“These were the conditions of entry for many of the European companies that went to China in the early days – you had to transfer technology. So we need to do a reverse-China on China,” he said.

data.title: Mortgage interest bills for home movers hit 17-year high
data.description:
Mortgage interest bills for home movers have hit a 17-year high as higher borrowing costs make it harder to move up the property ladder.

People who moved house in July spent 14.4pc of their income on mortgage interest, up from 13.5pc a year earlier and the highest proportion since November 2008, according to figures from UK Finance.

This was double the 7.8pc of their income they spent on mortgage interest four years ago.

The data track borrowers who have previously held a mortgage, which means they are not first-time buyers but are upsizing or downsizing.

Their average age was 41, suggesting they were primarily families moving house.

These buyers will also not benefit from Andy Burnham’s new Your First Home scheme, launched in an attempt to boost activity in the housing market.

Your First Home is focused on first-time buyers, offering them a 20pc government-backed equity loan when purchasing a new-build home.

Lucian Cook, of Savills estate agents, warned that “second-steppers” – people who are looking to move on from their first home – are having “real difficulty trading up the housing ladder”.

These buyers are facing not only rising mortgage costs, but have largely failed to accumulate any housing wealth, Mr Cook said, “particularly those who have been living in flats where actually they may have seen some of their equity eroded”.

Borrowing costs have soared because of the war in Iran, which has brought fears of a new wave of inflation.

Bank of England data last week showed rates on new mortgages climbed to 4.65pc in August, the highest level in nearly two years and almost triple the average 1.58pc rate at the start of 2022.

This has both increased the cost of moving and reduced homeowners’ ability to benefit from house price growth.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics show house prices fell by 3.3pc year-on-year in July.

Mr Cook said London was suffering the most as “people who bought flats as their first property who are probably going to be selling at a loss in a lot of circumstances”.

Including their capital repayments, home movers taking out new loans in July paid 21.2pc of their income on their mortgage bills, up from 17.8pc four years ago and also the highest level since 2008.

These buyers took out mortgages over record-high 26.7-year terms, up from 25.9 years in July 2022, to reduce their monthly costs.

Taking out loans for a longer period is a way to lower monthly repayments by spreading them out, but it means that borrowers will spend more money on interest overall.

The UK Finance figures also show home movers now make up a much smaller share of the mortgage market than they did historically.

In 2012, buyers who had previously held a mortgage made up 65pc of new loans. This has dropped to 45pc.

Bank of England data published last week showed mortgage approvals for home purchase dropped to 54,900, down from 55,900 in July and the lowest figure since December 2023.

data.title: Airlines banned from charging parents to sit next to their children
data.description:
Airlines will be banned from charging parents extra to sit with their children on flights.

The Government has proposed a set of rules requiring airlines to seat children under the age of 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge.

According to the Department for Transport, it can cost a parent up to £104 to arrange to sit next to their child on a return journey.

Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking to correct a mistake.

It is thought ministers will bring in the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays.

MPs are debating a new set of rules for travel companies as the Civil Aviation (Consumer Protection and Regulatory Reform) Bill makes its way through Parliament.

The proposed law will give ministers powers to draw up a list of passenger rights and a list of duties which both airlines and airports must undertake.

‘Giving people room to breathe’

Andy Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.

“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them.

“This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”

Rory Boland, the editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together.

“Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”

Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights.

The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children between two and 11 years old to pay to reserve what it referred to as a mandatory family seat. Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge.

The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority found.

At the time, Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair, said its previous policy was “the most progressive and transparent in Europe”.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the Government, airlines and trade unions working on a system to share information about disruptive passengers.

Airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, government figures show, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted.

Using the information-sharing system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.

“Everyone deserves to travel knowing their flight isn’t going to be disrupted by bad behaviour from a small minority,” Ms Alexander said.

“These common-sense reforms will make flying safer for staff and passengers and protect people from unnecessary charges, whoever they fly with.”

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Putin has ordered ‘General Armageddon’ to smash the bridges of Kyiv. This is why
data.description:
As winter approaches, Vladimir Putin is resorting to the one weapon he has consistently used when his armies fail on the battlefield: terrorising civilians and smashing cities. He has just brought in General Sergei Surovikin – aka “General Armageddon” who flattened the Syrian city of Aleppo, killing thousands of civilians in the process – to do the same to Kyiv.

Putin needs something to change in Ukraine, as the Russian offensive in the Donbas has been in serious trouble for months. Ukrainian forces are pushing back around Pokrovsk and Lyman, while Russian casualties remain extraordinary. President Volodymyr Zelensky has claimed that more than 10,000 Russian soldiers were killed in a single week.

Whether that precise figure is ultimately verified or not, there is no doubt that Putin is paying a staggering price for very limited territorial gains. And now he is running short of men: it is getting difficult to recruit enough volunteer “kontraktniki” contract soldiers to replace the losses.

In theory, Putin could simply launch a mobilisation, which would yield huge numbers of new troops. But the Kremlin knows that another major mobilisation, potentially involving hundreds of thousands of Russians, could be politically explosive. The dictator therefore needs a dramatic change in the military equation before he is forced into a decision that could threaten his grip on power.

His answer is becoming increasingly obvious: if Russia cannot defeat Ukraine’s army, it will try to break the Ukrainian people and nation this winter. This is not a new tactic. Putin supported Bashar al-Assad’s brutal campaign in Syria, where I saw first hand what happened when hospitals, schools and civilian areas became targets for Russian firepower.

The calculation was simple: kill, wound and brutalise enough civilians – make their lives dangerous and horrible enough – and eventually they will demand that their own government ends the war. It failed in Syria. It is likely to fail in Ukraine too.

Kyiv is now under almost relentless attack. There were 18 air raid alerts in the capital on Tuesday alone. Russian missiles and drones are striking deep into the city, damaging civilian infrastructure and even hitting the National Academy of Sciences.

The seven bridges across the Dnipro are obvious targets. Kyiv, like most capital cities, is a major road and rail nexus. If it can be cut in half, that has a paralysing effect on the whole of northern Ukraine: imagine the effect on south eastern England if every bridge in London (including those on the M25) were down.

This is not the behaviour of a man preparing to end his war. It is the behaviour of a dictator preparing his population for a longer one.

The danger is that Putin has identified a vulnerability. Ukraine’s stocks of air-defence munitions are under enormous pressure. High-end interceptor missiles such as the US Patriot are in particularly short supply. Moscow knows this. It is therefore adapting its tactics, moving beyond military targets and increasingly seeking to cripple the infrastructure that allows Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities to function.

This is precisely why the West must understand what Putin is attempting before it is too late. His calculation has always been brutally simple: can Russia outlast its opponent? Putin believes it can.

He has shown an extraordinary willingness to sacrifice Russian soldiers. To the Kremlin, human life is a cheap commodity. Russia has a far larger population than Ukraine and has progressively placed its economy on a war footing. Putin therefore believes that Russia can absorb casualties for longer than Ukraine can stand the punishment and, crucially, for longer than Western governments can maintain public and political support.

That last is the real battle. The question is not simply whether Ukraine can hold Pokrovsk or Lyman. It is whether Britain and Europe have the political stamina to ensure that Ukraine is still standing next year, and the year after that.

I am not convinced that our Government fully understands this. The Prime Minister has explicitly stated that, to him, social security is more important than national security. His priorities are upside down. You cannot deliver social security if you are not secure as a nation.

The West must dramatically increase supplies of air-defence missiles, radars, drones and electronic-warfare systems. But we should also be prepared to consider measures that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago.

If Russia deliberately targets civilian infrastructure on an industrial scale, Nato must consider how its overwhelming air power could be used to protect Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure without directly entering the war. That does not necessarily mean declaring a traditional no-fly zone tomorrow. It means seriously examining whether Nato aircraft could help defend defined areas or critical infrastructure in extremis, particularly where the alternative is allowing Russian missiles and drones to slaughter civilians with impunity.

The Geneva Conventions are clear: the proper laws of war – not overblown human rights rules, but the regular laws of war – forbid deliberate targeting of civilians without any military purpose. Just when Ukraine appears to be gaining momentum on the battlefield, Putin is attempting to move the war on to ground where he believes Russia has the advantage: a test of civilian endurance.

We must not let him.

Ukraine’s army is fighting back in the Donbas. Its soldiers are inflicting enormous losses on the Russian military. This is precisely the moment when the West should be leaning forward, not stepping back. Putin understands strength, but understands weakness even better.

If we allow him to discover that bombing Kyiv works, he will do more of it. If, instead, Britain and Europe demonstrate that Ukraine’s cities will be defended, its people will be supported and its army will be supplied for as long as necessary, Putin may finally understand the one thing he has so far refused to accept: Russia cannot bomb and meat-grind its way to victory.

data.title: Boots sold for £7bn to family behind Primark
data.description:
Boots has been sold to the billionaire family behind Primark for nearly £7bn.

The high street pharmacist, which was founded in 1849, has been bought by the Canadian arm of the Weston family, Wittington Investments, for $8.9bn (£6.7bn).

The deal comes just a year after the private equity firm Sycamore bought Walgreens Boots Alliance, for $24bn.

Galen Weston, the chairman of Wittington, who will become chairman of the high street chain, said: “Boots is one of Britain’s most enduring businesses, with a rich heritage, a trusted name and a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland.”

The Westons, a Canadian business dynasty, are one of the world’s richest families.

The Canadian branch of the family, which will take control of Boots, owns Loblaw, the country’s largest supermarket. The UK arm of the family, meanwhile, owns brands including Fortnum & Mason and Primark-owner Associated British Foods.

Under the terms of the deal, Wittington will acquire Boots’s retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. Boots has 1,800 stores across the UK.

Sycamore and the Italian billionaire Stefano Pessina, who originally helped take Boots private in 2007, will retain ownership of the Boots Group’s other operations, Farmacias Benavides in Mexico and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland in Germany.

The deal is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027.

Boots was sold to Mr Pessina and the private equity firm KKR in 2007 in an £11.1bn deal.

At the time, it was Europe’s biggest leveraged buyout and the first instance of one of Britain’s leading listed companies being taken over by private equity.

Walgreens later bought the group in 2014 before Sycamore Partners took the chain private again last year.

Along with the Westons, the Canadian business Fairfax Financial, run by billionaire Prem Watsa, will take a 50pc stake in Boots as part of the deal.

Alex Baldock, chief executive of Boots, said: “Boots matters. Every day, our colleagues give millions of people longer, healthier and happier lives.

“Those customers and patients trust in Boots’ unmatched authority, capability and leadership across health, wellness and beauty. I’ve seen enough already of our colleagues’ passion and expertise to understand why they do.”

Mr Baldock, who is expected to stay on as chief executive, was recruited as Boots’s new boss from electricals retailer Currys only a month ago.

The retail executive has a reputation for steering turnarounds and is seen by analysts as key to bringing new focus to the sprawling Boots business.

Boots, which employs more than 51,000 people, was founded in Nottingham in 1849 by John Boot, originally as a seller of herbal remedies.

His son Jesse Boot led the expansion of the company, and by 1933 there were 1,000 stores across the UK. Its cosmetics brand No7 was launched two years later.

The various branches of the Weston family are all descended from George Weston, the Toronto tycoon.

The Canadian branch, headed by his great-grandson Galen Weston Jr, operates more than 200 companies. The Canadian Westons also previously owned the department store Selfridges until 2022.

The separate UK offshoot of the family is led by another great-grandson and Galen’s cousin, the British businessman George Garfield Weston.

The British branch of the Westons owns a majority stake in Primark’s parent company. It has been exploring a listing of the budget clothing retailer.

Mr Pessina, an Italian entrepreneur, has been involved with Boots for 20 years, helping to take the business private in 2007.

data.title: ‘Unfair’ warehouse tax will hurt retailers, Tesco says
data.description:
The boss of Tesco has urged John Healey to exclude retailers from “fundamentally unfair” plans to mount a tax raid on large warehouses in the Budget.

Ken Murphy, the chief executive of Tesco, said the current business rate regime had already left the retail sector paying four times more than it should given its size within the overall economy.

Asked on Thursday about the prospect of higher rates on warehouses, Mr Murphy said: “The business rates system is fundamentally unfair.

“Retailers are paying four times more than their fair share of rates and I would urge the Government for more equitable rates.”

He also called for an “exemption for all retail businesses from the new rateable value threshold”.

Mr Murphy said high street retailers should not have to pay a higher business rate multiplier on larger warehouses with a rateable value of more than £500,000.

Rachel Reeves introduced a higher rate surcharge for larger commercial properties in last year’s Budget. It came into force in April.

Andy Burnham has since signalled this so-called “Amazon tax” could be ramped up further on warehouses in the upcoming Budget.

This would help fund an announced 20pc rate cut for smaller businesses that “bring social benefit”, such as pubs and live music venues from next April.

However, retail bosses have warned the new rates could be passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices as high street supermarkets, rather than online retailers, occupy the majority of warehouse space.

Mr Murphy said: “We genuinely believe rates need to be reformed and we urge the Government to exempt retailers from the threshold put in place last year.”

Mr Murphy would not be drawn on whether an increase in rates would be passed on to Tesco shoppers.

However, last month James Bielby, the chief executive of Food and Drink Wholesale UK, told The Telegraph: “It’s very simple. If they put it on, it’s going to be passed on.”

Analysis by the consultancy firm Ryan showed that the 10 warehouses with the biggest business rates bills in the country are owned by Lidl, Tesco, John Lewis, Sainsbury’s and Marks & Spencer.

Mr Murphy’s comments came as Tesco increased its profit guidance on Thursday, with the retailer telling investors it expected to make between £3.15bn and £3.3bn in the year to February. In April it projected a range of £3bn to £3.3bn.

Like-for-like UK sales rose 1.5pc in the first six months of the financial year to the end of August, while for the group as a whole they were 1pc higher.

Operating profits climbed by 6.6pc to £1.7bn.

Mr Murphy also said he expected a less boozy Christmas than in previous years, with more sales of “low and no” alcohol drinks reflecting a trend towards healthier eating and drinking.

He said there has been a “general trend towards” healthier eating that dates back to the pandemic. Shoppers are also looking for meals with higher levels of fibre and protein, and smaller portion sizes.
