data.title: BT’s TalkTalk takeover is an omnishambles
data.description:
On the face of it, BT’s lightning swoop on TalkTalk during the weekend was a highly welcome last-minute intervention. The need to preserve the broadband services of millions of households and businesses was obviously critical.

TalkTalk’s incompetent board and an army of overpaid advisers had wasted months desperately trying to cobble together a convoluted rescue deal that seemed doomed from the very start.

As a long list of supposed “buyers” came and went, TalkTalk’s problems became more life-threatening until it was eventually just days away from collapse, without any safety net to ensure its customers remained connected.

These include tens of thousands of vulnerable elderly people who use medical telecare devices connected to Britain’s legacy copper network.

Somebody clearly had to step in to save the company from itself and those who so recklessly ran TalkTalk aground – primarily Sir Charles Dunstone, the founder, and his backers, private credit giant Ares and City investor Toscafund.

That the company lives on is where the good news abruptly ends. On every other measure, the TalkTalk saga is a complete omnishambles for all concerned.

Allison Kirkby, the BT boss, won’t believe her luck. Britain’s national telecoms champion has managed to pick up the carcass of the country’s fourth-largest broadband provider for next-to-nothing, shorn of its debts, and from under the noses of the rest of the market too – all aided and abetted by dozy ministers and a supine competition policeman.

No wonder BT’s rivals are spitting feathers. A former state monopoly that already has a vice-like grip on more than 30pc of the residential broadband market, and a scarcely believable two thirds of the wholesale broadband market, has been handed a further 2.5 million customers, including one million households on a plate.

The Government’s somewhat unconvincing argument for this obvious aberration is that ministers reserve the right to override competition rules because of the “unprecedented” nature of the situation and the risk to vulnerable customers if TalkTalk had been allowed to completely implode.

Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, has even invoked the powers granted to her by the Enterprise Act 2002 – which gives her the right to wave away competition concerns – to intervene, allowing BT to step in.

With the Competition and ‌Markets Authority given just a fortnight to report back to ⁠her, one suspects it is practically nailed on that Nandy will give the deal the Government’s official blessing.

So while we are meant to believe there will be a proper “regulatory review”, one suspects the outcome has as good as already been determined.

As Virgin Media says, this has “all the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest” with the rules “thrown out the window to allow TalkTalk to fall into BT’s lap”.

It is tempting to dismiss such concerns as a case of sour grapes from an arch rival who would have done exactly the same had it received the same tap on the shoulder from panicked government officials.

But Virgin’s main complaint – and an entirely legitimate one at that – is what it calls the complete absence of “a proper process”.

What ministers and regulators must explain is why BT was offered the opportunity to ride to the rescue on such favourable terms, yet not Vodafone or indeed Virgin.

It’s a less bad outcome than TalkTalk vanishing off the face of the earth, as it came very close to doing so. But of all the alternative scenarios, a deal that allows BT to emerge more powerful than before is a disaster in a world where deregulation was meant to put the rocket boosters under competition.

As Uswitch rightly says, your broadband and landline might carry on as normal, but BT must quickly explain “what this means for contracts, prices and service in the future”. It’s certainly hard to believe customers will end up with a better deal.

One could also argue the entire “alt-net” experiment – in which scores of plucky start-ups nibble away at the domination of a handful of major players, led by BT’s Openreach arm – is effectively over too.

It was already looking increasingly shaky as the sheer economics of building alternative networks from scratch proved insurmountable for new entrants. This, despite the billions of pounds of capital that have been poured into the alt-net market.

TalkTalk, together with its PXC wholesale arm, was what the industry calls a “multi-network customer” that directed its traffic to alternative providers, such as CityFibre. BT, on the other hand, has tended to favour Openreach for obvious reasons.

Investor appetite for pumping more money into the challenger broadband infrastructure sector has already been dented by the number of failures, so it’s probably fair to assume it will wane further now.

This rushed rescue deal also exposes the dreadful limitations at the heart of telecoms regulation.

There are obvious parallels with the energy market, insofar as TalkTalk was one of many constructs that emerged when the telecoms industry was opened up to competition.

Similarly, scores of upstart energy suppliers popped up when Ofgem set out to break the stranglehold of the Big Six more than a decade ago.

But the difference with the energy market is that it is propped up by a supplier-of-last-resort regime that ensures your gas and electricity stay on. It’s fairly straightforward too: either through a competitive process or direct instruction, Ofgem chooses a healthy replacement company that takes on the customers of the bust provider.

It’s been tested numerous times, most of all when scores of tiddlers gave up the ghost during the post-pandemic energy shock. There’s also a special administration regime that exists for systemic collapses, which proved effective when Bulb went under.

The absence of one for telecoms poses a massive strategic question for the Government. The telecoms network is clearly part of Britain’s critical infrastructure, increasingly so as the world becomes more digital. Why then have parts of it been allowed to end up in the hands of debt-laden players like TalkTalk? When will ministers start to take national resilience more seriously?

It is a mess of epic proportions, and that’s before you get to the real problem, which is why TalkTalk was ever allowed to reach the brink of collapse in the first place.

Even now, it’s hard to understand why Sir Charles, Ares and Toscafund took it private in 2021.

With the company’s share price suffering a massive, prolonged decline in the years leading up to the takeover, the impression is of a handful of dominant shareholders desperately chasing their losses.

But the cost of servicing the eye-watering debts that were piled onto the company initially, and through repeated refinancings, meant it was only ever going to end in tears.

Ares is meant to be a sophisticated Wall Street investor. What on earth was it thinking?

As for Sir Charles, his reputation as one of the UK’s top entrepreneurs will do well to survive a deal that has wiped out the bulk of TalkTalk’s creditors and required ministerial intervention. TalkTalk will be remembered as one of the great corporate car crashes of our times.

data.title: Banks brace for a punishment beating from Healey
data.description:
Sign up here for more exclusive insight from Jeremy Warner in our Economic Intelligence newsletter, delivered direct to your inbox every Thursday.

Come back Rachel Reeves, all is forgiven. There is a growing sense of resignation among bank bosses to the imposition of a higher banking surcharge in the forthcoming Budget.

They thought they’d dodged that particular bullet after convincing Reeves, the former chancellor, that it would damage growth and therefore be a counterproductive way of patching up the public finances.

But there has been no such reassurance under John Healey, her successor.

He was completely inscrutable at a meeting with leading bankers this week, leading one to conclude: “It’s pretty much a done deal. I suppose we’ve just got to suck it up.”

Merely returning the surcharge to its previous level of 8pc would raise £9bn across four years, according to trade-union analysis, while increasing it to 16pc might deliver a hefty £20bn over the same time frame.

Oh dear. I know the Chancellor is desperate for anything that might help relieve the pressure on the fiscal arithmetic from rising interest rates, but I really do wish people would stop making such formulaic assumptions about the supposed milch cow attributes of the City.

It is as if finance’s only purpose is that of supporting the leviathan of Labour’s welfare state. No, the social purpose of banking is not to fund overblown public spending but to put depositors’ money to good use by supporting growth in the wider economy.

Worse, Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, seems to think that the “Big Bang” reforms of the 1980s – which gave us the great wealth-creating dynamo of today’s City – are where everything went wrong for the UK.

Some time before New Labour’s landslide election victory of 1997, I had an eye-opening lunch with Alistair Darling, then Labour’s City spokesman, later to become chancellor.

The City, he told me, was not something to be demonised, which was the traditional Left-of-centre view, but a precious national resource which needed to be nurtured and encouraged as an economic powerhouse for the future.

I was somewhat taken aback by his remarks, which were a clear departure from the old Labour view, and they helped convince me that the party had indeed changed sufficiently to make it electable again.

In the event, Labour’s free pass to finance arguably went too far, culminating in the economic catastrophe of the financial crisis.

Banking has been on the naughty step more or less ever since. On one level, it is indeed entirely reasonable that the Government should seek to recoup at least some of the tens of billions it spent bailing the banking system out with somewhat higher rates of taxation than it imposes on corporate profits more widely.

Besides, thanks to much higher interest rates, banks are again generating positively avaricious levels of profit, helped by a widening in the net interest margin (NIM) – the difference between the interest earned on lending and that paid to depositors.

What’s more, at least some part of this profits bonanza comes directly from the taxpayer as a result of the interest paid on the central bank reserves created by more than a decade of quantitative easing.

Under an indemnity, the Treasury must reimburse the Bank of England for any losses sustained on this monetary voodoo. In recent years, these have been substantial, resulting in a transfer from taxpayers to the commercial banking sector worth tens of billions.

Healey has been toying with reform of the arrangement as an alternative to raising the surcharge on banking profits, but I’d be surprised if he went that way. Not least because it’s a flagship policy of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. Labour won’t want to give Farage any quarter whatsoever.

In any event, the banking crisis was a long time ago now, and the time for punishment beatings is over. Today’s economic challenges are nothing to do with the banks and the wider City.

Rather they are down to the Government’s inability to control its spending. Treating finance as a piggy bank may help temporarily plug the gap, but it is entirely alien to the growth agenda the country so urgently needs.

While the politicians yo-yo, constantly chopping and changing their policies, finance has become a rock of stability in an increasingly uncertain world and one of the few dependable engines of growth.

Beneath the radar, banks have been steadily expanding their lending to the wider economy, providing both households and small and medium-sized businesses with the sustenance that the Government has failed to provide. To interfere with this happy disposition by whacking up their taxes would be a desperately anti-growth initiative.

It’s all very well saying that the banks can afford it, that to them the sums involved are no more than a rounding error, but that’s not the way it works in the real world.

Stinging the banks for more in taxes is far from being the risk-free move Labour ministers fondly believe. Arithmetically, more tax equals less credit. It’s as simple as that.

A strong economy needs strong banks, and strong banks in turn need predictability in regulation, tax and government. Sadly, we are seeing it in none of these things.

Already, US-based banks are reaping a substantial competitive dividend from the lower capital and regulatory requirements that the Trump administration imposes on them.

It’s the same on tax. According to analysis by PwC, London-based banks already pay a marginal rate of 46.4pc once everything is taken into account, including standard corporation tax, levies, surcharges, irrecoverable VAT and uncapped employer National Insurance contributions. The read-across to a New York-based bank is just 27.9pc, 42.2pc in Amsterdam, 38.9pc in Frankfurt and 28.9pc in Dublin.

Restoring the 8pc surcharge would push the marginal rate on London profits to well in excess of 50pc.

And tax is just half of it; the burden of precautionary, safety-first regulation also keeps rising.

There comes a tipping point where all these concerns converge into a sudden loss of competitiveness that eclipses all the other supposed advantages London is meant to have as a home for international finance.

Most vocal in his warnings of the likely consequences has been Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan Chase.

He’s presumably going to have to go through with his threats if Healey acts. For JP Morgan, banking more business in Frankfurt, Paris, Milan and elsewhere in Europe is easily done.

During my time as a business journalist, I’ve seen astonishing change in finance and the City. Britain has managed brilliantly to ride this boom. It’s the sort of prize that other jurisdictions would almost quite literally kill for.

Yet we have a Government that speaks the language of growth but doesn’t seem to understand the first thing about it.

Turning the clock back to the world as it was before the boom began, as Burnham wants, may have some nostalgic appeal, but it won’t solve any of Britain’s problems.

data.title: Britain fires up gas power stations as wind power fails to deliver
data.description:
Britain will step up generation at its gas power stations as calm and cloudy weather conditions trigger a drop in renewable energy supplies.

In a notice issued late last night, the National Energy System Operator (Neso), which manages Britain’s electricity grid, said it had told power plants to notify it of any extra megawatt capacity.

The energy operator warned that electricity supplies may be tight on Monday evening but it did not signal that Britain was at risk of imminent blackouts.

Neso’s warning comes as the UK enters a period of “dunkelflaute” conditions, the German term for still and gloomy weather that causes renewable power generation to plummet.

Figures showed that just 16pc of the UK’s electricity was generated by wind at noon on Monday, while 58pc was being produced by gas.

Kathryn Porter, an independent energy analyst, said that a period of “low wind, low solar” was contributing to the latest warning from Neso, as well as higher energy demand in the evening as the nights begin to draw in.

The energy operator’s call for additional supplies, known as an electricity margin notice, was released at 11.30pm on Sunday.

Neso said supplies were expected to be particularly tight between 4pm and 7pm on Monday and warned that a “maximum generation service may be instructed”.

This is when it calls on power plants to exceed their usual energy generation limits for a short time to increase supplies. It does not signal that blackouts are imminent or that there is not enough generation to meet current demand.

Neso also called on neighbouring countries to send additional energy and questioned whether British suppliers could take steps to reduce demand.

The energy operator issued several calls for additional energy supplies over the summer as Britain’s network grappled with a series of sweltering heatwaves and a rise in electricity usage from air conditioning units and fans.

The latest warning came as a new report from Ms Porter warns that Britain is “increasingly depending on electricity imports” when renewable energy generation falls.

The report warned that this created a “material risk to security of supply”, especially as neighbouring countries such as Norway and France often experience similar weather conditions to the UK.

The energy operator later said it had cancelled the warning after receiving additional energy capacity from suppliers. 

A spokesman for Neso said: “Market participants have successfully restored the operating margin required for this evening’s peak period. The system is operating as normal and Great Britain’s electricity supplies remain secure.”

The Department for Net Zero and Energy Security was contacted for comment.

data.title: I travelled the ‘border’ between North and South. Here’s what I learnt
data.description:
A sign by the estuary warns of danger, but it’s hard to see much to be afraid of here apart from the nettles and a fairly ominous sky. Under the Severn Bridge, on a spit of land on the river’s west side, it seems peaceful enough. Traffic roars overhead, but you can’t see the cars from below. There’s birdsong and the smell of wet foliage, glimmering water fringed by sodden sand and then cracked earth. It doesn’t feel like a border, but I’m standing at the far western end of England’s North-South divide.

There is, of course, no official line across England’s midriff. No razor-wire fences or passport checks mark where the South ends and the North begins. But nor is the boundary a figment of our imagination. We’ve heard enough jokes about the Watford Gap to know that Southerners see the North – the people, the places, the culture – as somehow different. And we Northerners, admittedly, can be bloody-minded about our Northern identity.

But how entrenched does the North-South divide remain today, after years of political talk of levelling up, Northern powerhouses and ill-fated high-speed rail connections? How much does our geography still shape how we see those from elsewhere in the country? And where, actually, does the notional dividing line start and end?

Apparently, not where you might expect. Recent YouGov data from almost 46,000 adults in England revealed that many people along the borders of the areas classified as North, South and Midlands don’t place themselves in the same regions government maps would suggest. Feelings of “Northernness” extended south of the regional borders, the pollsters found, while in the parts of East Anglia that supposedly sit in the South, people don’t all feel Southern. In short, like many types of identity, it’s complicated.

With that in mind, I have set out to travel along an unofficial boundary line between the North and South of England – one commonly used in academic research – to interrogate these feelings and explore what the divide means today. My editor has suggested I walk the entire 340 miles from Beachley Point on the Severn estuary to the Wash, between Lincolnshire and Norfolk, possibly in one go. I have counter-suggested the use of a motor vehicle.

The journey is a personal one. Having grown up in Leeds, my Northern identity is one I have insisted on throughout my adult life (which I’ve spent mostly in the South). When I started writing my debut crime thriller novel, The House on Otley Road, I knew it had to be set in West Yorkshire. Home.

The tug of the North has never left me, and I spend much of my time on the East Coast Main Line, travelling to and from where I spent my youth. But I’m surprised to find that it supposedly begins more or less where I’m standing by the Severn. The first (and only) person I encounter on the footpath here is Justin Charnock, 37. He identifies as Southern (this is fair – he comes from near Bristol) and thinks “people in the North are a lot nicer than people in the South” (also fair). “More welcoming,” he says.

It’s a commonly held perception, mentioned frequently by those I meet on my journey – almost all of whom have strong ideas about how Northerners differ from Southerners.

Charnock thinks being Southern traditionally means being “wealthier; a lot more aloof; snobby; much less hospitable, welcoming, friendly or helpful”. Working in the South West (he won’t divulge his job), he never gets tipped and “often people are a bit snooty”.

‘It’s become very middle class here’

Behind the popular images of Northerners lie some dispiriting numbers. The North East remains the region with the lowest healthy life expectancy at birth (HLE), at 57 years, according to the most recent figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It has had the lowest HLE in every period since the ONS began measuring it. The South East remains the region with the highest HLE (63 years for men, 64.3 years for women).

A similar disparity can be seen in economic activity. In 2023, London had the highest gross domestic product per capita, at £69,077, while the North East had the lowest, at £28,583. It is worth noting, though, that the poverty rate is higher in London (26 per cent) than anywhere else in the country, according to figures from the charity Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

Meanwhile, perceptions of Northerners and Southerners that seem to stem from our economic histories – the North as industrial, the South as the country’s financial engine – have stubbornly persisted.

The first stop on my journey is Brockweir, a scenic Gloucestershire village on the river Wye. Old stone houses are painted in creamy yellow, pale blue and white, while green hills rise behind them. All the villagers seem to know each other. They all have dogs, and their dogs know each other too. The community owns its pub, the 16th-century Brockweir Inn.

“We tried to sell our bodies [to raise the money for it], but we’re all too old,” says Carol Knight, 76. (I think she’s joking.)

Her family has lived here for centuries. “It’s become very middle class,” says the suntanned, denim-dungaree-clad former English teacher, while clutching a bunch of Whitsuntide boss flowers and the leads of her two labradors. “Property prices have skyrocketed.”

Does this mean Brockweir must be Southern? House prices are, after all, a stark divider between North and South. Prices may be rising more steeply in the North at present, but the gap remains vast, even after removing London from the equation: in March 2026, the average house price across the South East and South West was £340,000, compared with £188,500 across the North East and North West.

‘We need more Northern leaders’

I travel onwards, trying to keep close to the Wye, down winding lanes bordered by verdant hedgerows and cow parsley. I stop at Upper Redbrook, where I can’t find a pub, or a shop, or a human, then Staunton, where the 18th-century pub isn’t open yet (it’s still too early). Traffic rattles through the village of silent modern houses.

In the Herefordshire village of Lea, I encounter a friendly pair of Scousers who decamped here long ago. Mike Tyson, a 46-year-old roofer and carpenter (“Yes, it’s my real name,” he says, for probably the millionth time), talks of his daughter’s “Northern attitude”.

What is it? “Friendlier, more easy-come, easy-go. ‘Chippy’ is the right phrase.”

The men are not the only ones to claim Northerners have a different (better?) sense of humour. But there’s uncertainty about whether we’re in the North or the South here – the consensus seems to be the middle – but Tyson believes there’s more money to be made down here than up in Liverpool.

Tied up with the question of economic activity and affluence is that of political power. Devolution to England’s cities and regions has given some control to communities far from Westminster. Whether it has helped those communities feel less overlooked is uncertain. Phil Henesey, 71, who is drinking in a beer garden with Tyson in the late-afternoon sunshine, says the North still feels farther (figuratively) from Westminster decision making.

“That’s why we need more Northern leaders,” he says.

He is speaking not long before the enthroning of a Northern leader in Downing Street. Andy Burnham, the Liverpool-born former Mayor of Greater Manchester, has made much of his links to, and concern for, the North of England. The new PM has created a No 10 North. In doing so, he has set himself up to be judged on how successfully he makes Northerners feel more connected to the centre of power. Also on how he does this without alienating the South.

‘There’s more chivalry in the North’

It’s raining when I reach Ledbury, the sky a grey-white sheet. The Tudor buildings are picture-perfect and well preserved. “It’s very much Middle England,” says a shopkeeper on the high street who doesn’t want to be named. “Did you ever see Keeping up Appearances? It’s full of Hyacinth Buckets [here].”

He identifies as a Southerner. “When you go up North, it’s dark,” he says. “It’s a funny old thing, that divide.”

Declan Butler, a 68-year-old Irishman who moved to Britain in the 1970s and now runs a gift shop down the road, thinks Ledbury is “probably more Southern”, judging by its disposable income.

“I had a couple in here from North Yorkshire at the weekend and they spoke to me as if we were old friends, whereas people from the South East are much more reserved,” he says. “If I was to choose a Southerner or a Northerner to be friends with, I’d choose a Northerner, because they’re friendlier. They’re probably harder workers. They’re grafters.”

He concedes that Cockneys and people from Essex can be friendly, too. Has he been to the North much? “I’ve been to Birmingham,” he offers.

Crossing into Worcestershire, I see the grey-blue shadow of the hills rise up ahead. I pass an old roadside chapel and an abandoned filling station, and arrive at Bredon, where the local Spar sells cider on tap.

“I thought the North started at Crewe,” muses Steve Fowler, an ex-Army man, inside the still-quiet Royal Oak pub, where there’s horse racing on the TV. He’s surprised to hear that by some definitions he is in the North right now. A Southerner by birth (Surrey), he awards the North another point for humour. “The funniest comedians are Northerners,” he says.

“I think [people] are more materialistic in the South,” says David Gray, a semi-retired gardener from Scotland. “There’s a lot more chivalry in the North.”

“It’s all about survival in the North,” chips in Paul Sefton, a retired butcher. He came here from North Wales 30 years ago “purely because someone said to me my kids would never get a proper job up North”.

‘The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties’

The North-South divide has been with us for a long time, chronicled and perpetuated by our art and culture. Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South (published 1855) contrasts England’s tranquil, idyllic South with a grimy industrial North plagued by poverty and suffering. Almost 150 years later, David Peace evoked a dark and lawless North in his fictional Red Riding quartet. There was always something harder and edgier about the most famous Northern bands than their Southern counterparts. Contrast the Beatles with the Kinks, Oasis with Blur.

Yet in today’s hyperconnected society, how long can such differences last?

“It’s flattened out quite a bit by sheer mobility,” says Steve Fowler. And, he says, by exposure to the internet. “You would have to go very deep into the countryside, to very isolated communities, to find residual differences.”

In the Plough Inn in Stretton-on-Fosse, Warwickshire, Gordon Everett, 59, says, with both sadness and pride, “This is one of the last old-fashioned drinking pubs.” Local accents are waning a lot, he says, touching on the most overt marker of Northern or Southern identity. When he was a boy, you could tell the difference in accents between people from two local villages that lay just three miles apart. “Now, everyone’s got this flat English accent.”

Non-locals, he says, have come to the area and changed it. “The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties.”

Still, tracing this line across the country is a lesson in the extent to which our villages and small towns either cling to their past or else are haunted by it. Between Bredon and Stretton-on-Fosse, I pass houses with names such as the Old Bakehouse, the Old Stoves. A croquet club and a country clothing store. Less picturesque: a dead badger on the A44.

In Brackley, Northamptonshire, there’s a similar nostalgia in evidence. On the high street, there’s the Old Bakery and the Old Hall Bookshop. The sign for Brackley Community Shops is painted in old-fashioned fairground colours. One of these shops offers tattoos, but still.

In the Courtyard Shops farther along, I’m reminded of one of those mock-Victorian streets you find in museums, except there’s a vape shop here. Browsers are welcome, says a sticker in the window, and they’re also on CCTV.

A 75-year-old woman I meet in the town, when I ask what Northerners are like, suggests they’re either industrious farmers or else they work in “industrial places”. I don’t have the heart to tell her that no one I know in West Yorkshire does any such thing.

Did you know Brackley is in fact north of the North-South divide, I ask Anne Mellor, a volunteer in a local charity shop? “No,” she says, “we thought we were in the middle, surrounded by HS2.”

Depending on where you are in the North, transport links can be a sore point – and another marker of difference from the South. Burnham might be proud of his re-regulated Bee Network buses in Manchester, but raise the subject of the still-non-existent tram service in Leeds and that fabled Northern grit might give way to heavy sighs of Northern frustration.

In the North East, poor transport links were said last year to put more than 30 per cent of the region at risk of poverty. In 2022, lack of transport connectivity was found by the Centre for Cities to cost the North £16bn a year in productivity losses. Against this backdrop, HS2 has become a punchline, not an answer.

‘They’re parochial and territorial’

I’m travelling to Silverstone, Northamptonshire, which is famous for a different sort of transport. Pictures of motor-racing heroes adorn the walls of the village pub, the White Horse. I pass through a familiar landscape of roundabouts and roadworks before arriving. A poster on the village noticeboard invites me to become the best version of myself. (I decline.)

Gary Baird, 38, who runs the pub, thinks the North is more working class, while the South attracts more tourism. No one, he argues, goes to Hull on holiday.

Onwards to Rushden, Northants, a “historic boot and shoe town”, passing en route an American diner, a Starbucks, a Travelodge, a McDonald’s, a Toby Carvery and a new-build housing estate. I could be anywhere now. I don’t know whether I’m North or South, my senses are scrambled, or numbed by the dreary uniformity of our in-between spaces.

But in Rushden, for the first time, I feel I could be in the North. Behind the bar in the town’s Working Men’s Club, 30-year-old Tomethia Bartley confirms, “They’re Northerners here.” (She’s not – she’s from London.) “They’re all in a community together. Everyone knows everyone.”

She’s wearing a T-shirt saying, “Don’t like me? F--- off. Problem solved.” I don’t know how Northern or Southern this sentiment is.

Howard, 67, a former helicopter pilot enjoying a pint in the club with his partner, Lynette Keirnan, says: “I was married to a woman from Lancashire. She was bloody weird, actually. They seem to see things differently up there. They’re very parochial and territorial.

“They eat food like barm cakes [a bread roll from the North West] and black peas,” he adds. “They feel disenfranchised, I think.”

But out on the high street, it doesn’t feel so different here from many post-industrial towns further North, with grand old Victorian buildings and the sense of better days being behind it. There’s a kebab shop and an amusement arcade now. A nail bar, a Poundstretcher and, curiously, a large reptile specialist called House of Venom.

Deeply ingrained perceptions

The land flattens out as I enter Lincolnshire, stopping briefly in Market Deeping for a scalding portion of battered fish. “Sunny days are here at last,” it says on a small blackboard inside the Market Gate Deli. Outside, a fine rain falls. An unseasonable chill hangs in the early June air.

My odyssey ends in Norfolk, where I meet arable farmer Richard Ward, 55. “Where am I?” I ask.

“You’re probably North more than anything, because that’s the North Sea,” he says, pointing to the horizon, where I can’t see anything but farmland. A few years ago, a bomb squad came to remove a load of Second World War ordnance found in the fields. “It was quite a hairy experience,” says Ward.

Do people fish out there? I ask, pointing vaguely to where the sea should be. No, he says. “It’s dead vegetation and horrible black, boggy clay soil.”

I finish my journey not far from this, by a soggy field overlooking some marshland. The sun has finally emerged. Some desultory wasps buzz above the glistening wet grass. A crow caws, a cockerel crows and my feet are becoming very wet.

The conversations I’ve had along my journey have shown that, despite our increasingly homogenised culture, perceptions of differences between Northerners and Southerners remain deeply ingrained. Perhaps we will always retain these in some form.

As Richard Collett writes in his book Along the Borders, “We carve landscapes apart to define our very sense of self and identity.”

I recognise this impulse. And I’m not going to claim it’s all grim down South, but I’ll always be Northern and proud.

The House on Otley Road by Rosa Silverman (£16.99, HQ/HarperCollins) is out now.

data.title: The BBC programmes I would axe
data.description:
There’s terrible news for Britons who still watch or listen to the BBC: to save £500m, the corporation is axing much-loved programmes. Radio 4’s You and Yours is the latest to go, after 56 years.

Yet most of us still pay the licence fee, so surely we deserve a say in what goes next. Here are six that I think should go.

Have I Got News For You

No one is sure when it started, but everyone knows it stopped being funny in the late 1890s, shortly after Ian Hislop ran out of Oscar Wilde material. What remains is half an hour of centrist dads making centrist dad jokes about everything centrist dads despise: Brexit, Trump, Farage, Brexit, and Nigel “Brexit” Farage, in that order.

The audience laughs at the word “Reform” before the punchline arrives. Its one lasting achievement was making Boris Johnson a star, which it has regretted ever since. Paul Merton’s expression hasn’t changed since the Major government, leading concerned viewers to ask whether he is still alive. Google says he is touring an improv show, which is oddly inconclusive.

Newsnight

Not because it is Left-wing, though it is, but because it is pointless. In 2024 it was cut to half an hour and lost its reporters; even the BBC’s then head of news wasn’t sure it was worth keeping. Its finest hour (in 1997!) was Jeremy Paxman asking Michael Howard the same question 12 times; today it couldn’t afford such a long segment.

Emily Maitlis, its more recent star, left to make a podcast that does Newsnight better than Newsnight. Put it out of its misery, or give it the whole £500m.

Antiques Roadshow

Not because it’s bad: it remains oddly gripping. But it has become a weekly bereavement, because antiques are now worth nothing. “A complete Wedgwood dinner service, from 1805, not a chip on it. Magnificent! A fiver on eBay, if you pay the postage.” “A solid mahogany Georgian bookcase. Superb. With gas prices what they are, I’d burn it.”

The owner always replies: “Oh, we’d never sell it.” Just as well. Fiona Bruce, who also presents Question Time, spends all week watching people discover their most treasured possessions are worthless, and it’s starting to affect her persona. Enough.

The One Show

Probably the most honest show on TV, because it is officially named after the number of interesting things said on it. The format never varies: a star perches on the sofa to plug a film, then sits through a report on a man in Lincolnshire who has built a Spitfire out of Twiglets. Should anything interesting threaten to happen, the credits roll. Katy Perry was once cut off mid-anecdote, presumably because it was getting good.

Celebrity MasterChef

I love real MasterChef, officially the world’s most successful cookery format, which has turned more than 100 amateurs into professional chefs, and some pro chefs into ones with Michelin stars. But the celebrity version turns nobody into anything.

This year’s line-up included a Gladiator, a former ballet dancer and a YouTuber called TommyInnit (no, me neither), and absolutely nobody cares whether they can do aubergine five ways. The winner will not open a restaurant. At best, they will open a packet of instant noodles when they get home.

Wild card: Gardeners’ Question Time

Since 1947, its panel has given precisely one answer: it depends on your soil. Blackfly on the broad beans? Depends on your soil. Clematis wilt? Soil. Husband run off with the woman from the allotments? Definitely the soil. Axe it, play the words “it depends on your soil” on a loop on Radio 4, and spend the savings bringing back the brilliant Big Train, and all its brilliant writers.

data.title: Burnham to nationalise Avanti West Coast
data.description:
Avanti West Coast will be nationalised from next year, the Transport Secretary has announced.

Heidi Alexander will use her speech to the Labour Party conference on Monday to outline plans to bring the rail firm into public ownership in March next year, when its contract is expected to expire.

The line, which Andy Burnham uses to travel between London and Manchester, has been beset by frequent delays and cancellations in recent years.

Since the general election two years ago, the Labour Government has been nationalising rail services across the country as contracts have ended.

Nationalisation will be supported by a plan to improve infrastructure, reduce delays and improve passenger experience, the Government said.

Avanti West Coast had the highest proportion of cancellations in Britain this summer at 12.6 per cent – double the national average.

The operator was also worst performing in terms of punctuality, with just 32 per cent of trains arriving on time.

Last month, Avanti drivers were handed a 3.6 per cent pay rise from the Government after threatening to strike, as well as a £720 bonus if they agree to work a fifth day in a given week.

Mr Burnham was one of those entitled to compensation when his train from Manchester to London was delayed in June, as he travelled south to take up his seat in Parliament before ultimately dethroning Sir Keir Starmer.

‘Passengers, not shareholders, will come first’

In a post on social media on Sunday evening, the Prime Minister wrote: “Enough is enough.

“For years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti’s cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again.

“So my Labour government is bringing Avanti West Coast into public ownership at the earliest opportunity in March next year.

“That means passengers, not shareholders, will come first. More investment, fewer delays, and a renewed focus on getting the basics right.

“We’re putting essential services back in public hands and building a railway that actually works for the people who use it.”

Ms Alexander said: “For years, we’ve heard stories of Avanti underperforming, with passengers left paying the price. Enough is enough.”

“This Labour Government is committed to putting essential services back in public hands, connecting people to opportunity and delivering growth in every postcode and this move reflects that commitment,” she added.

“We will also introduce a comprehensive improvement plan, focused on delivering for passengers, not shareholders.”

Andy Mellors, the managing director of Avanti West Coast, said: “We’re proud of what we’ve achieved over the last six years – from refurbishing our Pendolino fleet and introducing our new Evero trains to running more services than ever before.

“Together, these improvements have given customers greater choice, more capacity and better connectivity, while we’ve continued to innovate to shape the future of the West Coast and wider rail industry.

“Over the coming months, we’ll work closely with the Government to ensure a seamless transition into public ownership while remaining focused on delivering for our customers and communities.”

data.title: Healey urged to launch £1.5bn ‘Amazon tax’ raid on retailers
data.description:
John Healey should mount a £1.5bn raid on Amazon and other online retailers in the Budget to fund a high-street tax cut, a Labour-linked think tank has said.

The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which has helped shape Labour policies, said a new online sales tax could raise billions of pounds for the Chancellor to cut business rates for shops, pubs, restaurants and other high-street businesses.

Andy Burnham has signalled that Labour will ramp up a so-called “Amazon tax” to help fund a tax cut for “businesses that bring social benefit”, such as pubs and restaurants.

The IPPR urged the Prime Minister and Chancellor to consider a new 2pc tax on online sales by large retailers and 1pc for click-and-collect purchases that it said would raise at least £1.5bn a year.

Under the think tank’s proposals, the first £500,000 of a business’s remote sales each year would be exempt in a move designed to protect smaller firms.

It estimates the changes could save smaller businesses an average of around £1,400 a year and larger firms around £2,500.

The proposal comes amid growing concern about the burden of business rates on the high street, with the IPPR arguing that Britain has an unusually heavy reliance on property taxes.

OECD data show property taxes account for 10.5pc of UK tax revenues, compared with an average of 5.1pc.

Business rates alone raise more than £27bn a year.

Aditi Sriram, of the IPPR, said: “Britain’s tax system was built for an era when the location where you did business was closely linked to how much business you did. That is no longer the case.

“As people have moved their shopping online, high street shops and restaurants continue to face large, fixed tax bills simply because they need physical premises.

“The Government should shift some of the tax burden from bricks to clicks and use the money to cut bills for the businesses that bring people on to our high streets.”

However, executives and retail groups have warned that an online sales tax could push up the cost of living.

The British Retail Consortium has highlighted that high-street retailers occupy a large share of warehouse space and that higher taxes could ultimately be passed on to shoppers through higher prices.

A Treasury spokesman said: “The Chancellor is fully focused on his priorities, which will boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode.

“As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

data.title: The barrister who cast Britain’s biggest lawsuit into chaos
data.description:
Thomas Goodhead’s 40th birthday party was an extravagant affair.

Hosted at the Wallace Collection, an art gallery in Mayfair, the black-tie gathering was held to honour the British barrister and the law firm he co-founded, Pogust Goodhead.

As guests sipped champagne and dined on fine food, the Oxford-educated lawyer had good reason to celebrate.

His law firm was at the time in control of the biggest lawsuit in British legal history, representing thousands of Brazilian victims in a £36bn class action lawsuit against two of the world’s largest mining companies.

Goodhead’s work on the case had propelled him into a fast-paced lifestyle involving regular trips between Britain and Brazil.

“I don’t do very well on my carbon footprint, I’m afraid, because I’m just commuting across the Atlantic, but I like to think it’s for a good cause,” he once said.

The case involved work on behalf of thousands of victims from one of the worst environmental disasters in history.

A burst dam near Mariana in southern Brazil had flooded local villages in toxic mud in 2015, killing 19 people.

BHP and Vale have been held liable for the calamity, with hundreds of thousands of claimants now seeking compensation from the companies.

Goodhead and his firm were spearheading the claim for around 700,000 of the victims until it all unravelled last year.

The British barrister was booted out of his firm after a row with Gramercy Funds Management, the US hedge fund financing the claim.

It meant the barrister was cut out of the litigation. But now he is fighting back.

The High Court will shortly rule on who represents the majority of the claimants: Goodhead’s former firm (Pogust Goodhead) or his new law firm.

At stake are hundreds of millions of pounds’ worth of fees.

Goodhead first heard about the Mariana disaster during a chance encounter with a Brazilian lawyer at a conference and soon became captivated by the idea it might be litigated in the High Court.

By chance, he met Harris Pogust, a high-profile American litigator, at a Super Bowl party in Hawaii shortly after.

It led to them launching Pogust Goodhead only a few months later, with the specific aim of launching the £36bn Mariana Dam claim.

“I don’t know if it was his idea, my idea, but we decided let’s just start a firm and see where we can take this thing, and it kind of exploded pretty much immediately,” Pogust said.

The nascent firm grew rapidly, taking on a series of similar class action lawsuits, including the so-called “dieselgate” claim against carmakers.

But it was the Mariana claim which pushed the law firm into the stratosphere – and Goodhead into the firing line.

Like most class action lawsuits, the funding to pay for the case came from a hedge fund, in this case Gramercy.

Goodhead and Gramercy came to loggerheads last year – leading to Goodhead leaving the firm he founded.

The circumstances of the departure are disputed.

Goodhead says Gramercy wanted to settle the case for a smaller sum than the victims deserved, while Gramercy has claimed he was misspending millions worth of legal funds.

Goodhead has denied these misspending allegations, saying the outgoings were part of the ordinary business of the law firm or paid for by himself with no client money involved.

Pogust – Goodhead’s former partner – has defended the spending, saying any top executive in a large law firm would have similarly sizeable expenses.

“It’s b------t. You look at any managing partner of any firm in the US that’s 600 people and you look at what they’re saying, they’re going first class, staying in five-star hotels. When you travel 200 days a year, you’re entitled to do that. You give up your life for the clients. So don’t expect him to sit in the toilet,” Pogust said.

The row with Gramercy might have ended the career of most high-flying lawyers, but behind the scenes Goodhead was working to regain the centre stage.

Last month, Goodhead revealed he was working with a new law firm, Bailey Glasser International (BGI), which now claims to be representing most of the victims.

At the start of September, Bailey Glasser said 400,000 claimants had switched to work with it, rather than Pogust Goodhead, after a committee of victims voted to transfer the case.

The committee claims Pogust Goodhead is now effectively owned and controlled by Gramercy and that its interests fundamentally clash with those of its clients because the hedge fund wants to settle the case.

A spokesman for Pogust Goodhead said the claim was incorrect and the law firm acts “independently and in the best interests of its clients”.

“Gramercy is a funder of the firm, but it does not direct or control the conduct of the Mariana litigation,” it said.

“The suggestion that [Pogust Goodhead] is seeking to bring the litigation to an end prematurely is also inconsistent with what the firm is actually doing.”

Further litigation has followed, with Pogust Goodhead suing the committee, claiming they lacked the authority to switch firms.

Pogust also has asked for his surname to be taken out of its name and sent a cease-and-desist letter to his former firm, requesting the change of name. He says the legal clash risks damaging his own reputation as a lawyer.

“These people lost everything in this disaster – their houses, their family members, their possessions, their pets, everything. And the last thing they need is the people they think they trust the most to sue them,” Pogust said.

Pogust Goodhead has begun changing its name to PGMBM. A spokesman for the law firm said: “Neither of the former founders has any role in the firm today, and we believe the name should reflect the firm as it exists now.”

The firm added: “Should the court ultimately recognise the client committee’s authority to transfer representation of the wider claimant group, PGMBM will pursue all appropriate legal remedies to protect its rights.

“The rights and obligations arising from almost eight years of legal work cannot simply be disregarded, irrespective of which firm ultimately represents the claimants.”

It will now be for the High Court to decide who should run the biggest case in the history of Britain’s courts.

BGI was contacted for comment.

data.title: The dismal track record of Britain’s state-owned water companies
data.description:
To many, the solution to England’s water industry crisis is full-fat public ownership.

In his emotional address to the Labour Party conference in Liverpool last week, Andy Burnham drew applause for paving the way for nationalisation. Labour, he told delegates, would repeal Margaret Thatcher’s “ideological ban” on state ownership of England’s water companies.

The water industry is in chaos. Thames Water is drowning in a debt pile of almost £20bn, and last year England’s water companies spilt sewage for 1.9 million hours.

But what would water nationalisation look like? We can look to Northern Ireland, Wales and Scotland to see how well things go without the profit motive – and the case for state control of water is murky.

Scotland, the wettest part of the UK, ought to be way ahead when it comes to tap-water quality. But official data suggest it isn’t.

Tap water is of a slightly lower quality in Scotland than England. The Drinking Water Inspectorate rates 99.97pc of England’s tap water as meeting required standards. Yet in Scotland, the country’s own water quality regulator rates Scots’ tap water at 99.88pc compliant.

As in the rest of England, the infrastructure north of the border is showing its age. But because Scottish Water is state-owned, it can only turn to customers’ bills or taxpayer funding, rather than private investment. The average Scottish Water customer bill is £532, cheaper than the typical English bill at £602.

Steve Reed, the former environment secretary, found himself at the sharp end of Scots’ ire when he sad the nation’s water was not as clean as it might be. The UK’s statistics agency also cautioned him for an “overly selective” use of data to make his point.

Another embarrassment for Scottish Water is the leaks. Scottish Water loses 453 million litres per day, more than 30pc of its daily water supply. In England, about 19pc is lost.

England’s pipe network is so porous that water companies have been forced to roll out satellite monitoring to find patches of damp ground, and use acoustic sensors to find leaks.

Part of this investment drive is down to oversight by Ofwat, the water regulator for England and Wales, whose authority ends at the Scottish border.

In England, water companies now monitor 100pc of their sewer overflows. But with Scotland outside Ofwat’s remit, it has historically lagged by years, only recently improving monitoring to about 34pc.

Sewage is being spilt, but in Scotland it is impossible to know how bad the situation is.

Nonetheless, in its latest annual report, Scottish Water admits it had 199 pollution incidents in 2024 to 2025.

Scottish Water bosses argue they are up against it. A spokesman noted its network is more than 30,000 miles long, “which adds to the complexity of managing and maintaining a water network”.

Welsh Water

Wales has its own system. Dŵr Cymru Cyfyngedig – Welsh Water – is a privately operated, not-for-profit business. It has no shareholders and pays no dividends.

But despite the lack of profits, customers in Wales have long complained that their water bills are rising. At £683 per year, Welsh customers pay more than Londoners for the pleasure of being Thames Water customers.

Henry Tufnell, the MP for Mid and South Pembrokeshire, tells The Telegraph that Welsh Water’s “executives are very well remunerated”. Roch Cheroux, the new chief executive, could take home up to £894,000. While this is admittedly much less than the highest-paid bosses of English water companies, who can earn up to £3.3m, that pay packet puts him above the likes of Dave Hinton, the former boss of South East Water. Meanwhile, Alex Plant of Scottish Water is on around £430,000.

Tufnell, a Labour MP, has reservations about state control. “I would caution anyone who thinks that a change of ownership model to something like Welsh Water would be a silver bullet,” he says.

Welsh rivers are generally cleaner than English waters, but there are caveats.

Three years ago, Natural Resources Wales, which uses the same metrics as the Environment Agency, hit Welsh Water with a two-star “requires improvement” rating, and it has been stuck with it ever since.

This rating puts it in the same basket as English suppliers Yorkshire Water and United Utilities. It also trails behind Severn Trent.

Last year, Welsh Water had nine serious pollution incidents and was hit with a £44.7m fine for failing to maintain wastewater treatment works.

According to Ofwat, Welsh Water is deemed “lagging” when set alongside 17 competitors. It trails with the likes of Thames Water and Southern Water.

A Welsh Water spokesman defended the record. The company said it recognised room for improvement and planned to invest £4.2bn between 2025 and 2030. As in Scotland, Welsh Water faces the challenge that many of its customers are in sparsely populated areas.

In Northern Ireland, meanwhile, people pay no water bills.

The Northern Ireland Executive spends around £340m a year subsidising water and sewerage operations at Northern Ireland Water (NI Water). But the trouble with the public not paying is predictable. Owing to a lack of funds, investment has historically been inadequate.

According to the Northern Ireland Chamber of Commerce, the situation has left an £11bn hole in the economy, and £200 of capital expenditure per person isn’t enough to plug it. House building, for instance, has been limited because water infrastructure isn’t there.

Because of these limited funds, about 80pc of storm overflows in Belfast, according to the campaign group, Ulster Wildlife, are in poor condition, making sewage pollution a significant problem. Some 20 million tons of sewage pollution is spilt every year, and only 14pc of Northern Irish loughs, in part owing to sewage, are deemed to be in good condition.

On leaks, Northern Ireland sits between England and Scotland, losing 155 million litres of drinking water per day, which equates to 25pc of the total supply.

Northern Ireland is upfront about its plight. According to a spokesman, Northern Ireland Water “continues to face significant funding challenges”.

On the state of England’s water industry, meanwhile, a spokesman for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “This situation can’t continue, which is why this Government will give the public more control.” But what that means still isn’t clear.

Sir Jon Cunliffe, in his report on water in England, said: “We pushed very hard for evidence that shows that other ownership structures are systemically better. The results were mixed.”

For Burnham’s supporters, the argument for seizing the water industry from its woeful private owners is obvious. In reality, the evidence in favour is clear as mud.

data.title: Kemi Badenoch’s carefully calculated conference wardrobe
data.description:
Unlike many politicians, Kemi Badenoch has spent this Conservative conference looking as though she cares about the way she dresses. It’s a rare politician who realises it’s possible to discuss British fashion as a precious generator of jobs and the Hamas attacks on Israel three years ago to the day, then announce a significant policy such as scrapping inheritance tax, without any of these subjects cancelling out the others. But she might be one of them.

So, to itemise those outfits: on October 3, arriving in Birmingham, she wore a loose brown pinstriped M&S suit with wide trousers, the one she bought after seeing it on the M&S catwalk at London Fashion Week. Message: Everywoman, in an accessible but also aspirational brand.

The next day came pale-blue Reiss tailoring. She loves a bit of Reiss. She wore one of its khaki jumpsuits to the Burberry show. Message: modern, but nothing to scare the horses. Interesting in light of a recent interview in which she compared the Conservative Party to a heritage brand, an observation that makes even more sense of her attendance at both the Burberry and M&S fashion shows during London Fashion Week last month.

On Monday, it was a raspberry-pink fitted dress by The Fold, a growing British brand founded by Polly McMaster, who has worked day and night to turn it into a £20m-a-year business and has ambitions to make it much bigger, therefore creating more UK jobs. The Fold has become Badenoch’s go-to for smart tailoring. On Tuesday, her crisp white trouser suit was also from The Fold.

For her closing speech on Wednesday, she chose The Fold again, its Elaria dress in stretch teal crepe. By the way, she does choose her own clothes. “Lots of online shopping and lots of returns,” she told me when I met her at that Burberry show last month.

On that point, politicians at London Fashion Week are vanishingly rare. Not that anyone wants an influx of them. But fashion is a £60bn-a-year industry in the UK, albeit one that has been hit by Tory-instigated Brexit, Labour’s rise in National Insurance and the refusal of both parties while in power to reinstate tax-free shopping, which has sent tourists shopping in Paris or Milan instead of London.

Badenoch, of course, announced on the day of that Burberry show that her party would restore it if it got back into power, which would be a significant boost to hospitality as well as retail. Let’s see.

Badenoch’s two Fashion Week appearances were, naturally, anything but haphazard. They’re part of a strategy to prove she grasps the importance of our creative and cultural industries. The two shows she watched were carefully chosen and then wrapped into relatable nuggets for her speech.

“M&S has been around for 100 years,” she told the hall. (Is this the first time a party leader has talked about Fashion Week in a conference speech?) “Not so long ago people said they were a bit stuffy and stuck in the past,” she continued. “Some were even questioning whether the brand could survive. Do you see where I’m going with this? But now M&S is back in fashion… people are flooding back, including me. But like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes and make people feel good about us.”

There’s nothing accidental about her clothes either. She has used a stylist in the past, but told me it wasn’t entirely helpful. Is she sure? Without being strident, the colours register from the back of a conference hall, and suit her. More unusually, they properly fit her. They appear to have been ironed or steamed. She dresses with confidence but also with something that looks suspiciously like pleasure.

“I’ve always liked fashion,” she told me. An avid reader of Alexandra Shulman’s British Vogue, she is, I note, a follower on Instagram of Collagerie, the online fashion and interiors platform founded by two former Shulman-era Vogue staffers whose tagline is “The One Thing Over Everything”. Message: buy better, buy less.

You’d think taking care of your appearance would be normal for someone in the public eye who needs to project an aura of confidence, competence and, oh please God, flair. No one’s asking them to be fashion plates, but if they could demonstrate a rudimentary understanding that first impressions are formed almost instantly and that they matter, that would be an excellent start. Not least because we, the public, have to look at them endlessly in our homes on TV. Also, when they appear on a world stage, it would help our confidence if they at least looked tidy.

Andy Burnham emitted crisp authority in his made-to-measure navy Oliver Brown suit at the recent Labour conference. But many politicians seem to go out of their way to prove they’re above the visuals, although they’re perfectly happy to indulge in an inane photo op.

Badenoch seems to understand it’s possible to have style and substance. That’s why she wasn’t afraid to open her speech by talking about Jeffrey Archer and how he would frequently message her not just about her speeches but her outfits. Bold to eulogise a former party chairman who went to prison, perhaps even bolder to mention their fashion chats.

But then, she doesn’t consider fashion trivial. “We should think about what story we’re telling with our clothes,” she told me at Burberry. “I like to tell a story about determination, confidence in who I am and who our country is.”

According to journalist and author Plum Sykes, who took part in a panel discussing the importance of the UK fashion industry to the economy during the Tory conference this week (another first), consistency is part of Badenoch’s strength.

“Kemi doesn’t change her image much and I think that’s a better move,” she says. “Only influencers change their style every five minutes. Hers is authentic. Burnham’s T-shirt often looks like cosplay.”

Sykes is right about the consistency – of both Badenoch and Burnham. There’s no doubt Burnham’s cultivated “friendly northerner” look is effective. Badenoch’s strong colour, precise tailoring, defined waist and proper-shoes approach is too. Her personal poll ratings are high, even if her party is still lagging.

And the light-touch way she dresses distances her from her predecessors. Theresa May loved fashion but could look fussy and unprepared. Liz Truss’s clothes were a mess. Rishi Sunak’s fashionably short trousers and Adidas Samba trainers didn’t go down well with core Tory voters either.

“The style that I have is very, very much me,” Badenoch told me. “I like things that are bold and striking, contemporary. I don’t think that we all need to dress in a frumpy sort of fashion just because we’re in politics.”

data.title: HSBC to axe UK wealth managers in AI push
data.description:
HSBC is planning significant job cuts across its UK wealth management division after replacing staff with AI for its richest clients.

The London-headquartered bank, which is Europe’s biggest lender, has started a consultation process affecting managers and specialist advisers.

Around 70pc of the division’s financial advisers will be eliminated, while roughly half of its managers and specialists are set to disappear from its ranks, according to the Financial Times, which first reported the move.

Affected employees are expected to depart by the end of October.

The bank has not said how many jobs are at risk and has not published any headcounts for the division; however, it is thought to employ hundreds of relationship managers across the country.

HSBC had previously embarked on a hiring drive in 2024, with plans to add hundreds of relationship managers to a 400-strong team at the time.

That expansion was designed to double the UK wealth management arm’s assets to £100bn by 2030 and propel it into Britain’s top five wealth managers.

At the end of 2025, its retail banking and wealth division grew by £9bn to total more than £62bn.

Jose Carvalho, who led the UK retail banking and wealth arm, left his post three weeks ago after four years.

The restructuring comes after Georges Elhedery stepped in as chief executive in September 2024 with a mandate to cut costs.

Mr Elhedery has put AI at the heart of his efforts to boost productivity. In May, he told investors in Hong Kong: “We all know generative AI will destroy certain jobs and will create new jobs.”

Bloomberg reported in March that as many as 20,000 jobs at HSBC could be at risk globally as part of its push to use AI.

This would represent around 10pc of its workforce, which consists of about 211,479 staff.

It comes after rival Standard Chartered, which is also headquartered in the UK, set out plans to cut around 7,800 roles by 2030 as part of a drive to use more AI.

A spokesman for HSBC said: “HSBC UK is a long-established, leading UK wealth manager and premium banking provider. We’re continuing to evolve to deliver more digitally-enabled products and journeys, to support our best-in-class wealth service and meet the changing needs of our customers.”

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Surging Gulf oil flows may be too late to stop a ‘terrifying’ winter
data.description:
It sounds like good news.

For the first time since Donald Trump attacked Iran eight months ago, oil exports from the Persian Gulf are nearly back at pre-war levels.

This should herald a return to normality for the world’s bruised energy markets, in theory at least.

However, with a barrel of Brent still trading above $100, it seems optimism hasn’t yet fed into the markets – a worrying sign as Britain prepares for winter of soaring energy bills and possible diesel shortages.

Goldman Sachs revealed the extent of the Middle East’s oil recovery earlier this week by claiming that exports have hit 98pc.

This came after 23.3 million barrels of oil were shipped out of the region on average each day, on par with last year’s figures and at least 10 million barrels higher than in March.

The figures highlight how oil producers have effectively acclimatised to conflict in the region, either by finding ways to bypass the Strait of Hormuz or by relying on the US military for an escort.

Today, around 40pc of Gulf oil is exported without passing through the Strait, according to Kpler, compared to just 17pc before the conflict broke out.

Goldman Sachs struck an upbeat tone in a note released on Wednesday: “We estimate that the global oil market is roughly balanced in September.

“The remarkable adaptation of both Middle East supply and China import demand supports our base case that Brent prices moderate to $85 by year-end and to $80 in 2027.”

With the war in Iran still raging, this will serve as a glimmer of hope for a global economy starting to feel the strain.

Countries like Britain had been fearful of energy shortages this winter if global supplies fail to improve, threatening households with power cuts, higher interest rates and surging food prices.

This may all be avoided if Goldman’s prediction is right.

But not everyone is convinced, including oil traders who fear that hostilities between the US and Iran could escalate at any point.

“If oil exports carry on at these levels for, say, the next month, then I think we’ve got signs of optimism,” says Ashley Kelty, a research analyst at Panmure Liberum.

“Everyone wants to have good news because if you actually look at the reality of it all, you realise how terrifying this winter could be.”

Some have argued that growing oil flows out of the Middle East suggest Trump has the upper hand and is on the cusp of winning the war.

Others are less sure.

“In terms of the maritime picture, it’s clear that the Americans are enabling Gulf exports, and the blockade on Iran has had a material impact on its own exports falling to a fraction of pre-war levels,” says Darius Barik, at the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation.

“But that has come at great cost in terms of resources on the American side.”

Barik also points out that the level of Gulf oil exports can all change quickly dependent on Iran’s military appetite.

“Iran the capacity to strike regional energy infrastructure or US forces in the region,” he says. “It’s not clear that that has been diminished. Ultimately, it’s about who can absorb pressure for longer.”

He believes that many observers underestimate how much pain Tehran is willing to endure.

Importantly, allowing Gulf nations to export more oil also benefits Iran because it keeps their regional trading partners afloat, Barik adds.

“Beyond tolerating those flows, there’s a sense among the Iranian leadership that they can sustain the economic costs that come with the attritional war for longer than many might expect,” he says.

All of which paints a complex picture that has made even the most ardent oil analysts give up, with markets still racked by geopolitical confusion and uncertainty.

JP Morgan, the world’s largest investment bank, recently had to concede to clients: “For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don’t have a baseline view.

“We simply don’t know how to model the endgame.”

As for the latest increase in shipments from the Middle East, this was boosted by resurgent exports from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

But analysts are still wary about whether this will ease pressure on the world’s economy.

For one, transporting oil barrels around the world has become excruciatingly expensive because of the war, fuelled by a new premium on safety.

This has propelled the tanker industry to the “highest profitability in its history”, according to analysis by Lloyd’s List.

Greg Miller, of Lloyd’s, said this was unlikely to change regardless of whether the war de-escalates.

Manny Newman, at Onyx Commodities, adds: “It’s definitely a loading problem in the Middle East. The oil is there.

“It’s able to be loaded if it can be done safely. But logistically there’s just a huge cost to doing so at the minute. That’s being baked into the prices.”

The oil trader says the unpredictability is nearing levels at the start of the war, when she and her colleagues at the most extreme stayed in the office overnight taking power naps in sleeping bags.

“It feels like we’ve reverted to March/April times in terms of what’s going on with price action, the volatility and the market’s behaviour, but that can change again very, very quickly,” she says.

Unsurprisingly, many hedge funds are looking to exploit this volatility, with some deeming prices detached from the physical market.

This is particularly relevant when it comes to current pricing, which remains high despite exports returning to normality.

The cost of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose by 4.7pc to $102 on Thursday, up from lows of just under $60 at the start of the year.

These prices reflect futures contracts one month ahead, while the actual cost of securing oil on the spot market is at $120.

Kelty warns that if anything, there is too much hope priced in.

The actual constraints on the market mean prices should be even higher, he believes.

He warns that volumes may be rising, but many countries that have depleted their stockpiles will be rushing to replenish them.

‘Demand is going to help keep prices high’

There is also concern over the fact that exports of diesel and gasoline from the Middle East are still only at 58pc of pre-war levels.

“We’ve taken what 400 million barrels out of strategic reserves so far, plus whatever China and the like have used up, which they don’t disclose,” he says.

“That demand is going to help keep prices high, because everyone’s going to say we’ve got to replenish these stores for the next time there is a falling out between Iran and somebody.

“Everyone’s so desperate for good news that they’re not looking at the reality.

“The markets are seizing on any hints of good news. It’s probably the most divorced from the physical markets I’ve seen in a long time.”

This may spell trouble for Britain this winter when gas and electricity bills are poised to hit £2,000.

Andy Burnham warned of an energy crisis in the coming months, and said the Middle East conflict still “needs to command a lot of our attention”.

One can only hope the optimists are on to something if we are to avoid a “terrifying” winter.
