data.title: Lisa Nandy under fire after backing BT’s TalkTalk deal
data.description:
Lisa Nandy is under fire for backing BT’s rescue deal for stricken broadband business TalkTalk.

Lutz Schüler, the chief executive of rival Virgin Media O2 (VMO2), has written to the Culture Secretary asking her to explain why the Government intervened to clear the way for BT’s £400m takeover.

Mr Schüler wrote in the letter, seen by The Telegraph: “Protecting customers does not, in our view, require government to predetermine who should ultimately own TalkTalk’s consumer and wholesale businesses; credible alternative arrangements should be fully explored.

“Given the exceptional intervention, we would welcome clarity on the evidence relied upon by the Secretary of State.”

BT swooped to buy TalkTalk out of administration on Monday in a move that saved the debt-laden broadband provider from imminent collapse.

In normal circumstances, the former state monopoly would likely be blocked from buying up its rival, the UK’s fourth-largest broadband company, because of concerns about its market power.

TalkTalk serves about 1.5 million households, as well as a further one million customers through its wholesale division.

But Ms Nandy intervened using pandemic-era legal powers to override competition concerns in mergers and acquisitions to maintain public health.

The Government stepped in over fears TalkTalk’s collapse would have put tens of thousands of vulnerable customers at risk, as well as some critical national infrastructure.

TalkTalk had been in discussions with several other potential suitors but negotiations fell through.

Ms Nandy has ordered the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to report back on the BT deal by Oct 19 before she makes a final decision.

Allison Kirkby, BT’s chief executive, described the crisis at TalkTalk as a “genuinely unprecedented situation” and warned of “catastrophic” consequences if it had been allowed to go under.

But VMO2, BT’s largest rival, has called the process a “stitch-up” and demanded further scrutiny.

Mr Schüler said the competition watchdog should examine the significant debts owed by TalkTalk to BT’s network division, Openreach, which were written off as part of the rescue deal, and to what extent they influenced the negotiations.

He added that the deal’s timing also raised a “question of consistency”, coming just days after the CMA threatened to block a proposed £2bn takeover of broadband start-up Netomnia by VMO2’s owners.

Mr Schüler, who called for an urgent meeting with the Culture Secretary, said BT’s takeover should not be allowed to go ahead without measures to safeguard competition.

VMO2 is understood to be calling for BT to divest TalkTalk’s wholesale arm, PXC, and launch a sale process for retail customers in areas covered by both BT’s and VMO2’s networks.

Mr Schüler warned that TalkTalk’s collapse was a symptom of Britain’s “fragile” broadband market, echoing warnings from Ms Kirkby that further collapses of debt-laden start-ups could follow.

The telecoms boss added that government intervention in the market could put future investment at risk.

TalkTalk’s biggest lender, the private credit giant Ares Management, was handed £100m as part of the BT rescue deal but will still lose around half of its initial investment.

Ares’s true losses are believed to be even higher when interest is factored in, while scores of other creditors owed hundreds of millions of pounds have been wiped out in the administration process.

The BT takeover has piled further pressure on VMO2’s already strained finances as investors fret about the company’s ability to service its £22bn debt pile.

VMO2’s junk bonds dropped to record lows because of concerns that the Netomnia deal could be blocked. The telecoms giant is now bracing for job cuts to reassure investors.

Other rivals including Vodafone and CityFibre are understood to be concerned about the BT takeover.

Opus, a broadband challenger that had bid for TalkTalk’s customer base, also sounded the alarm about BT’s rescue deal.

It said: “After months of due diligence and negotiation, Opus had a live offer for the consumer business which had not been rejected. Opus’s acquisition had also been cleared by government under the National Security and Investment Act.

“That offer would have protected customers, including vulnerable customers, and avoided the competition concerns.”

Opus said its interest in the consumer business “remains unchanged”.

However, Enders Analysis described BT as a “buyer of last resort” and warned the ramifications of a TalkTalk collapse would have been “very serious”.

Its analysts wrote: “Some of BT’s competitors may well protest but unless they actually make an alternative offer for the company, the failing firm theory is proven.”

The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport was contacted for comment.
